## 10 Minute Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/10-minute-typing-test.html

Test true typing endurance with a full 10 minute typing test. Ten minutes measures how well you hold speed and accuracy over long sessions - the closest test to a real workday of writing or data entry.

On this page
10 minute typing test
Who needs a 10 minute test?
How to pace a 10 minute test
Reading your 10 minute result
Preparing for a 10 minute typing test
What 10 minutes measures that 1 minute can't
The 10 minute decay curve
Training for the 10 minute format
When employers and exams use long tests
Taking a ten minute typing test online
Why the five-character word matters for endurance scores
The 10 minute typing test is the ultimate endurance check. Ten minutes exposes fatigue that short rounds hide: most typists slow 5-15% between minute one and minute ten, so your score here reflects what you can truly sustain. Warm up first with a 1 minute typing test or a 5 minute typing test.
Anyone whose work is long-form typing - transcriptionists, writers, coders, data entry clerks. If you will type for hours, a 10 minute result predicts your real-day speed better than any sprint. Build up to it with structured typing practice sessions.
Start about 10% slower than your 1 minute speed and settle into a rhythm you can hold. Sit up, keep wrists neutral, and take micro-pauses at sentence breaks. Finishing strong matters more than an early burst that fades.
Your ten-minute score tells two stories: the headline WPM, and the fade between your fastest and slowest minutes. A drop under 10% means solid endurance; 10 to 20% is normal and shrinks with practice; more than 20% points to tension — usually raised shoulders or held breath — rather than weak fingers. Check whether errors cluster late in the round, which signals fatigue, or scatter throughout, which signals an accuracy habit; then train the weakness with focused typing practice sessions.
A 10 minute typing test is an endurance event, not a sprint. Almost everyone finishes 10-15% slower than their 1 minute speed, and that is expected rather than a failure.
Set posture first - feet flat, wrists neutral, elbows near 90 degrees. Discomfort at minute three becomes lost accuracy by minute seven.
Pace, do not sprint - open at roughly 90% of your comfortable speed and hold it. Sprinting the first minute reliably costs more than it gains.
Stop correcting every slip - for an endurance score, constant backtracking costs more WPM than the error itself.
Breathe and relax the shoulders - tension is the main cause of late-round slowdown.
A one-minute test measures your working speed — fresh fingers, no fatigue, a sprint by any other name. Ten minutes measures something employers actually care about more: whether your speed survives contact with real work. Almost everyone is fast for sixty seconds; the tenth minute is where sloppy posture, death-grip tension and uneven rhythm come due.
Expect your ten-minute score to read 5–15% below your one-minute score. That gap is not a failure — it is your fatigue profile, and it is the most honest single number about your typing. A small gap means your technique is sustainable; a large gap means you are borrowing speed from muscles that will not lend it for eight hours.
Ten minutes has a shape, and knowing it is half the pacing battle. The table below breaks the test into its natural segments — where speed comes free, where the wall hits, and what to do in each.
Segment | What happens | What to do
Minutes 1–2 | Warm-up; rhythm forms | Start at 90% of sprint pace, settle early
Minutes 3–6 | Cruise zone; your real speed | Hold even rhythm, eyes one word ahead
Minutes 7–8 | The fatigue wall; errors spike | Drop 5% pace, do NOT fight through at full speed
Minutes 9–10 | Second wind or collapse | Hold form, finish clean — last-minute errors cost most
Most people lose the test in minutes 7–8, not because they are slow but because they refuse to downshift. The professionals' secret is unglamorous: planned deceleration. Losing 5% of pace for two minutes costs far less than the error cluster that full-speed fatigue produces.
Endurance is trainable, and the training is boring on purpose: one long round per week at the full ten minutes, watching where your accuracy starts to slip. That slip point moves later and later over a month of weekly rounds — from minute five, to seven, to clear through ten. The decay curve flattening is the clearest progress signal in endurance typing.
Two supporting habits matter more than extra rounds. Posture checks at minute five — shoulders down, wrists floating, grip relaxed — because tension is what you are actually fighting in the back half. And a ten-second hand shake between practice rounds, so you learn to release tension instead of carrying it into the next round.
Short tests dominate hiring screens, but the long formats show up wherever the job itself is long: transcription and captioning assessments (sustained audio work), data-entry simulations for volume roles, and court or administrative exams in several countries that set five-to-ten-minute passages specifically to measure endurance.
If your target role involves continuous typing, your ten-minute score matters more than your one-minute best — and the typing speed requirements table shows which roles weight endurance heavily. Practise the format you will be tested on: the 5 minute typing test is the natural stepping stone if ten minutes still breaks you today.
This ten minute typing test runs the full 600 seconds in the browser with no sign-up and no round limit, so you can repeat it as often as you like and keep every result in your own local history. Ten minutes is long enough that pacing, posture and fatigue decide the score more than raw finger speed does, which makes it the honest format for testing whether a speed you hit in one minute survives real work.
Use it as an endurance check rather than a daily drill: one ten minute run after a warm-up, compared against your own one minute result from the same week. A gap of 5 to 15 percent below your short-round speed is normal. A gap wider than that is a posture or tension problem, not a speed problem, and the fix is a slower pace with relaxed wrists rather than more force.
Long rounds are only comparable if the unit is fixed. This test scores every five characters as one word, the convention documented for words per minute, so a ten minute result can be set against a one minute result from any other test that uses the same rule. Change the unit and the drop you are measuring stops being fatigue - it becomes an artefact of the formula.
If ten minutes is more than you need, the two-minute test covers the length most interviews use.

## Chinese Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/chinese-typing-test.html

Test your Chinese typing speed with real Chinese sentences. Measure your words per minute and accuracy instantly. Free, no sign up.

You do not type Chinese characters directly on a standard keyboard. You type a romanised or structural code - pinyin being the common case - and then choose a candidate from a list. Speed therefore depends on two skills: the keystrokes of the code, and how quickly you pick the right candidate.
That is why a Chinese WPM figure is not comparable to an English one at face value. A pinyin typist producing 40 characters per minute is typing maybe 120-160 keystrokes, and the character count is what gets reported.
Candidate selection. Common words appear first; rare characters require scanning or extra keystrokes. Practising your own vocabulary beats practising random text.
Phrase versus character input. Typing whole phrases (词) rather than single characters roughly halves the candidate selections, which is where most of the gain is.
Homophones. Pinyin maps many characters to one syllable, so accuracy depends on choosing correctly rather than on hitting the right key. An input-method error is a wrong character, not a typo.
Structural methods - Wubi (五笔), Cangjie (倉頡), Zhengma - encode the shape of a character rather than its sound. They have a much steeper learning curve but avoid candidate selection almost entirely, which is why professional Chinese typists often use them.
For most people pinyin is the right choice: it is already installed, it matches how you think, and the ceiling is high enough for office work. Switch only if you type Chinese for hours a day and the candidate list is demonstrably your bottleneck.
Use the Sentences mode and type the characters as they appear, committing each phrase with the space or number key your IME uses. The score panel reports characters per minute; multiply by 60 for characters per hour, and remember that the five-characters-per-word convention was designed for alphabetic scripts.
For a job that quotes words per minute, ask whether they mean characters or words. A 60 WPM requirement in a Chinese-language role usually means 60 characters per minute, which is a different target from 60 English words per minute.
## Chinese typing test FAQ
Usually in characters per minute, because each character carries a syllable. Multiply by 60 for characters per hour. The five-characters-per-word convention was designed for alphabetic scripts.
Wubi and other structural methods have a higher ceiling because they avoid candidate selection, but they take far longer to learn. For office work, pinyin's ceiling is usually enough.
Rare characters sit deep in the candidate list, so you scan or type extra keystrokes to reach them. Input-method errors produce a wrong character rather than a typo, which is why they are harder to notice.
40-60 characters per minute is comfortable for office work with pinyin; experienced typists reach 80-120. Professional structural-method typists exceed that, but they are a different population.
Yes - the Chinese comma and full stop (， 。) are part of the passage, and in full-width form they are separate keystrokes from their Latin counterparts.

## Hindi Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/hindi-typing-test.html

Test your Hindi typing speed with real Hindi sentences in Devanagari script. Measure your words per minute and accuracy instantly. Free, no sign up.

Hindi is written in Devanagari, where consonants carry an inherent 'a' vowel and other vowels appear as matras - marks placed before, after, above or below the consonant. A single written syllable can require two or three keystrokes, so your characters-per-minute is not the same as your syllable rate.
Add conjuncts (क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ) and the nasal marks (ं ँ) and you have a script where accuracy depends on sequence, not just key location. That is why Hindi typing tests feel different from English ones even at the same WPM.
Indian typing exams usually specify a layout, and the three you will meet are Krutidev, Remington (often called the typewriter layout) and Mangal/InScript. They map Devanagari to the keyboard in completely different ways: Krutidev and Remington are legacy layouts built for typewriters and phototypesetting, while InScript follows the script's logical order.
Layout | Where you meet it | Learning cost for a QWERTY typist
Krutidev | Many state government exams, court work | High - keys do not match the script order
Remington | Older exams, some typing institutes | High - typewriter-era mapping
InScript / Mangal | Modern government and Unicode work | Moderate - follows the script logically
Check the notice before you practise. Learning the wrong layout is worse than not practising, because the reflexes conflict.
Hindi typing tests commonly ask 25-30 words per minute, with 30 WPM the figure used where English requires 35. Some posts quote key depressions per hour instead, and the mistake allowance is usually around 5%.
Because the same passage can be scored as WPM or as key depressions, convert before comparing yourself to a friend's score: 30 WPM is 9,000 key depressions per hour under the five-character convention.
Practise on the layout your exam uses, on a keyboard you do not own, with a passage that includes the danda (।) and the numerals. Then time yourself for the full ten minutes rather than in one-minute bursts: conjunct errors cluster late, when attention thins.
If you are starting from English touch typing, expect two to four weeks before the Devanagari reflexes stop interfering with your Latin ones. Do not alternate layouts within a session; the interference is real and it slows both.
## Hindi typing test FAQ
Commonly 25-30 words per minute, with 30 WPM where an English requirement would be 35. Some posts quote key depressions per hour instead, usually with a 5% error allowance.
Whichever your exam notice specifies - Krutidev, Remington or InScript/Mangal. They map Devanagari completely differently, and learning the wrong one creates conflicting reflexes.
Matras and conjuncts mean one written syllable can take two or three keystrokes, so characters per minute and syllables per minute diverge. Accuracy also depends on sequence rather than single key location.
Yes. It is part of the passage, like a full stop in English, and an omitted character counts as an error on every mainstream test.
Yes, once the layout is installed in your operating system. The physical keyboard stays the same; only the mapping changes.

## Arabic Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/arabic-typing-test.html

Test your Arabic typing speed with real Arabic sentences. Measure your words per minute and accuracy instantly. Free, no sign up.

Arabic is written right to left and the letters join, so what you see on screen is not one glyph per keystroke: most letters have isolated, initial, medial and final forms, and the renderer picks the form as you type. Your speed is still one keystroke per letter - the joining is the font's job, not yours.
Four features decide accuracy: the hamza forms (أ إ آ ؤ ئ), ta marbuta (ة) versus ha (ه), the alif maqsura (ى) versus ya (ي), and the Arabic comma ، and semicolon ؛ which sit where a Latin keyboard puts different characters. None of these are optional if the text is right-to-left formal writing.
The standard Arabic layout keeps the Latin letters on the same physical keys and adds Arabic legends, so touch typists can switch between languages without moving their hands - the muscle memory transfers, only the output changes. That is good news for anyone who already types English.
The part that catches people is direction. In a right-to-left field the cursor moves left as you type, and mixing Arabic with Latin words or numbers reverses the visual order of the run. If your accuracy collapses when a sentence contains a number or an English product name, that is bidi handling, not typing speed.
Most Arabic typing tests report words per minute using the same five-characters-per-word convention as English, so the two numbers are broadly comparable - with one caveat: Arabic words are shorter on average than English words, so a text of equal character count contains more words. Compare CPM rather than WPM when you are comparing across languages.
CPM | WPM (÷5) | Reading
150 | 30 | Beginner, hunt-and-peck
200 | 40 | Comfortable office speed
250 | 50 | Fast for Arabic formal text
300+ | 60+ | Professional, transcription level
Start with sentences without tashkeel (diacritics), because everyday writing omits them and typing them slows you down for no gain. Add them only if your work requires vocalised text - religious, educational or children's material.
Then practise the pairs that cause errors: ة versus ه at word ends, ى versus ي, and the hamza carriers. Ten repetitions of one word beat one pass through ten words, because the goal is a corrected reflex rather than exposure.
For the English side of the same skill, see the English typing test; for the general benchmark, average typing speed.
Government and clerical posts in the Gulf and Egypt commonly ask for a certificate or a timed sample, often 20-30 words per minute for data entry and higher for secretarial work. Because the requirement is set per employer, read the posting rather than assuming a national standard exists.
If a test is proctored, expect an unfamiliar keyboard with Arabic legends. Practise at least twice on a different machine: key travel and legend placement change your error rate more than practice volume does.
## Arabic typing test FAQ
Letters - one keystroke per letter. The joined forms you see on screen are produced by the font, not by extra keystrokes.
Mixing right-to-left Arabic with left-to-right digits reverses the visual order of that run. It is a bidirectional text issue rather than a typing-speed problem; check your output rather than your speed.
Only if your work needs vocalised text. Everyday Arabic writing omits them, and typing them slows you down without improving the result.

## Touch Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/touch-typing-test.html

Free touch typing test and practice. Train yourself to type without looking at the keyboard: home row drills, real sentences, and a 60 second test that scores your speed and accuracy. The practice text is drawn from touch typing lessons, so what you read is what you learn. No sign up, works in your browser.

A touch typing test measures how fast and how accurately you type without looking at the keys. Touch typing means all ten fingers work from the home row, and your eyes stay on the screen the whole time. This free test runs for 60 seconds, scores your words per minute (WPM) and accuracy live, and highlights every error so you can see exactly which keys still trip you up. Because the practice sentences are taken from real touch typing lessons, taking the test is itself a lesson.
Muscle memory is built by frequency, not by marathon sessions. A daily 60 second touch typing test is enough to keep the home row fresh and to expose the two or three keys that always slow you down. Track your WPM across a week and you will see the pattern: accuracy climbs first, and speed follows a few days behind. When your accuracy passes 98 percent, you know the keyboard has finally moved into your fingers.
Start by resting your index fingers on the small bumps on F and J, with the other fingers curling onto the home row beside them. Type the sentence on screen without glancing down; if you must look, look only after the line is finished. Keep your wrists floating and your shoulders down. After the test, read the error report: those keys, not your fastest ones, are your next practice targets.
The full picture: is it hard to learn touch typing, how long to learn touch typing, the easy way to learn touch typing, and touch typing for adults.
Three numbers, once a week, same test length and time of day: net WPM, accuracy, and consistency (how much your speed varies second to second). Progress in touch typing usually shows up in accuracy first, then consistency, then speed - in that order.
If speed rises while accuracy falls, you are trading one for the other and the net result is flat. That is the most common false plateau, and the fix is a week of accuracy-only rounds rather than more speed work.

## Typing Tutorial
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-tutorial.html

Free typing tutorial for beginners. Step by step touch typing lessons in your browser: home row first, then every finger, then real speed. Each tutorial sentence is also your practice text, so reading the lesson is doing the lesson. No sign up, no cost.

On this page
The path, and what each stage is for
What to skip, and in what order
A four-week schedule that fits a working day
How to know the tutorial worked
When a stage will not click
How long each stage actually takes
Stage | What you do | Move on when
1. Home row | asdf jkl; until the fingers return without looking | 95% accuracy, no glances
2. All rows | Top row, then bottom row, one at a time | 30 WPM on ordinary words
3. Modifiers | Shift for capitals, punctuation in sentences | 96% accuracy with punctuation intact
4. Digits | Number row with correct fingers; keypad if relevant | 97% accuracy on a numbers round
5. Speed | 30-second sprints plus slow accuracy rounds | Sprint peak 10-15 WPM above sustained
Skip alternative layouts (Dvorak, Colemak) until you are past 60 WPM on QWERTY. Switching early means paying the learning cost twice and measuring neither. Skip code typing until you can type sentences without looking, because brackets make a hard task harder.
Do not skip the digits stage even if your job seems prose-only. Every real document contains a date or an amount, and the number row is where untrained typists lose the most accuracy.
Week 1: two minutes home row, three minutes normal text, one minute covered. Week 2: add the row you miss most, keep the covered round. Week 3: punctuation and capitals in sentences, plus a numbers round every other day. Week 4: five-minute rounds and one full test as a checkpoint.
Fifteen minutes a day is enough. The variable that predicts progress is not session length but the number of days you show up.
Two checks. First, you can type a sentence with your hands covered at 90% of your normal accuracy. Second, your five-minute net score improved by at least 5 WPM since the start.
If neither happened, the cause is almost always that the covered round got dropped. It is the least pleasant part of the tutorial and the only part that removes the ceiling.
Every stage has a characteristic failure, and each has one fix that works better than repeating the same drill:
Symptom | What it usually means | Fix
Accuracy collapses when you cover your hands | The key map is visual, not spatial | Two weeks of covered rounds at 30 seconds, no target
Speed rises but errors rise faster | You are typing ahead of the buffer | Drop to 85% pace for a week; one error per round allowed
Fine on sentences, lost on digits | The number row was never drilled | Two minutes of Numbers mode daily, graded on errors
Good in practice, worse in tests | The countdown itself is the problem | Practise with the timer visible every session, same length as the test
These are typical ranges for an adult practising fifteen minutes a day, not guarantees. The spread between people is wide, and the variable that predicts progress is how many days you show up, not how long each session is.
Home row secure: 1-2 weeks.
All rows without looking: 3-4 weeks.
Capitals and punctuation not breaking rhythm: 5-6 weeks.
45 WPM sustained on normal text: 2-3 months.
60 WPM: 4-6 months for most adults starting from two-finger typing.
If you are outside those ranges by a lot, the cause is almost always one of the four symptoms above rather than talent.

Yes. Dates, amounts and reference codes appear in almost every real document, and the number row is where untrained typists lose accuracy first.
The covered round. It is the only one that removes the look-at-keyboard habit, which is what caps most people at 35-40 WPM.
Yes, with no account. Each stage links to the test mode it needs, and results stay in your browser.
Each stage has a characteristic failure: a visual key map (fix with covered rounds), typing ahead of the buffer (drop to 85% pace), undrilled digits (two minutes of Numbers mode), or test anxiety (practise with the timer visible).

## Typing Tutor
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-tutor.html

Free typing tutor with live feedback. Pick a drill, type for sixty seconds, and the tutor scores your WPM, your accuracy, and names the exact keys that slowed you down. Every drill is also your practice text, so the lesson is the workout. No sign up, no cost.

Software measures output: WPM, accuracy, which keys you miss. A tutor watches process: posture, whether the same hand presses Shift, whether you look down before or after an error, whether you tense your shoulders when the timer starts.
That distinction matters because most adult blockers are process problems. A typist who types at 45 WPM with all ten fingers and no looking has a posture or tension problem, and no amount of drill volume fixes it.
Baseline: five-minute net WPM, accuracy, and the same on a numbers round.
Technique observations: finger assignment, Shift hand, looking frequency, wrist position.
Error pattern: which characters cluster in the error report, not just how many.
Prescription: two or three drills, not a course. Anything more will not be done.
If an assessment gives you a number and a course to buy, it is a sales funnel rather than a diagnosis.
A good tutor will ask what you type and why before testing you, and will spend most of the first session watching rather than timing. Ask whether they teach touch typing from scratch or fix existing habits - the second is harder and rarer.
Self-tutoring works if you follow three rules: measure the same way every week, change one variable at a time, and keep a covered round in every session. The data does the diagnosing; you just have to write it down.
Run a five-minute test at the start of each week and record net WPM, accuracy and the two slowest keys from the results panel. That is enough data to see whether a drill is working after three weeks.
For the drills themselves, the touch typing course is structured, and the typing speed exercises page covers the ones that target specific weaknesses.
## Typing tutor FAQ
Not if you are progressing: weekly measurements and a covered round are enough. A tutor helps when you are stuck at the same speed for months with correct technique, or when posture and tension are the problem.
Mostly observation: a baseline five-minute score, finger assignment, Shift hand, how often you look down, and where your errors cluster. A number alone is not a diagnosis.

## Learn to Type: Free Typing Tutorial for Beginners
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/learn-to-type.html

Learn to type for free, from the very first key. This beginner typing course starts at the home row and adds one row at a time, and every practice line is written as a first lesson, so the text you type teaches you how to type. Sixty seconds a day, instant feedback, no sign up.

On this page
learn to type
Your first lesson in learning to type
How long does it take to learn to type?
Learn to type without looking
A one-week learn-to-type plan
Learn to type on a laptop keyboard
To learn to type you only need two things: the home row, and the patience to be slow for a week. This free course teaches touch typing from absolute zero, and every practice sentence is a lesson about learning itself, so your practice text coaches you while you type it. Sixty seconds a day in your browser, with live WPM and accuracy feedback, no account and no cost.
Rest your left fingers on A S D F and your right fingers on J K L ;, thumbs on the space bar. Feel the small bumps on F and J; they are the only map a beginner needs. Type words made from the home row only, slowly, and let each finger return home after every key. If you must look, look after the word, never in the middle of it. That is the entire first lesson, and everything after it is just practice.
Most people own the home row in a week and reach a comfortable 40 to 60 words per minute in three to four weeks of daily practice. The mistake beginners make is chasing speed early; accuracy is the foundation and speed is the building that arrives later. End every session on your slowest, most careful line, and your hands will learn faster than you expect.
Looking at your hands feels faster for about a week and caps you near 30 WPM forever, because every glance breaks the loop between what your eyes read and what your fingers do. Break the habit deliberately: cover your hands with a cloth for one short round a day, accept the slower score, and let the home row do the work. The full method is on the how to type without looking page.
Day one: home row only, slow, eyes on the screen. Day two: add the top row with the correct fingers. Day three: bottom row and the shift key. Day four: short common words. Day five: full sentences at a comfortable pace. Day six: numbers and punctuation. Day seven: one timed round to see where you are — not to pass a target. Fifteen minutes a day is enough; the schedule matters more than the minutes.
When the week ends, move to structured typing practice and check the result panel for the keys that are slowing you down.
Laptop keys have shorter travel, which makes light, quick presses easier and heavy presses slower. The home row is the same, but the keyboard is often narrower, so your hands sit closer to centre. If the built-in keyboard is uncomfortable, the mechanical keyboard for typing guide covers what actually matters — key travel and actuation force — without the marketing.
For a step-by-step version of this page, the typing tutorial runs the same five stages with a checkpoint at each one.
## Learn to type FAQ
Yes. This course is completely free, with no sign up, no account, and no paywall. Every lesson is a timed practice you can repeat as often as you like, and your results stay in your own browser.
That is exactly who this page is for. It starts at the home row, assumes nothing, and adds one row at a time. Being slow in the first week is not a setback; it is the lesson.
The home row: A S D F J K L ; with your thumbs on the space bar. Find the bumps on F and J with your index fingers, and practice words made only from those keys until you never look down.
Usually one to two weeks for the home row, and three to four weeks before the whole keyboard feels automatic. Covering the keyboard with a cloth speeds this up, because it removes the option of cheating.
Accuracy, always. Speed is a byproduct of accurate repetition. A fast wrong keystroke teaches your hand the wrong address for a key, which you then have to unlearn.
Ten to fifteen minutes every day. Short daily practice builds muscle memory far better than one long weekly session, because the hands learn by frequency, not by total minutes.
You can learn the correct finger positions in a week, and most people reach a usable 30-40 WPM within three to four weeks of daily practice. Reaching 60 WPM usually takes two to three months of consistent short sessions.

## Typing Trainer
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-trainer.html

Free typing trainer with drills and practice plans. Sixty second training sets, live WPM and accuracy, and your best scores saved locally so every session has a target to beat. The practice text is written as training instruction, so each drill coaches you while you type it. No sign up.

A typing trainer gives you the two things practice alone never will: a plan and a record. This free trainer runs sixty second drills, scores your live WPM and accuracy, and keeps your best result in the browser so each session has a number to beat. The practice lines are written as training instruction, so while you type, the drill teaches you about training plans, muscle memory, and logging progress. No sign up and no cost.
Week one is diagnosis: run three drills a day and read the error report without trying to fix anything. Week two, drill your two weakest keys twice as often as the rest. Week three, run the full minute at a speed where you make no errors, and live there. Week four, chase your personal best once a day and log it. Five words per minute each week is the only target, because tendons keep their own pace.
Practice is typing a lot; training is typing the right thing a lot. The difference is the log. When you record your WPM and accuracy side by side each day, a speed that costs accuracy shows up immediately as a bad trade, and the drill that fixed your weak keys shows up as a permanent step up. Your hands will plateau; the trainer's answer is variety and rest, not more effort.
Technique before speed: touch typing tips that fix form, and finger placement typing drills.
Trainer drills work best inside a plan: online typing practice lays out the daily 10-minute structure by goal — speed, accuracy, exam or a new language.

Sixty seconds per set, with short rest between sets. Keep total training under thirty minutes a day; a tired hand practices its own mistakes.

## Custom Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/custom-typing-test.html

A fully customizable typing test: pick your duration from 15 seconds to 10 minutes, switch between sentences, quotes, numbers and words, set the language, theme and line width, then type and get instant WPM. Everything is configurable, nothing to sign up for.

On this page
Four ways people actually use a custom test
What to paste, and what not to
Settings that matter
Limits worth knowing
When a custom test is the right measurement
How pasted text behaves in the engine
Interview rehearsal - paste a passage in the style of the employer's test (legal clause, medical note, code snippet) and practise at the same length.
Weak-key drilling - paste the words you keep missing, twenty times each, and run a minute on them.
Domain vocabulary - drug names, part numbers, legal defined terms. Typing your own vocabulary beats typing random sentences.
Classroom use - paste a passage from the week's reading so practice reinforces content rather than competing with it.
The custom text is stored in your browser for the session; nothing is uploaded, which is what makes the classroom use case workable.
Paste plain text. Formatting, smart quotes and non-breaking spaces can all produce characters your keyboard cannot type, which turns a practice round into a hunt for a Unicode symbol.
Keep it between 100 and 400 words. Shorter and the round repeats, which makes memorisation inflate your score; longer and you will never finish a five-minute round.
Setting | Use it when
Duration | Match the real test length; use 60 seconds for warm-ups only
Text mode | Sentences for prose, Numbers for codes and amounts
Layout | QWERTY by default; change it if you actually type on Dvorak or Colemak
Theme and width | Comfort only - they do not change the score
A custom test cannot tell you whether the passage is representative. If you paste easy words, you will score higher than on an employer's test and believe you are ready.
Use it for targeted practice, and the standard tests for benchmarking. For the benchmark itself, see the one-minute test or the five-minute test.
A custom test is valid for practising a specific text. It is not valid for comparing yourself to a benchmark, because the passage you chose is not a neutral sample.
Use it for: rehearsing the exact format of an employer's test, drilling your own domain vocabulary, and reproducing a text you keep mistyping. Do not use it to decide whether you are fast enough for a job - use a standard sentence test at the same length as the employer's, because that is what their test will be.
The text is split on whitespace and typed word by word. Punctuation inside a word (hyphens, apostrophes, brackets) is counted as part of that word, so a passage full of citations will score lower than the same character count of plain prose - correctly, because it is harder to type.
Two things to watch when pasting: smart quotes and non-breaking spaces from a word processor can produce characters your keyboard does not have a key for, and a very long single line will wrap in a way that makes the cursor jump. Paste plain text, and keep paragraphs under about 400 words.

If you write in more than one language, your typing speed is not one number; it is five, and the only way to know each one is to test it in that language.
Most typing tests assume English, but a keyboard is not the same in every language. Chinese and Hindi use input methods that add a composition step between keystroke and character. Arabic reverses direction and changes letter shapes mid-word. Spanish adds accented vowels. Testing in the language you actually write in is the only way to measure the speed that matters to you.
Run the same one minute test in each language on the same day, and write the five numbers down. Most people are fastest in their dominant language and ten to twenty percent slower in the others, and the gap shrinks fast with a few minutes of daily practice in the weaker languages. Re-run the same set next month and the comparison is honest, because the test itself never changed.

This page generates a typing certificate from your most recent round. It is free, needs no account, and is produced entirely in your browser - nothing is uploaded, which is also why there is no verification code on it.
The certificate is a printable record of one test: who typed, when, at what speed and accuracy, on what test length. It is a convenience for applications that want a number, not an accredited credential. The honest version of that distinction is spelled out on the certificate acceptance page.
Field | Content | Why it is there
Name | Whatever you type in the name field | An employer needs to attach the number to a person
Date | The date you generated it | Typing speed drifts; a dated result is checkable
WPM | Net words per minute from that round | The number most postings quote
CPM | Characters per minute | Data-entry roles quote characters, not words
Accuracy | Percentage of correct characters | The part employers actually weight
Length and mode | e.g. 5 minutes, sentences | Makes the score comparable - a 15-second burst is not
Paper: A4 or US Letter both work; the layout uses standard margins and no bleed.
Colour: it prints correctly in black and white, which is what most offices will do anyway.
Browser print settings: turn off headers and footers so the URL and date stamps do not appear over the artwork.
Digital copy: print to PDF rather than photographing the screen - the text stays selectable and the file stays small.
If the result panel is still open, the certificate uses that round. If you have closed it, take a new round first: the certificate is generated from the round in the current session, not from your history.
Use a five-minute test and quote the net figure. A one-minute result reads 5-10 WPM higher and is the first thing a careful employer discounts. If you are applying for a role quoted in keystrokes per hour, convert first: 45 WPM is 13,500 KPH, and the converter does it both ways.
If your accuracy is below 97%, run an accuracy round before generating the certificate. A certificate showing 55 WPM at 92% invites the question of how many of those words were right.
Private-sector recruiters commonly accept a dated result as a screening signal and then test you themselves. Public-sector, court, dispatch and hospital roles usually require a proctored test or a certificate from an approved centre, and the posting states the wording.
Plan for the re-test: if your certificate says 58 and their test reads 52, that is normal and consistent. If it says 70 because you quoted a 15-second burst, it looks like a discrepancy.
Nowhere. The round is measured in your browser, the certificate is composed in your browser, and the print dialogue is your operating system's. There is no server-side record, no account, and no way for us to look up a certificate - which is exactly why a verification ID is not printed on it.

## Dvorak Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/dvorak-typing.html

Practice and measure your typing in Dvorak. The on screen keyboard below is already set to the Dvorak layout, with finger guidance mapped to Dvorak hand positions, so what you see matches what your system layout produces. Use the QWERTY / Dvorak switch in the keyboard toolbar any time. Switch your operating system to Dvorak, take the test, and get WPM, accuracy and consistency.

Most typing tests show a QWERTY keyboard, which is useless when you practice Dvorak typing: the label you need to find is not on the key you press. This test flips the on screen keyboard to the Dvorak layout, keeping the physical key positions of QWERTY and relabelling every key, so the hand you need to move matches the finger guide on screen exactly as a Dvorak user sees their own keyboard.
Nothing is installed and nothing changes your system: the test only draws the Dvorak keyboard on this page. Switch your operating system input to Dvorak, start typing, and the test scores you exactly as it would in QWERTY, because the measuring logic reads the characters your layout produces, not the keys.
August Dvorak designed the layout in the 1930s so the most common letters sit on the home row, which means less finger travel between rows for almost every English word. Typists who switch usually report less strain in long sessions, and many reach a higher comfortable speed once the new muscle memory settles, which takes roughly two to four weeks of daily practice.
The honest trade off: Dvorak helps most for people who type a lot of English prose. Shortcuts that assume QWERTY positions stay where they were physically, and shared or public keyboards are QWERTY by default, so most Dvorak users keep a fast way to switch back.
Set your operating system layout to Dvorak first, otherwise you would be typing QWERTY text while looking at a Dvorak keyboard. Start with short sessions of two to five minutes, and resist the urge to look at your hands: the finger guides on this page exist exactly to replace that habit.
Expect your speed to drop well below your QWERTY speed for the first week; that drop is the switch cost, not a sign Dvorak is wrong for you. Track your WPM here each day and compare accuracy rather than raw speed, because accuracy recovers first and speed follows it.
Considering the switch? Dvorak vs QWERTY weighs the evidence honestly — and why technique usually beats layout.
## Dvorak typing FAQ

The vowels A, O, E, U, I move to the middle row under the left hand, and common consonants like T, N, S and H move to the right hand. The full relabelling is drawn on the on screen keyboard above.
Evidence is mixed: most studies show a modest speed gain at the high end and clearer reductions in finger movement and strain. The main benefit people report is comfort in long typing sessions rather than a guaranteed speed jump.

## One Hand Typing
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/one-hand-typing.html

Learn and measure one hand typing on a normal keyboard. Whether you type with one hand because of an injury, a permanent condition, or simply a hand that is busy holding a coffee, the technique below lets you reach useful speeds without special hardware or chording software. Take the test with one hand and see where you are today.

One hand typing on a standard QWERTY keyboard is a real, learnable skill. The idea is not to hunt and peck with one finger, but to assign each finger a fixed zone of the keyboard so your hand develops a repeatable map of where every letter lives. With practice, single hand typists reach 40 to 70 WPM, which is fast enough for almost all desk work.
You do not need a one handed keyboard or chord input software. The regular keyboard you already own is enough, because the technique is about hand position and practice, not hardware.
Put your four fingers on the home row of the side you use: left hand on A S D F, right hand on J K L semicolon. The thumb works the space bar. Each finger owns the keys in its column plus the row above and below, and the index finger stretches across the middle column to cover the keys on the far side.
The stretch is the hard part at first, especially the keys farthest from your little finger. Slow drills at first are normal; speed comes from accuracy, because a hand that returns to home row after every key does not need to look down.
Beginners hunting with one finger sit near 15 to 25 WPM. With proper finger zones and a few weeks of short daily sessions, 35 to 50 WPM is common. Experienced one hand typists who type all day reach 60 to 70 WPM and occasionally higher.
Measure honestly with the test on this page: run a one minute test with one hand only, and record your accuracy beside your WPM. Accuracy below 90 percent usually means you are reaching for speed before the map is settled, so slow down until accuracy rises and let speed follow.
## One hand typing FAQ
Yes. With fixed finger zones and practice, one hand typists commonly reach 40 to 60 WPM and experienced ones 70 WPM or more. The key is using all fingers of that hand, not one finger hunting.
No. The technique works on any standard QWERTY keyboard. Specialised hardware can help for some people, but it is not required to reach useful speeds.
Use the hand you have. The finger zone method works symmetrically for either side; the test here does not care which hand presses the keys.
Basic fluency in two to four weeks with fifteen to twenty minutes a day. Getting back to your two hand speed takes longer, but useful working speed arrives faster than most people expect.
The test is self paced and as short as 15 seconds, so you can use it within whatever your recovery allows. It is not medical advice; follow your clinician's guidance about how much to type while healing.
Results are saved in this browser automatically, so run a one minute test every few days and watch the history table for your WPM and accuracy trend.

## Privacy Policy
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/privacy-policy.html

This page explains what Typing.Rerivo does and does not collect. The short version: nothing about you is collected at all.

Nothing. There is no account system, no sign up, no email collection and no contact form on the typing test itself. We do not run analytics scripts, advertising pixels, fingerprinting or any third party tracking on this site.
When you take a test, your text input, your typing speed and your accuracy are computed entirely inside your own browser by JavaScript running on this page. The results are never transmitted to any server.
Your typing history, your chosen settings and your high score are saved in your browser's localStorage, which lives on your device only. Clearing your browser data or using a private window removes all of it. Nothing of yours reaches a database, because there is no database.
If you use the print certificate feature, the certificate is generated in your browser and sent straight to your printer or to your browser's save as PDF dialog; it is not uploaded anywhere.
The site is hosted on GitHub Pages, so GitHub may record standard request logs (IP address, timestamp, requested URL) as part of serving the pages, as any web host does. Those logs are governed by GitHub's own privacy policy and are not shared with or used by us.
We submit page URLs to IndexNow so search engines can discover the site faster. That submission contains only public URLs, no personal information.

## About Typing.Rerivo
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/about.html

Typing.Rerivo is a free typing speed test that runs entirely in your browser. No account, no paywall, no upload: pick a duration from 15 seconds to 10 minutes, type, and get your WPM, accuracy and consistency instantly.

On this page
Why this site exists
How the measurement works
Contact
Sources and standards we use
About this page
How we decide what to publish, and how we fix mistakes
Most typing tests on the web are heavy pages that ask you to sign up, show ads between every test, or hide your results behind an email wall. This one is built the opposite way: one fast page, one test, one result, and everything stored in your own browser so your history stays yours. The full list of what we publish is on the typing tests directory.
It started as a single page and grew by listening to what people actually searched for: timed variants from 15 seconds to 10 minutes, practice for punctuation and capital letters, number and symbol drills, a certificate you can print, a Dvorak keyboard that matches your layout, and one hand typing practice for people who type with a single hand.
WPM uses the industry standard of five characters per word, counted from correctly typed characters divided by elapsed minutes. Accuracy is the share of correct keystrokes, and raw WPM counts every keystroke including mistakes, so the gap between the two shows how much correcting you do. Consistency measures how stable your speed was across the whole test rather than just the peak.
The text you type never leaves your browser, and there is no server-side scoring because there is no need for one: JavaScript on this page does all of it.
Questions, corrections to a practice text, or ideas for the next typing drill are welcome at hello@rerivo.com. If you would like the site in your language, that is the fastest way to make it happen. What we store and why is set out in the privacy policy.
Where a page on this site makes a factual claim about typing speed, the claim traces to one of these references. We cite them so you can check the numbers rather than trust a test page.
Words per minute - the five-character word convention and the reference bands used on our benchmark pages.
Touch typing - the home-row method and its history, which underpins the finger charts and hand-position guides.
Dvorak keyboard layout - the 1936 patent and layout design, used for the Dvorak practice page.
Colemak - the 2006 layout and its home-row share, used for the Colemak practice page.
Numeric keypad - the ten-key layout behind the ten key and number typing tests.
O*NET 43-9021.00, Data Entry Keyers - the occupational profile we point to when describing data entry job requirements.
Benchmarks that come from commercial assessment vendors are linked with rel="nofollow" because we are not endorsing their paid tests; the free references above carry ordinary links.
Last updated 2026-10-20. This page documents the methodology behind every benchmark on the site.
Every number on this site falls into one of three categories, and the page always says which: a measured figure with a primary source and a DOI (for example the CHI 2018 typing study), an official standard quoted from a notice or exam authority, or a market range drawn from job advertisements and labelled as a range rather than a measurement.
Nothing else is published. There are no traffic numbers, no leaderboard statistics and no "average by country" table, because those would require data we do not have and could not verify. The benchmarks page states the same rule for the data it carries.
When a source is superseded or a figure turns out to be wrong, the page is revised and its date changes. The date you see at the bottom of every page comes from the site's own version history, and the same date is emitted in the page's structured data, so a page claiming to be current actually is.
What this site does not claim: it is not an accredited testing centre, it does not proctor anything, and a certificate printed here is explicitly self-issued. Those limits are spelled out on the certificate acceptance page rather than hidden in a footer.

The site is built and maintained by the Typing.Rerivo team, which is the author declared in the structured data on every page. Contact is hello@rerivo.com; corrections to practice texts are welcome and are usually fixed in the next build.

## Average Typing Speed
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/average-typing-speed.html

The average typing speed is about 40 to 50 words per minute (WPM) with roughly 92% accuracy. 45–60 WPM is good, 60–80 WPM is above average, and only about 1% of people type faster than 100 WPM. Test your own speed below, then compare it with the benchmarks.

On this page
The number, and where it comes from
Why published averages disagree
What counts as good, fast and exceptional
Average typing speed by age
Average typing speed by profession
Why your score differs from these numbers
Test yourself against the bands
The most-cited modern measurement is Dhakal, Feit, Kristensson and Oulasvirta, "Observations on Typing from 136 Million Keystrokes" (CHI 2018). It recorded 136,857,600 keystrokes from 168,960 volunteers and reports a mean of 51.56 WPM with a standard deviation of 20.2, an uncorrected error rate of 1.17%, and 1.173 keystrokes per character. The paper is open at doi.org/10.1145/3173574.3174220.
Most pages still quote 40 WPM. That figure comes from older, smaller samples of office workers and students, and it has been copied forward without being re-measured. Both describe real populations: 40 WPM is closer to "typical office worker on a work task", 51.56 WPM to "person who chose to take an online typing test".
Search "average typing speed" and you will find 40, 45, 50, 52 and 60 WPM on the first page. They are not all wrong - they describe different populations, measured different ways. This is the table that reconciles them:
Figure | What it describes | Where it comes from
~40 WPM | Office workers on work tasks, older and smaller samples | The legacy figure quoted in most business and career articles; no single modern study
51.56 WPM | People who chose to take an online typing test | Dhakal et al., CHI 2018 - 136,857,600 keystrokes from 168,960 volunteers, doi.org/10.1145/3173574.3174220
36.17 WPM | The same task on a touchscreen | Palin et al., MobileHCI 2019 - 37,370 volunteers, doi.org/10.1145/3338286.3340120
60-70 WPM | "Good typists" in job advertising | Advertised requirements, not a measured population
So the honest answer to "what is the average" is: 51.56 WPM if you mean people who take typing tests, about 40 WPM if you mean office workers on work tasks, and 36 WPM if you mean phones. None of those is a national average, and nobody has measured one recently.
Which should you use? For a job application, use the figure in the posting - employers compare against their own floor, not against a population. For a personal target, use the percentile table above, because it tells you where you sit among people who actually type for a measured minute.
Band | Net WPM | Percentile (approx.) | What it means
Slow | under 26 | bottom 10% | Hunting for keys; typing is the bottleneck
Below average | 26-40 | 10th-28th | Two-finger or untrained touch typing
Average | 40-52 | 28th-50th | Enough for most office work
Good | 52-65 | 50th-75th | Comfortable all-day typing
Fast | 65-78 | 75th-90th | Above most job requirements
Top decile | 78-100 | 90th-99th | Professional typists, developers, transcribers
Exceptional | 100+ | top 1% | Competitive typing, world-record territory
The percentile column is a normal approximation of that distribution, and it reproduces the study's own reported deciles to within about one point. The percentile page does the arithmetic for any score.
Speed peaks in the late teens to thirties in most published samples and declines slowly after that, but the spread within an age band is far larger than the difference between bands. A 55-year-old who touch types beats a 20-year-old who does not, every time.
The practical reading: age is a weak predictor compared with whether someone was ever taught to touch type. If they were not, the gap is trainable at any age - the age breakdown has the numbers by decade.
Data entry: 45-65 WPM, often quoted as 13,500-19,500 KPH, with 97-98% accuracy.
Administrative and secretarial: 50-70 WPM depending on seniority.
Transcription: 65-80 WPM sustained over audio, which is harder than the same speed over visible text.
Software developers: no formal requirement; most sit above 70 WPM, and code typing differs because of brackets and symbols.
Writers and journalists: 60-80 WPM, where the limit is usually thinking rather than typing.
Role-by-role figures, in the units employers actually use, are on the typing speed requirements page.
Test length: a 15-second burst reads 5-10 WPM higher than a five-minute run. Text type: random words score lower than sentences, code lower again, digits are a different skill. Scoring: gross WPM is higher than net. Keyboard: a laptop chiclet keyboard is slower than a mechanical one for most people.
So before concluding you are below average, check what you measured. A five-minute net score on sentences is what this page's bands refer to; a one-minute gross score on random words is not comparable.
Run a five-minute sentence test, then read net WPM and accuracy from the results panel. Compare the net figure against the table above, and check whether accuracy is inside the 97-98% band most employers require - a fast score at 92% accuracy is not the same asset as a slightly slower clean one.
The source table behind these bands, plus the phone average and the raw CSV, is on the typing speed benchmarks page.
Reading about averages is not the same as measuring yours - a free typing test on this site reports net WPM and accuracy against these bands in one minute.
## Typing test FAQ

It is around the 28th percentile of the CHI 2018 distribution and clears the floor for most clerical and reception roles. It is below the 50-70 WPM band that legal, medical and transcription roles ask for.
Above 78 WPM puts you in the top 10% of the measured population. Above 100 WPM is roughly the top 1%, and competitive typists exceed 130 WPM in short bursts on known text.
Slightly, and far less than the variation between people of the same age. Whether someone was taught touch typing predicts speed much better than age does.
The first thirty seconds are warm-up pace you cannot hold. A five-minute net score is typically 5-10 WPM below a 15-second burst, and the longer number is the one that reflects a working day.

## CPM Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/cpm-typing-test.html

This CPM typing test measures your speed in characters per minute. CPM counts every correct keystroke, so because one word is five characters, CPM = WPM &times; 5. Type the passage below to see your live CPM, WPM and accuracy.

On this page
What is CPM (characters per minute)?
CPM to WPM calculator
WPM, CPM and KPH: the conversion table
CPM vs WPM: which should you use?
How this CPM test measures you
The hidden cost of errors in CPM
What is a good CPM typing speed?
How to raise your CPM
Drills that move your CPM
CPM and KPH benchmarks for jobs and exams
CPM for data entry, exams and language typing
CPM for non-English and symbol-heavy typing
CPM test: take a characters-per-minute test in one minute
Why characters are the more portable unit
Sources for the numbers on this page
About this page
CPM counts how many characters you type in one minute — every letter, number, space and symbol you produce. It is the rawest possible measure of typing output, which is why data-entry and transcription work quote speed in CPM or its hourly sibling KPH (keystrokes per hour) rather than in words.
On this site the conversion is the standard one used across the typing industry: five characters count as one word. So CPM is simply your WPM multiplied by five — no rounding tricks, no alternate formulas.
Type in any box: CPM, WPM or keystrokes per hour. The conversions are CPM ÷ 5 = WPM, WPM × 5 = CPM, and CPM × 60 = KPH, so the three boxes always agree.
The unit that matters depends on the posting: typing tests quote WPM, data-entry adverts quote keystrokes per hour, and exam notices in some countries quote characters per minute. Converting before you compare avoids the most common application mistake - quoting a number in the wrong unit.
Use this table to convert between the three units employers and exams quote. The formula is exact: CPM = WPM × 5, and KPH = CPM × 60.
WPM | CPM (WPM × 5) | KPH (CPM × 60)
20 | 100 | 6,000
30 | 150 | 9,000
40 | 200 | 12,000
50 | 250 | 15,000
60 | 300 | 18,000
80 | 400 | 24,000
100 | 500 | 30,000
120 | 600 | 36,000
Two reference points make the table easy to use: an average adult types about 40 WPM, which is 200 CPM or 12,000 KPH; the office-standard 60 WPM is 300 CPM or 18,000 KPH. Data-entry job postings asking for '8,000–10,000 KPH' are therefore asking for roughly 27–33 WPM — much less intimidating than the big number sounds.
Use WPM when you are comparing yourself with the classic typing benchmarks — schools, résumés and most online tests all quote it. Use CPM when the work itself is measured in keystrokes: numeric data entry, transcription, coding-adjacent tasks, and any language where 'word' is a fuzzy concept.
That last case matters more than it seems. In Japanese or Chinese, one character carries the meaning of a whole English word, so WPM understates the real work; CPM stays honest across scripts. The same is true for number-heavy documents, where a 'word' of five digits is far denser than a word of prose. If your job involves mixed text and figures, track both numbers for a week and see which one predicts your real output better.
The timer starts on your first keystroke, and the live display tracks your character rate as you type. When the clock stops you get two figures: net CPM, which is your correct characters per minute with errors deducted at the standard weighting, and raw CPM, your gross keystroke rate before any penalty. The site uses the same five-characters-per-word standard across every page, so your CPM here converts directly to the WPM shown elsewhere with no second-guessing.
You also get the consistency score, which measures how even your keystroke timing is, and the per-key report showing which letters you miss and which ones slow you down. For character-rate work the slow-key list is gold: a single hesitant key — a bracket, a digit, a shifted symbol — taxes every word that contains it. Drill that one key and the whole character rate lifts.
Results save privately in your browser, building a history you can compare week to week. Because CPM is more granular than WPM, real progress shows up in the numbers sooner — a five-CPM gain is visible long before a one-WPM gain would be.
Errors hurt twice in a character-based score. The mistyped character does not count, and the correction costs further keystrokes — a backspace and a retype at minimum, roughly two extra keystrokes for every mistake you actually fix. Unfixed errors are worse: they sit in the text and get deducted from your net figure at the end.
Run the arithmetic and the pattern is obvious. A raw 310 CPM at 94% accuracy nets below a controlled 290 CPM at 99%, and the cleaner run also produces better real documents. This is why every experienced data-entry trainer gives the same advice: find the speed where your accuracy stays above 97%, hold it until the character rate climbs on its own, then lift the ceiling a little. Accuracy is not the enemy of speed — it is the mechanism of it.
One more reason CPM deserves a place on your dashboard: it reacts to practice faster than WPM does. Because the unit is five times finer, a genuine improvement shows up as a visible CPM gain within days, while WPM might not tick over for weeks. That faster feedback loop keeps motivation honest — you can see the practice working, in keystrokes, almost as it happens.
Scaled from the standard WPM bands: around 200 CPM is the average adult, 300 CPM is good office-standard speed, 400 CPM is fast — the top ten percent — and 500 CPM or more is elite territory. The accuracy rule scales too: whatever your CPM, keep it above 97% accuracy, because every corrected error costs far more time than it saves.
WPM | CPM (= WPM × 5) | Level
20 WPM | 100 CPM | Beginner
40 WPM | 200 CPM | Average adult
60 WPM | 300 CPM | Good / office standard
80 WPM | 400 CPM | Fast
100 WPM | 500 CPM | Top ~1%
Watch your net figure, not the raw one. This test shows net CPM with errors deducted alongside your raw keystroke rate; the raw-minus-net gap is the clearest signal of whether you should push speed or tighten accuracy.
CPM rewards exactly one thing: more correct keystrokes per minute. Anything that removes hesitation raises it — home-row discipline, eyes on the screen, and drilling the specific keys your weak-key report flags after each round. Anything that creates backspaces lowers it, so type a touch slower than your panic speed and let accuracy do the compounding.
Symbols and digits carry more CPM weight than people expect, because they break letter rhythm. A few rounds in numbers or quotes mode each week keeps punctuation from collapsing your character rate. Short daily rounds on the 1 minute typing test build the base speed; then check the same run here to see it expressed in keystrokes.
Different text types train different parts of your character rate. Numbers mode is the fastest way to raise digit-heavy CPM — the kind that data-entry and spreadsheet work actually measure. Quotes mode drills the punctuation and capitals that break letter rhythm in prose. Words mode strips away sentence flow and measures pure per-word burst speed, which is useful for diagnosing whether your ceiling is vocabulary or technique.
Structure the week around your weak-key report. Two or three 15-second sprints as a warm-up, one full minute for the measurement, then five minutes drilling whichever keys the report flagged. Alternate prose days with numbers days if your work involves figures. Once a week, take a longer run — three or five minutes — and watch how your character rate decays; stamina is trainable, and the decay curve flattening over weeks is the clearest sign of real progress.
Data-entry job postings usually quote KPH — keystrokes per hour — with typical requirements between 8,000 and 12,000 KPH, plus an accuracy cutoff near 98%. Converted at the standard rate, that is roughly 130 to 200 CPM, or 27 to 40 WPM: demanding for a hunt-and-peck typist, comfortably reachable for anyone with a few weeks of touch-typing practice. Clerk, banking and court exams in several countries score short passages the same way, in keystrokes with an accuracy threshold.
Transcription and captioning sit higher, often expecting the equivalent of 300 CPM or more with near-perfect accuracy, because the work is continuous. Wherever a target is quoted in keystrokes, practise in CPM so the number on test day needs no mental conversion. Because this site uses the industry-standard five-character word, scores you measure here transfer directly to those requirements.
Data-entry employers quote KPH targets — typically 8,000 to 12,000 keystrokes per hour — and exams for clerk and banking posts often score passages in keystrokes with an accuracy cutoff. Practising directly in CPM removes the mental conversion on test day. The keystrokes per hour test shows the same score in KPH, and the typing speed calculator converts any result between the three units instantly.
If you type in more than one language, CPM is also the only fair cross-language scoreboard: WPM shifts with each script's idea of a 'word', while characters are characters everywhere. The words per minute test page explains the word-based view in more detail.
Words are a comfortable unit in English, but they get slippery elsewhere. Japanese and Chinese text has no spaces between words, so a 'word count' depends on a segmentation algorithm, not anything a typist can see. Agglutinative languages like Turkish or Finnish pack whole phrases into single long words, pushing WPM down even when finger speed is high. Code and data files invert the problem: brackets, operators and digits are dense with keystrokes but sparse with 'words'.
Characters never have this problem. A keystroke is a keystroke in every script and every file type, which is why CPM travels where WPM cannot: comparing your speed across languages, across prose and numbers, or across a week that mixed emails with spreadsheets. If you work in more than one language, CPM is the only scoreboard that treats them all fairly.
The same logic applies to accuracy. One mistyped character costs exactly one character of net score whether it sits in English prose, a Hindi conjunct or a line of figures — so the accuracy habits that raise your CPM transfer to every script you type.
A CPM test scores the same one-minute round as a WPM test, but reports characters instead of words - which is why CPM appears roughly five times larger than the equivalent WPM figure. Take the test above, type for sixty seconds, and the result panel shows characters per minute, words per minute and accuracy side by side so you never have to convert by hand.
CPM is the fairer unit when your language or your work is not English prose. WPM depends on an arbitrary five-character word, so scripts that write without spaces, and data entry that is mostly digits and symbols, produce WPM numbers that cannot be compared across languages. Character counts have no such convention: 200 CPM means 200 characters typed correctly, in Tokyo, Berlin or Bangalore alike.
The five-character word is a convention, not a measurement: words per minute standardises a word to five characters including spaces and punctuation precisely so that different passages produce comparable numbers. Character counts skip the convention entirely, which is why a CPM score travels across languages and across numeric keypad work, where the numeric keypad contributes most of the keystrokes.
Speed and accuracy figures quoted here follow the largest published study of everyday typing: Dhakal et al., CHI 2018, Observations on Typing from 136 Million Keystrokes, which measured 136,857,600 keystrokes from 168,960 volunteers. It reports a mean of 51.56 WPM (SD 20.2), a mean uncorrected error rate of 1.17%, and a mean keystrokes-per-character rate of 1.173. Those are the numbers this page's bands are checked against.
The claim that finger consistency and keypress preparation predict speed — more than which finger presses which key — comes from Feit, Weir and Oulasvirta, CHI 2016, a motion-capture study of 36 typists. The two studies disagree on how much formal touch-typing training matters, and this page says so where it matters rather than picking the tidier result.
Where a figure is an estimate rather than a measurement — job requirements, age bands, exam cut-offs — it is drawn from the ranges employers and exam boards publish and is labelled as an estimate. Nothing on this page is a benchmark we ran ourselves.
Last updated 2026-10-20. Written and maintained by the Typing.Rerivo team; scoring formulas, sources and corrections policy are documented on the about page.
## Typing test FAQ
CPM stands for characters per minute - the number of correct characters you type in one minute, counting letters, numbers, spaces and symbols. It is a finer-grained measure of typing speed than WPM.
Divide CPM by 5, because a word is defined as five characters. So 300 CPM equals 60 WPM and 200 CPM equals 40 WPM. To go the other way, WPM × 5 = CPM.
The average adult types about 200 CPM (40 WPM). A good CPM is 250–300 (50–60 WPM), and 400+ CPM (80+ WPM) is fast. Numeric data-entry roles often require at least 165 CPM.
Numeric data entry is done on the number keypad where whole words do not apply, so speed is measured in characters (or keystrokes) per minute. Employers commonly ask for at least 165 CPM with 95%+ accuracy.
Neither is better - they measure the same thing on different scales (CPM = WPM × 5). WPM is the standard for prose typing; CPM is more common for numeric and data-entry work.
Yes. The headline CPM is a net figure with errors deducted, so it matches what an employer measures. Your raw keystroke rate is shown separately, and the gap between the two tells you whether to push speed or accuracy.
It is the same one-minute test reported in different units. CPM counts every correct character; WPM divides that count by five and by the elapsed minutes. A 300 CPM result equals 60 WPM, so neither number is more accurate - only differently scaled.

## Typing Practice for Programmers
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-practice-for-programmers.html

Programmers type a lot of symbols, brackets and camelCase &mdash; the exact characters most typing tests skip. Most developers type 50&ndash;70 WPM on prose, but what really matters is fluent symbols and a low error rate. Practise the way you code: paste your own code with custom text, or drill punctuation and numbers below.

A good typing speed for a programmer is 50-70 WPM, but coding is not a typing race - you spend far more time thinking than typing. Speed matters where it removes friction: the faster your fingers find brackets, operators and names, the less a thought is interrupted on its way to the screen. Accuracy matters even more, because a mistyped symbol is a syntax error you have to hunt down. For why that friction compounds across a whole codebase, see programmer typing speed.
Code is dense with characters that ordinary typing practice never covers - brackets, semicolons, operators, and numbers - plus naming styles like camelCase and snake_case that break your rhythm. The fix is to practise those specific characters, not more prose.
What you type in code | Why it is slow | Practise it here
Brackets & symbols () {} [] ; = > | Rare in word tests; awkward reaches for the pinkies | Punctuation test
Numbers & operators | Top row and keypad use different muscle memory | Number test
Your real code | camelCase, indentation and your stack&rsquo;s idioms | Custom text
Paste a real file you work in using custom text and type it for accuracy, not speed. Spend a few minutes on the punctuation and number drills so symbol reaches become automatic. Keep your fingers on the home row and let the weak pinkies own the bracket and semicolon keys. Ten focused minutes a day beats one long session.

## How to Type Without Looking at the Keyboard
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/how-to-type-without-looking.html

To type without looking, rest your fingers on the home row &mdash; left hand on ASDF, right hand on JKL; &mdash; feel the small bumps on F and J, and let each finger own its own keys. The skill is called touch typing, and it comes from short daily practice, not talent. Here is exactly how to build it, then test yourself below.

You look because you do not know where the key is. Fix: the on-screen keyboard and home-row drills, with the guide visible.
You know the key but look anyway to confirm. Fix: covered rounds. This is the stage that lasts longest, and the only cure is typing with the hands hidden.
You look when you make a mistake. Fix: finish the word before checking. Most "looks" happen after errors, not before them.
Most people are stuck in stage two and believe they are in stage one. The test is simple: type a sentence with your hands under a cloth. If accuracy collapses, you are in stage two and the fix is covered practice, not more key drills.
Each glance costs an eye movement, a re-focus and a re-orientation - roughly a quarter of a second, plus the risk of losing your place in the text. At one glance per word, that is 15-25 seconds of lost typing per minute.
It also prevents the mental map from forming. The map is built by reaching for a key and being right, which is exactly what looking replaces with a visual shortcut.
Days 1-3: one covered round a day, 30 seconds long, no target. Just get through it. Days 4-7: two covered rounds, 60 seconds. Days 8-11: covered rounds on the words you miss most, then a normal round to compare. Days 12-14: one covered round per session, permanently.
Expect accuracy to fall by 10-20% during the covered rounds. It recovers within a week and the resulting speed is higher than where you started, because the glance was the ceiling.
If a particular key keeps failing, practise that key in isolation for thirty seconds, then return to text. If the whole round collapses, shorten it - a 15-second covered round you finish beats a 60-second one you abandon.
And keep one normal round per session. The goal is to type without looking, not to type under a cloth forever.
## Typing test FAQ
Two to four weeks of covered rounds, at 30-60 seconds a day. Accuracy dips 10-20% for the first week before recovering above where you started.
That is the confirmation habit, and it is the longest stage. Key drills do not fix it; only typing with the hands hidden does.
Yes for the covered rounds - a cloth or a sheet of paper. Partial covering lets you cheat by peeking, which keeps the habit alive.
No. Accuracy drops for about a week, then speed rises above your previous ceiling because the glance was the limiting factor.
Shorten the round and read one word ahead rather than one line ahead. Losing place is usually a reading-ahead problem, not a typing problem.

## Colemak Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/colemak-typing.html

Practice and measure your typing in Colemak. The on-screen keyboard below is already set to the Colemak layout, with finger guidance mapped to Colemak hand positions, so what you see matches what your system layout produces. Use the QWERTY / Dvorak / Colemak switch in the keyboard toolbar any time. Switch your operating system to Colemak, take the test, and get WPM, accuracy and consistency.

Most typing tests only draw a QWERTY keyboard, which is useless for Colemak typing practice: the label you are hunting for is not on the key you press. This test flips the on-screen keyboard to the Colemak layout, keeping the physical QWERTY key positions and relabelling every key, so the finger guide on screen matches exactly what a Colemak typist sees.
Nothing is installed and nothing changes your system. The page only draws the Colemak keyboard; you switch your operating system input to Colemak, start typing, and the test scores the characters your layout produces - so your WPM, accuracy, consistency and the per-key heatmap are all measured for real Colemak typing.
Colemak was published in 2006 as a middle path between QWERTY and Dvorak. It keeps the common shortcut keys Z, X, C and V in their QWERTY places and changes only 17 keys, so the switch is far gentler than Dvorak while still putting the most-used letters under your fingers.
On the same English passage, Colemak keeps about 73% of letters on the home row (QWERTY is near 36%) and cuts repeated same-finger presses to roughly 1.5%, versus about 7.9% on QWERTY. Less finger travel usually means more comfort over long sessions; it does not guarantee a higher top speed, which still depends mostly on practice.
Set your operating system input to Colemak first, otherwise you would be typing QWERTY characters while looking at a Colemak keyboard. Start with short two-to-five minute sessions and resist looking at your hands - the finger guide and on-screen keyboard exist to replace that habit.
Expect your speed to drop well below your QWERTY speed for the first week or two; that is the switch cost, not a verdict on Colemak. Track accuracy here before speed, because accuracy recovers first and speed follows it. Compare Colemak with Dvorak and QWERTY on the keyboard layouts page.
