## Keyboard Layouts Compared
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/keyboard-layouts.html

QWERTY, Dvorak, Colemak and Workman compared on home-row use, finger travel and same-finger presses &mdash; so you can see which keyboard layout fits you before you commit weeks to switching. Try any of them on the test below with a layout-matched on-screen keyboard and finger guide.

A keyboard layout is just the map of which letter sits under each key. QWERTY has been the default since the 1870s, but alternative layouts rearrange the letters so the most common ones sit on the home row, cutting finger travel. Here is how the four best-known layouts compare on the same English text.
Layout | Introduced | Finger travel* | Home-row use | Same-finger
QWERTY | 1870s | 153 m (baseline) | 36% | 7.9%
Dvorak | 1936 | 88 m (&minus;42%) | 71% | 3.2%
Colemak | 2006 | 89 m (&minus;42%) | 73% | 1.5%
Workman | 2010 | 84 m (&minus;45%) | 67% | 2.0%
Home-row share and same-finger figures below are modelled from a fixed English passage. For the documented history and design intent of each layout, see keyboard layout, Dvorak keyboard layout (patented 1936) and Colemak (released 2006, 74% of typing on the home row against 32% for QWERTY).
There is no single best layout, because less finger movement is not the same as faster typing. QWERTY wins on familiarity: it is on every shared computer and every shortcut assumes it. Dvorak alternates hands the most (about 67% of keystrokes), which many typists find rhythmic for long English prose. Colemak keeps the most letters on the home row (73%) and the fewest awkward same-finger presses (1.5%) while leaving Z, X, C, V and most shortcuts in place, so it is the usual pick for QWERTY users who want to switch. Workman trims total finger travel the most by also minimising sideways stretches.
For almost everyone, practice and accuracy move your WPM far more than the layout does. A fast QWERTY typist will beat a beginner on any layout. Switch for comfort and reduced finger travel, not for a guaranteed speed jump.
Switching costs you one to four weeks of slower, deliberate typing while new muscle memory forms, and shared or public machines will still be QWERTY. The payoff is less finger travel and, for many people, more comfort in long sessions. It is worth it mainly if you type a lot of English every day and own the keyboards you use most.
If you want the gentlest change, start with Colemak because it keeps your common shortcuts. If you love hand-alternation, try Dvorak. The honest answer for casual typists is that staying on QWERTY and practising is the higher-return move.
You can practise two of these layouts right now with a matching on-screen keyboard and finger guide: take the Colemak typing test or the Dvorak typing test, or measure your current speed on QWERTY with the main typing speed test. Each shows WPM, accuracy, consistency and a per-key heatmap so you can compare how a layout feels for you.
Layout decisions: Dvorak vs QWERTY — evidence, retraining cost, and who should switch.
## Keyboard layouts FAQ
No layout is reliably fastest for everyone. Modeling shows Dvorak, Colemak and Workman cut finger travel by roughly 42 to 45% versus QWERTY, but measured typing speed depends far more on practice and accuracy than on the layout. The world's fastest typists use several different layouts, including QWERTY.
Dvorak puts about 71% of letters on the home row versus QWERTY's 36% and alternates hands more, which many typists find more comfortable for long English text. Studies show modest speed gains at best, so the main benefit is reduced finger movement and comfort, not a guaranteed speed jump.
Colemak keeps more letters on the home row (about 73%) and the lowest same-finger rate (about 1.5%), and it changes only 17 keys while keeping Z, X, C and V in their QWERTY places, so it is easier to switch to than Dvorak. Dvorak alternates hands more. Which feels better is personal.
Code uses far more punctuation, brackets and symbols than English prose, so prose-optimised layouts help less. Programmer variants such as Programmer Dvorak and Workman Programmer rearrange the number and symbol rows. Many developers stay on QWERTY because editors, shortcuts and pair-programming all assume it.
Most people reach usable speed again in one to four weeks of short daily practice, and return to their old speed over one to three months. Accuracy recovers before raw speed, so track accuracy first.
Yes. This site has a free Dvorak typing test and a free Colemak typing test, each with an on-screen keyboard relabelled to that layout and a matching finger guide, so you can practise and measure your WPM without installing anything.

## 10 Key Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/ten-key-typing-test.html

A 10 key typing test measures how fast you type on the numeric keypad &mdash; the number pad on the right of a full-size keyboard &mdash; using the fingers of your right hand. It is the standard speed test for data entry, accounting and finance work. Take the timed number-pad test below and get your speed instantly.

10 key typing (also written ten key typing or 10-key) is touch typing on the numeric keypad: the number, arithmetic and Enter keys on the right of a full-size keyboard. Instead of hunting for digits across the top row, a 10 key typist keeps the right hand anchored on 4 5 6 with the index, middle and ring fingers, and reaches every other key from there. It is the skill behind fast data entry, bookkeeping and banking work.
This page runs a numpad typing test in numbers mode, so the practice text is digits, decimals, dates and amounts - exactly the characters a 10 key operator types all day. Switch the Time chips to 15 or 30 seconds for a quick check, or run 3-5 minutes for a stable result.
Rest your index finger on 4, your middle finger on 5 and your ring finger on 6 - these three usually have a raised bump or a dot so you can find them without looking. The index finger also covers 1 and 7, the middle covers 2 and 8, the ring covers 3 and 9, and the little finger handles 0, . and Enter. Your thumb rests on the 0 key on many layouts.
The golden rule of ten key typing is the same as touch typing on the letter keys: eyes on the screen, fingers always returning to 4 5 6 between digits. Speed comes from never looking down.
10 key speed is usually quoted in keystrokes per hour (KPH) or characters per minute (CPM), not words per minute. A comfortable 10 key speed for data entry is about 8,000-10,000 KPH (roughly 130-165 CPM), and strong operators reach 12,000-15,000 KPH with 99%+ accuracy.
Level | 10 key speed
Beginner | 3,000-5,000 KPH
Average | 5,000-8,000 KPH
Data entry ready | 8,000-10,000 KPH
Fast / professional | 12,000-15,000+ KPH
This test reports your characters per minute live; multiply by 60 to get an approximate keystrokes-per-hour figure, or use the dedicated keystrokes per hour test.
The top number row and the numeric keypad use completely different muscle memory. Typing letters fast does not make you fast at the number pad, and many people lose a data entry job interview on the 10 key portion alone. Practising the numpad on its own trains the right hand to hit 0-9 and the decimal point without a single glance at the keyboard.
If you need both, warm up with this 10 key typing test and then check your general speed on the number typing test or the main typing speed test.
Numeric keypad work is usually scored in keystrokes per hour, but the same minute of typing can be read three ways: keystrokes per hour, characters per minute, and the five-character words per minute used by general typing tests. Because digits and operators are single characters, ten key speeds look far higher in KPH than the same effort looks in WPM - convert before comparing yourself with anyone quoting a different unit.
## 10 key typing FAQ
A 10 key typing test measures how quickly you type on the numeric keypad (the number pad on the right of a full-size keyboard) using your right hand, keeping the fingers anchored on the 4, 5 and 6 keys.
For data entry work, aim for at least 8,000 keystrokes per hour (about 133 characters per minute). Experienced operators reach 12,000 to 15,000 KPH with 99% accuracy or better.
It is touch typing applied to the numeric keypad. You keep your eyes on the screen, rest the fingers on 4 5 6, and let each finger own its column of digits.
Practise a few minutes a day with your eyes off the keyboard, keep the index, middle and ring fingers on 4, 5 and 6, and prioritise accuracy - errors cost more time than a slightly slower but clean run.
On laptops with no dedicated keypad you can use an external USB numeric keypad, or practise the digits with the number-typing mode instead, which uses the top number row.

## Data Entry Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/data-entry-typing-test.html

A data entry typing test checks the two things employers screen for: typing speed and accuracy. Data entry roles typically ask for 50&ndash;70 WPM (or 8,000&ndash;10,000 keystrokes per hour) with 97&ndash;99% accuracy. Take the timed test below and see where you stand.

Data entry and clerical jobs usually expect 50-70 WPM with 97%+ accuracy. Numeric-heavy roles are often measured in keystrokes per hour instead, where the bar is about 8,000-10,000 KPH. Some employers use a 10 key (numeric keypad) test rather than a text passage.
Metric | Typical data entry requirement
Typing speed | 50-70 WPM
Accuracy | 97-99%
Numeric (10 key) | 8,000-10,000 KPH
Test length | 1-5 minutes
Benchmarks reflect commonly published data entry job requirements; actual figures vary by employer.
In data entry, a wrong digit is worse than a slow one, so most employers score net speed - your speed after errors are subtracted - and many set a hard accuracy floor. Practise typing clean the first time rather than relying on backspace, and let speed rise on its own as the keystrokes become automatic.
Take the test at the length the employer uses. Most screening tests run 1 to 5 minutes, so warm up with a 1 minute test and then do a 3 minute or 5 minute run.
Practise with real text that includes numbers, punctuation and capitals, because that is what the passage will contain - not a clean word list. If the role is numeric, train the number pad separately with the 10 key typing test. Sit comfortably, keep your fingers on the home row, and do two or three warm-up runs before your scored attempt so you are at your normal speed.
Every result here is saved in your browser, so you can watch both WPM and accuracy improve over the days before an interview. Your history is private and stays on your device.
Most data-entry postings quote 8,000–12,000 keystrokes per hour with ~98% accuracy — about 27–40 WPM — and professional numeric roles can reach 12,000–15,000 KPH. For the full requirements table across every scenario, see typing speed requirements by job and exam.

## Data entry typing FAQ

Aim for 97% to 99% accuracy. Many employers score net speed (errors subtracted) and set a minimum accuracy threshold, so a clean 60 WPM beats a sloppy 75 WPM.
Employer screening tests are usually 1 to 5 minutes. Practise at 3 minutes for a balanced check, and use shorter runs to warm up.
Many do. Roles that are mostly numeric use a numeric keypad (10 key) test measured in keystrokes per hour, while text-heavy roles use a words-per-minute passage.

## Keystrokes Per Hour Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/keystrokes-per-hour-test.html

A keystrokes per hour (KPH) test measures typing speed the way many data entry employers do &mdash; in keystrokes over an hour, not words per minute. Data entry roles commonly require 8,000&ndash;10,000 KPH. Type the passage below and convert your result to KPH instantly.

On this page
What is keystrokes per hour?
KPH vs WPM vs CPM
What KPH do data entry jobs require?
How do KPH requirements convert to WPM?
Where KPH scores lead
Sources for the numbers on this page
Keystrokes, characters and words are three units
What is the average keystrokes per hour?
8,000 key depressions per hour in WPM
Key depression and keystroke are not always the same thing
Keystrokes per hour (KPH or KSPH) counts how many individual key presses you make in an hour, counting every character including spaces. It is the standard measure for data entry and numeric keypad work because it does not depend on how long the words happen to be. A fast data entry operator reaches 10,000-15,000 KPH.
If you know your characters per minute (CPM), multiply by 60 to get KPH: a steady 160 CPM equals 9,600 KPH. This test shows your characters per minute live, so you can read your KPH straight off the result.
All three describe the same typing, just at different scales. WPM counts words (5 characters each) per minute; CPM counts characters per minute; KPH counts keystrokes per hour. Because a &lsquo;word&rsquo; is standardised as 5 characters, the conversions are fixed:
Your speed | WPM | CPM | KPH
Average | 40 | 200 | 12,000
Good | 60 | 300 | 18,000
Fast | 80 | 400 | 24,000
Elite | 100 | 500 | 30,000
The table assumes no error penalty; employers usually apply a net-accuracy penalty, so your effective KPH is lower than the raw figure.
Job postings for data entry and clerical work often ask for 8,000-10,000 KPH with a high accuracy rate; some set the bar at 12,000 KPH. Numeric roles may test the number pad specifically, so pair this test with the 10 key typing test. Measure your text speed here and your WPM on the words per minute test, then check the requirements in the typing test for jobs page.
Divide by 300: WPM = KPH ÷ 300, so a 10,000 KPH posting is asking for about 33 WPM. For the complete table of KPH, CPM and WPM requirements by job and exam, see typing speed requirements by job and exam.
Put your KPH to work: online typing jobs that quote KPH, and data entry job requirements by the numbers.
Speed and accuracy figures quoted here follow the largest published study of everyday typing: Dhakal et al., CHI 2018, Observations on Typing from 136 Million Keystrokes, which measured 136,857,600 keystrokes from 168,960 volunteers. It reports a mean of 51.56 WPM (SD 20.2), a mean uncorrected error rate of 1.17%, and a mean keystrokes-per-character rate of 1.173. Those are the numbers this page's bands are checked against.
The claim that finger consistency and keypress preparation predict speed — more than which finger presses which key — comes from Feit, Weir and Oulasvirta, CHI 2016, a motion-capture study of 36 typists. The two studies disagree on how much formal touch-typing training matters, and this page says so where it matters rather than picking the tidier result.
Where a figure is an estimate rather than a measurement — job requirements, age bands, exam cut-offs — it is drawn from the ranges employers and exam boards publish and is labelled as an estimate. Nothing on this page is a benchmark we ran ourselves.
Numeric keypad work is usually scored in keystrokes per hour, but the same minute of typing can be read three ways: keystrokes per hour, characters per minute, and the five-character words per minute used by general typing tests. Because digits and operators are single characters, ten key speeds look far higher in KPH than the same effort looks in WPM - convert before comparing yourself with anyone quoting a different unit.
Around 12,000 KPH is the middle of the working population, because that is what 40 WPM produces and 40 WPM is close to the median office speed. The bands below convert the WPM distribution into keystrokes per hour using KPH = WPM × 300.
Keystrokes per hour | WPM equivalent | Reading
6,000 | 20 | Beginner; hunt-and-peck
9,000 | 30 | Below average, workable for simple entry
12,000 | 40 | The common data-entry floor and close to the median
15,000 | 50 | Above average; comfortable for full-time entry
18,000 | 60 | Fast; upper band for entry work
24,000 | 80 | Top decile; numeric-heavy roles
The distribution behind those WPM figures is the CHI 2018 sample (mean 51.56 WPM, SD 20.2, n = 168,960), summarised on the benchmarks page. The conversion is arithmetic, so the uncertainties are in the WPM band, not in the multiplication.
8,000 KPDH ÷ 300 = 26.7 WPM (or 133 keystrokes per minute). That is the figure Indian SSC DEO posts use, and it is deliberately modest because the scoring counts every keypress - including backspaces.
That distinction is the whole difficulty. In a keystroke-per-hour test, a correction is another keystroke against your hour, so a typist who produces 35 WPM but backspaces constantly can score below someone at 30 WPM who types it right first time. If you are preparing for a KPDH test, practise without correcting: alphanumeric drills are the closest format.
Key depressions per hour | WPM (÷300) | Keystrokes per minute
6,000 | 20.0 | 100
8,000 | 26.7 | 133
10,000 | 33.3 | 167
12,000 | 40.0 | 200
A keystroke in this site's measurement means a character typed correctly. A key depression in examination scoring means any key pressed down, including Shift, Tab, Enter and backspace. The two numbers differ most for typists who correct a lot.
So when a posting says "8,000 key depressions per hour", assume it counts everything, and treat your KPH score from this page as an optimistic version of it. When a posting says "keystrokes per hour" without qualification, ask - the difference is worth several WPM.

## Typing Speed Calculator
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-speed-calculator.html

This typing speed calculator tells you how your typing speed converts between WPM (words per minute), CPM (characters per minute) and KPH (keystrokes per hour). Measure your real speed with the test below, then use the formulas and table to convert any figure. Everything runs in your browser.

Enter the characters you typed, the errors you left uncorrected, and the seconds elapsed. The calculator returns gross WPM, net WPM, CPM, keystrokes per hour and the approximate percentile of the net score.
The percentile uses a normal approximation of the CHI 2018 distribution (mean 51.56 WPM, SD 20.2). It is an approximation - real typing speed is mildly left-skewed - and it reproduces the study's reported deciles to within about one point. The percentile page has the full curve.
Typing speed in words per minute (WPM) is worked out with one simple formula: WPM = (characters typed ÷ 5) ÷ minutes. Every five characters count as one &lsquo;word&rsquo;, so longer words are worth more. Net WPM subtracts your errors first: net WPM = ((correct characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes). Employers use net WPM, because a mistake you have to fix costs time.
To get your own numbers, just take the timed test above - it computes WPM, raw WPM, CPM and accuracy for you, so you can read your result straight off the scoreboard.
The three common typing-speed units are all fixed multiples of each other, so you can convert any of them by hand:
From | To | Formula
CPM | WPM | WPM = CPM ÷ 5
WPM | CPM | CPM = WPM × 5
CPM | KPH | KPH = CPM × 60
WPM | KPH | KPH = WPM × 300
WPM | | WPM = (characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes
So 60 WPM = 300 CPM = 18,000 KPH. These are the standard conversions used by typing certificates and data entry employers.
If you type 300 characters in 1 minute, that is 300 ÷ 5 = 60 WPM (or 18,000 KPH). If you type 1,200 characters in 3 minutes, that is (1,200 ÷ 5) ÷ 3 = 80 WPM. If you make 12 mistakes over that run, your net speed is (1,200 &minus; 12) ÷ 5 ÷ 3 = 79 WPM.
Want the measured number instead of the maths? Run the words per minute test for WPM, the CPM typing test for characters per minute, or the keystrokes per hour test for KPH.

Divide characters per minute by 5. So 250 CPM is 50 WPM, and 400 CPM is 80 WPM.

Gross WPM counts every character you typed; net WPM subtracts your errors first. Employers almost always use net WPM because it reflects usable output.

## Quick Brown Fox Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/quick-brown-fox-typing-test.html

The &lsquo;the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog&rsquo; sentence is the most famous pangram in typing practice &mdash; a sentence that contains every letter of the alphabet. Typing it is the traditional warm-up and a quick way to check that every key on your keyboard works. Take the test below and measure your speed and accuracy.

&lsquo;The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog&rsquo; is a pangram: a sentence that uses all 26 letters of the alphabet at least once. Because it covers the whole keyboard it has been the standard typing drill for over a century, and it is still used to test typewriters, keyboards and fonts. Practising it warms up every finger before a longer typing test.
Type it a few times here - the test scrolls through alphabet-rich sentences in the same spirit, so your warm-up trains every letter rather than only the common ones.
Ordinary sentences repeat the same handful of common letters and rarely touch q, z, x or j. A pangram forces every key into the run, which is exactly what you need before a speed attempt: it surfaces the awkward keys while the stakes are low. That is why &lsquo;quick brown fox&rsquo; games appear in almost every typing tutor and school typing class.
For a targeted version, the keyboard typing test highlights the next key and the correct finger, and the easy typing test uses simple high-frequency words if the pangram still feels hard.
Because the pangram contains every letter, typing it is the fastest way to confirm that no key is broken or stuck: if a letter is missing from the output, that key is faulty. Try it with capitals and punctuation too - &lsquo;The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.&rsquo; - to exercise the shift keys and the full stop. Then move on to a full typing speed test to get your WPM.
## Quick brown fox FAQ

Because it uses all 26 letters, it exercises every key and finger in one short line, making it an ideal warm-up and a fast way to check that your keyboard works.

## Home Row Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/home-row-typing-test.html

The home row is the row of keys your fingers rest on &mdash; A S D F for the left hand and J K L ; for the right. Every key on the keyboard is reached from here, which is why home-row practice is the first lesson in touch typing. Take the timed test below to drill the home row and track your progress.

The home row (also called the home keys) is the middle row of the keyboard where your fingers rest between keystrokes: A S D F for the left hand and J K L ; for the right hand. The F and J keys have small raised bumps so your index fingers can find home by feel alone, without looking down.
Home-row typing is the foundation of touch typing. Each finger owns a column of keys and always returns to its home key, so the hand never has to hunt for a letter. Start by typing only home-row letters until they feel automatic, then add the rows above and below.
Home key | Finger | Also reaches
A | Left pinky | Q, Z, 1
S | Left ring | W, X, 2
D | Left middle | E, C, 3
F | Left index | R, T, G, V, B, 4, 5
J | Right index | Y, U, H, N, M, 6, 7
K | Right middle | I, comma, 8
L | Right ring | O, full stop, 9
; | Right pinky | P, slash, 0
The thumbs rest on the space bar. Keeping this assignment is what lets you type without looking - see the full method on how to type without looking.
Effective home-row practice repeats the eight home keys in short, varied bursts rather than long paragraphs, so your fingers build the exact movements they need. Run this test for 1 or 2 minutes a day, aiming first for perfect accuracy and only then for speed. When the home row feels natural, move on to the touch typing test and the keyboard typing test, which introduce the surrounding rows with an on-screen finger guide.
Placement done right: proper hand position for typing and the typing finger chart.
## Home row FAQ
A, S, D, F for the left hand and J, K, L, ; for the right hand, with the thumbs on the space bar. F and J have raised bumps so you can find the row without looking.
It is the base position of touch typing. Every key is reached from home and the fingers return there, so you never have to look down to find a letter.
Left hand: pinky on A, ring on S, middle on D, index on F. Right hand: index on J, middle on K, ring on L, pinky on ;.
Most people feel comfortable within a few days of short daily practice, but full touch typing across all rows takes a few weeks of consistent practice.
No. Keep your eyes on the screen and use the F and J bumps to find home. Looking down slows the muscle memory you are trying to build.

## Typing Test for Adults
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-adults.html

This typing test for adults is built for grown-ups who want a quick, no-nonsense check of their typing speed and accuracy &mdash; no lessons, no cartoon mascots, no account. The average adult types around 40 WPM; take the test below and see where you land.

On this page
What is a good typing speed for an adult?
You can still learn to type faster as an adult
How to use this test as an adult
Why adults usually start below where they could be
Reasons adults actually have for improving
What to expect in the first month
The average adult typing speed is about 40 WPM. Reaching 60 WPM puts you comfortably above average and is enough for most office work; 80 WPM is fast, and 100 WPM+ is top-tier. Age or when you learned to type matter far less than how much you practise.
Adult typing level | WPM
Below average | under 35
Average | 40-50
Good (office standard) | 60-80
Fast | 80-100
Elite (top ~1%) | 100+
These bands come from published typing-speed studies; see the full average typing speed breakdown by age and profession.
It is a common myth that only children can build typing speed. Adults usually improve faster than children because they follow instructions, understand why accuracy comes before speed and can practise deliberately. The catch is unlearning years of two-finger habit: the fix is to slow down, keep the fingers on the home row, and look at the screen instead of the keyboard.
Ten to fifteen minutes a day is enough. Start with the home row typing test, then the touch typing test, and only push for raw speed once your accuracy is steady.
Decide what you need. For a job application, run a 1-3 minute test and check the requirement table in the typing test for jobs. For everyday comfort, test once a day at 1 minute and watch the trend in your saved history. For data entry or accounting work, add the 10 key typing test. Your results are stored only in your browser, so nothing is uploaded.
Almost every adult who types slowly learned by using a computer, not by being taught. That means the habits formed were whatever got the work done: two fingers, looking at the keyboard, backspacing through errors. None of those are permanent, but all of them are invisible until you try to type without looking.
The encouraging part is that adults learn the key map faster than children do - you already read and write fluently, so the bottleneck is motor habit rather than language. Two weeks of covered rounds typically produces the first real jump.
A job requirement - clerical, reception, dispatch, legal and medical support postings quote 40-60 WPM and often test it.
A return to work - the test is usually a five-minute sample with an accuracy floor, not a race.
Career change into admin or support - the typing bar is modest but the accuracy expectation is not.
Writing volume - reports, emails and documentation that used to be someone else's job.
Comfort - less hunting means less wrist and shoulder tension by the end of a day.
Week 1 is slower and frustrating: you are replacing a working habit. Weeks 2-3 bring accuracy up and speed back to where it started. Week 4 usually produces the first measurable gain, often 5-8 WPM, mostly from no longer looking down.
If you are over 50, add one thing: a five-minute break every half hour during practice, and stop at the first sign of hand or wrist discomfort. The skill builds fine at that pace; strain does not.

## Typing Test for Students
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-students.html

This typing test for students measures your WPM and accuracy in one minute and shows how you compare with other students. Typing quickly and accurately saves time on essays, notes and online exams &mdash; and many courses and jobs now expect 40&ndash;60 WPM.

On this page
What typing speed should a student have?
Why students should type faster
How to practise as a student
Where students actually lose time
Exam and coursework contexts worth rehearsing
A term-long plan that fits around coursework
Most students type between 30 and 50 WPM, and schools increasingly expect 40-60 WPM by the end of secondary school so that typing stops being a bottleneck for essays and exams. College students and anyone writing long assignments benefit most from reaching 60 WPM+.
Stage | Typical / target WPM
Primary / elementary | 15-30
Middle school | 30-40
High school | 40-60
College / university | 60+
Targets vary by school and country; the bands above reflect commonly published guidance. See the full average typing speed table for more detail.
Typing speed is study efficiency. At 60 WPM you can keep up with a lecturer in real time, transcribe notes without falling behind, and finish essays in less time while staying in flow. For out-of-class and online exams, slow typing can cost marks simply because you run out of time - not because you do not know the answer.
If you type with two fingers, the ceiling is low. Learning touch typing is a one-time investment: practise the home row, then the touch typing test, and your speed will follow.
Ten minutes a day beats an hour once a week. Warm up with a short drill, take a 1-minute test to record your WPM, then spend the rest of the time on whichever is weaker - speed on the typing practice page, or precision with the typing accuracy test. Every result is saved in your browser so you can chart your progress before an exam or application.
Not in essays. Students lose time in the small, repeated typing tasks: searching a database for a citation, writing lab notes, replying to a seminar email, formatting a bibliography by hand. Each is two minutes of typing, five times a day.
The measurable consequence is that typing speed correlates with how much written work gets finished, not with how good it is. A student at 35 WPM spends roughly twice as long on the same written output as one at 70 WPM, and that gap comes out of reading time.
Context | What is timed | What to rehearse
Timed online exam with typed answers | The whole paper, including thinking | Typing while composing, not copying - practise answering a question in 200 words at pace
In-class laptop notes | Nothing, but you fall behind the lecture | Speed with abbreviations and no backspace; lectures run 130-150 words a minute
Referencing and formatting | Your own patience | Repeat the same citation ten times rather than ten citations once
Language or typing exam (e.g. SSC, school boards) | A fixed passage at a fixed speed | The exact format: length, punctuation, error allowance
Ten minutes, four days a week, for twelve weeks. Weeks 1-4: home row and covered rounds - this is the only part that feels like a step backwards. Weeks 5-8: accuracy at speed, 30-second sprints plus one slow round. Weeks 9-12: real material - lecture notes, your own essay paragraphs, a citation style you actually use.
Do not practise on random word lists in week 9. By then the constraint is your vocabulary and your punctuation habits, and those only appear in your own subject's text.

## Typing Skill Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-skill-test.html

A typing skill test tells you how good you are at typing: your words per minute (WPM), your accuracy and your error rate, combined into one clear picture of your typing skill level. It is the same kind of test used for job applications and typing exams. Take it below and get your score instantly.

Three figures, not one. Net speed is the number employers quote. Accuracy is what they weight when the job involves records, codes or names. Consistency - how much your speed varies second to second - predicts whether the speed survives a five-minute test.
A single WPM number hides all of that. Two typists at 60 WPM can be a careful 99% accuracy operator and a 91% risky one, and the second is a liability in any role where a wrong digit matters.
Band | Net WPM | Accuracy | What it clears
Entry | 25-35 | 92-95% | Some dispatch and call-centre floors; personal use
Clerical | 35-45 | 95-97% | Data entry at 8,000-12,000 KPH; county clerk roles
Office standard | 45-55 | 97% | Reception, admin, general office postings
Fast | 55-70 | 98% | Legal secretary, medical admin, transcription entry
Professional | 70-85 | 98-99% | Transcription upper band, dispatch supervisor, court support
These bands come from advertised requirements, not from a certification body - no one certifies a typing skill level. They are useful because they match the numbers employers actually print.
Use a five-minute round on sentences, in one sitting, at the same time of day each time. Then repeat it on a second day before you believe the number: single-round scores move by 5-10 WPM for reasons that have nothing to do with skill.
If you only ever test on one-minute rounds, you are measuring your burst, not your skill. Five minutes is long enough for the warm-up advantage to fade and short enough to repeat weekly.
Most screen against a floor - 40 WPM is the common one - and then watch the work sample. A few use a platform test with a cut score, and public-sector roles often require a proctored result.
In practice the accuracy figure decides more outcomes than the speed figure, because it is the one that predicts rework. If you are choosing which number to improve, improve accuracy first: it is faster to move and it is what the job punishes.
Speed low? Work the habit ceiling - covered rounds and no-backspace rounds (see the plateau guide).
Accuracy low? Slow to 85% of your pace for two weeks and refuse to correct during rounds; the error list, not the score, is the thing to read.
Consistency low? Type ten rounds and look at the spread. Slow-hold rounds narrow it faster than any speed drill - the consistency page has the method.
## Typing skill test FAQ
A timed test that reports net speed, accuracy and often consistency, rather than a single WPM figure. It is meant to show what you can sustain, not your best burst.
45-55 WPM at 97% accuracy clears most office requirements. 55-70 at 98% opens legal, medical and transcription entry roles; above 70 with high accuracy is professional territory.
Five minutes on sentences, repeated on a second day. A one-minute round measures a burst, and a single round moves 5-10 WPM for reasons unrelated to skill.
For most jobs, yes. Accuracy predicts rework, and the roles that quote speed also quote an accuracy floor - typically 95-98%.
No universal one. Public-sector exams and some agencies issue certificates for their own requirements, but no body certifies a general typing skill level.

## Government Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/government-typing-test.html

Many government and clerical job applications include a typing test &mdash; usually 30&ndash;40 WPM for entry-level posts and higher for clerical and data roles, with strict accuracy requirements. Practise the timed test below and check the levels used by government typing exams. No sign-up, instant results.

Government typing requirements vary by post and country, but the common shape is: a minimum of 30-40 WPM for entry-level administrative roles, and 40-60 WPM with high accuracy for clerical, secretarial and data entry positions. Where the job is mainly data entry, the test may be a numeric one scored in keystrokes per hour instead.
Post type | Typical requirement
Entry / general clerical | 30-40 WPM
Clerical / admin | 40-50 WPM
Secretarial / stenography | 50-70 WPM
Data entry | 8,000-10,000 KPH
Speed is only half of it: government tests usually require 95-98% accuracy, and some subtract errors, so a clean run beats a fast messy one. Requirements differ by department and country - always check the official notification for your exam.
Government typing tests are timed, commonly 3 to 5 minutes, and scored on net speed - the words per minute remaining after errors are deducted. Many use a fixed passage, and some allow no backspace, so typing it correctly the first time is essential. Because the standard is net speed, accuracy training is the fastest route to passing, not raw bursts of speed.
Practise at the exam length. Warm up with a 1 minute test, then run 3 and 5 minutes to build the stamina a scored attempt needs.
Work on accuracy until you can complete a passage cleanly, then raise speed. Train the home row and touch typing so you are not watching your hands, and if the post is data entry, drill the keypad with the 10 key typing test. Test yourself under the same conditions as the exam - same length, no restarts - and check your standing against the average typing speed. Your practice history stays in your browser.
Government clerk and assistant exams usually qualify on a short timed passage around 25–35 WPM with capped errors. For the complete scenario-by-scenario table with conversions, see typing speed requirements by job and exam. For country-specific exam formats such as SSC, IBPS and court clerk tests, see the government jobs typing test guide.
## Government typing test FAQ
Entry-level government and clerical roles commonly require 30 to 40 WPM, while clerical, secretarial and data roles ask for 40 to 70 WPM with high accuracy. Check the official notification for your specific exam.
Government typing tests are typically 3 to 5 minutes long and are scored on net words per minute after errors are deducted.
Yes. Most government tests require 95% to 98% accuracy, and many subtract errors from your score, so accuracy matters as much as speed.
Data entry posts often use a numeric keypad (10 key) test scored in keystrokes per hour, while general clerical posts use a text passage measured in words per minute.
Practise at the exam length, prioritise accuracy over raw speed, learn to touch type so you do not look at the keyboard, and train the number pad if the post is data entry.

## Paragraph Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/paragraph-typing-test.html

Practise with full paragraphs instead of single words — the format real typing exams and job tests use.

A word-list test (the monkeytype style) shows one word at a time and rewards raw reaction. A paragraph test shows continuous prose, so it also measures reading ahead, punctuation, capitals, and the ability to hold a rhythm across sentences.
Employers test with paragraphs because that is what the job looks like: continuous text with full stops, names, commas and the occasional number. A word-list score is a training metric; a paragraph score is a work metric.
Three reasons. Punctuation and capitals add keystrokes that a word list omits. Sentence structure means the next word is predictable, but only if you read ahead - which most typists do not. And length means fatigue enters: errors in the fourth minute are usually attention, not technique.
The result is a score typically 5-15% lower than the same typist's word-list number, and 5-10 WPM lower than a one-minute burst on the same text.
Length | What it measures | Use it when
1 minute | Burst speed | Daily warm-up, quick comparison
3 minutes | Common screening length | Interview practice, exam rehearsal
5 minutes | Working pace | The number you quote; matches most job standards
10 minutes | Endurance | Transcription, data entry, long document work
Start with one minute to warm up, then run a five-minute round and record net WPM plus accuracy. If accuracy is under 96%, stop chasing speed and run accuracy rounds for a week - it is the cheaper fix.
For exam-style practice, use the same length as the exam and include punctuation. For a written job test, add one round of the quotes test, which is the closest thing to real document text. A paragraph score is only useful if you can reproduce it on a second attempt, at a different time of day, on a keyboard you have not warmed up on.
## Paragraph Typing Test FAQ
A test using continuous prose rather than a word list, so it measures reading ahead, punctuation and capitals alongside raw speed.
Punctuation and capitals add keystrokes, sentence structure requires reading ahead, and length introduces fatigue. A 5-15% lower score is normal.
Five minutes for a number you can quote, three minutes to match most screening tests, ten minutes for transcription and data-entry work.
Paragraphs, because that is what the work looks like. Word-list scores are useful for training but they are not what screening tools measure.
Yes. Paragraph, passage and prose tests all mean continuous text; the differences are length and difficulty, not format.

## Beginner Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/beginner-typing-test.html

New to typing? Start here: an easy, forgiving test that measures where you are today so you can watch yourself improve.

On this page
A first test that does not punish you
What a beginner should actually practise
Your first realistic targets
What to do after your first month
Your first week, day by day
Three beginner mistakes worth avoiding
The default round is short, the words are common, and the score is reported with accuracy beside it. A beginner's first number should be a baseline, not a verdict - most untrained adults start at 20-30 WPM with 90-95% accuracy, and that is normal.
If your accuracy is below 85%, the speed number is not meaningful yet. Slow down until errors are rare; the speed will follow within two weeks and it will be a real number rather than a lucky one.
Home row first. asdf jkl; until the fingers return without looking.
No looking down. One covered round a day. This is the single largest gain available at this stage.
No backspace. Finish rounds with mistakes in them. Corrections cost more than errors at beginner speed.
Ten minutes daily. Short and frequent beats a long weekly session, because the skill is motor memory.
Stage | WPM | Accuracy | What it unlocks
First week | 15-25 | 90%+ | Finishing a round without panic
First month | 25-35 | 95% | Comfortable email and messaging
Three months | 35-45 | 96-97% | Entry-level office requirements
Six months | 45-60 | 97%+ | Most clerical job floors
These are typical progressions for someone practising ten minutes a day, not guarantees. The variable that matters is consistency, not talent.
Move to the one-minute test for the classic benchmark, and add the home row test as a weekly check on technique. When you can hold 95% accuracy at 35 WPM, the 40 WPM plan is the next step.
Avoid jumping to hard text or code typing before the map is automatic - it moves the errors rather than removing them.
Day | 10 minutes | What to notice
1 | Find F and J by touch; type the home row slowly | Whether you can return to the home row without looking
2 | Home row words; one 30-second covered round | How much accuracy drops when you cannot see
3 | Top row added; short real words | Which finger reaches wrong first
4 | Bottom row added; one minute of normal text | Whether you are backspacing more than typing
5 | No-backspace round, then a slow accuracy round | How much the corrections were costing you
6-7 | One timed round per day, same length | The size of the gap between your two scores
Practising at the edge of frustration. If accuracy drops below 90%, the session is teaching you to make mistakes. Slow down until it is above 95%.
Chasing WPM in week one. The first two weeks are about the map, not the speed. Speed arrives as a side effect and then keeps arriving.
Switching keyboards or layouts mid-month. Each switch resets the motor learning you just built. Pick one and stay for a month.
The fourth mistake is invisible: practising only when motivated. Ten minutes, four days a week, beats a two-hour session every other Sunday by a wide margin.
## Beginner Typing Test FAQ
20-30 WPM is normal for an untrained adult, with 90-95% accuracy. Reaching 35-45 WPM within three months of daily ten-minute practice is typical.
Accuracy. At beginner speed corrections cost more than errors, and a sloppy fast habit is much harder to undo than a slow careful one.
Four to six weeks to type without looking, and two to four months to reach 60 WPM, assuming ten to fifteen minutes of daily practice.
Yes, no account, no ads inside the typing area, and results stay in your browser.
Yes. It is the anchor every other reach returns to, and skipping it is what produces the two-finger ceiling at 35-40 WPM.
Find F and J by touch, drill the home row, then add the top and bottom rows one at a time, keeping accuracy above 95%. One covered round a day from day two.

## Timed Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/timed-typing-test.html

A ticking clock is the fairest way to measure typing speed. Choose your length and see how many words you can type before the buzzer.

A timed test adds two things a free practice session does not: a fixed end point, and a score you can compare with someone else's. That is why employers use them and why practice rounds so often do not transfer - the pressure is part of the task.
The practical consequence is that you should practise under the same clock. A typist who only practises untimed will underperform by 5-10 WPM the first time a countdown appears.
Duration | What it measures | Typical use
15-30 seconds | Burst speed | Warm-up, key drills
1 minute | Short-form benchmark | Daily check, casual comparison
3 minutes | Screening length | Interview and exam rehearsal
5 minutes | Working pace | The number you quote; federal standard
10 minutes | Endurance | Transcription, data entry, long documents
Short rounds produce errors of haste: a skipped letter, a wrong key under speed. Long rounds produce errors of attention: a dropped capital in minute six, a comma missed when the sentence changes direction.
That is why the same typist can have 98% accuracy on a one-minute test and 94% on a ten-minute one. If your job involves sustained typing, the ten-minute number is the honest one.
Record the same length every week and compare against yourself. The only useful comparison across people is the same duration, the same text type and the same scoring method - change any of the three and the comparison is noise.
For the standard benchmarks by duration, see the WPM chart; for the length most employers use, the five-minute test.
## Timed Typing Test FAQ
A test with a fixed countdown, so the score reflects speed under time pressure rather than open-ended practice.
One minute for casual benchmarking, three minutes for screening and five minutes for formal standards such as the US federal clerical test.
No. The clock runs continuously, which is why corrections cost time and uncorrected errors cost accuracy - you choose which penalty to take.
Yes, from 15 seconds to 10 minutes. Keep the same length when comparing scores across weeks.
Long rounds produce errors of attention rather than haste - a dropped capital in minute six, a missed comma when the sentence turns. That is the fatigue effect the longer test is designed to reveal.

## Fast Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/fast-typing-test.html

Already comfortable on the keyboard? Measure just how fast you really are — and find the ceiling you can push past.

Fast is relative but the bands are stable: 60 WPM is the 66th percentile, 78 WPM starts the top 10%, and 100 WPM is roughly the top 1%. Anything above 60 clears every clerical job requirement; above 80, extra speed is a personal project rather than an employability gain.
Be careful with the word "fast" on a test that runs 60 seconds. A one-minute score reads 5-10 WPM higher than a five-minute score for the same typist, so a "fast" one-minute number can sit at average on a real working test.
Three factors, in order: whether they were ever taught to touch type, how much they type daily, and how they handle errors. Finger strength and keyboard quality matter far less than most people assume.
The error-handling difference is the one people miss. Fast typists let minor slips go in throwaway words and fix the ones that matter; slower typists backspace through both, which costs the time they just gained.
Covered rounds: one a day, hands hidden. Removes the look-down cycle that caps most people at 35-40.
15-second bursts: maximum speed, ten per session, twice a week. Trains the top end you cannot reach in a minute.
Bigram work: the twenty most common letter pairs (th, he, in, er, an, re). Practising transitions moves 50-65 faster than practising words.
Accuracy rounds: 90% of your pace with zero tolerance. The gains compound into the longer tests where numbers actually live.
Run the test in the conditions you will be judged in: same length, same time of day, an unfamiliar keyboard if an interview is coming. Then quote the number you can reproduce, not your best.
If a test shows a sudden 10 WPM jump, check whether the text was unusually easy or the length unusually short before believing it. Most "breakthroughs" are measurement changes.
## Fast Typing Test FAQ
60 WPM is above two thirds of measured typists, 78 WPM is the top 10%, and 100 WPM is about the top 1%. Above 80, no ordinary job asks for more.
The first thirty seconds are warm-up pace you cannot hold. A one-minute test reads 5-10 WPM above a five-minute test for the same typist.
No. Two-finger typing plateaus around 35-40 WPM because each keystroke needs a visual target. Past that, ten fingers and no looking are the requirement.
From 30 to 50 WPM usually takes one to three months of short daily practice; 50 to 70 takes longer; 70 to 90 is typically measured in months to years.
Slightly, for most people - shorter travel and clearer feedback. It is worth 3-8 WPM at best, well behind touch typing and error handling.

## Hard Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/hard-typing-test.html

Easy text hides weak fingers. This hard test adds capitals, symbols and numbers so every part of the keyboard gets a workout.

Four things, in order of impact: mixed capitals (Shift with the opposite hand, every time), digits (extended reaches with no tactile landmark), punctuation (often a two-key combination), and long words (more consecutive keystrokes with no space to reset).
A fifth factor is unfamiliar vocabulary. You cannot predict the next letters of a word you have never seen, so reading slows and the hands wait. That is why technical passages feel harder than their letter count suggests.
On easy text, speed is mostly finger speed. On hard text it is mostly error economy: typists at the same WPM diverge by 10-15% because one group backspaces through every slip and the other lets a throwaway word go.
It also exposes Shift discipline. Watch your accuracy fall on proper nouns and sentence starts: if it drops more than elsewhere, the opposite-hand rule is not yet automatic.
Slow to the pace where errors stay under 2%, and hold it for the full round. A clean 45 on hard text is a better signal than a sloppy 60, because the second number cannot be reproduced on a document that matters.
Do not skip capitals or punctuation to type faster. On every mainstream test an omitted character counts as an error, and in real work - a legal filing, an invoice, an email - it is worse than slow.
Move up when you can hold 97% accuracy on sentences at your target speed. If you are below that, hard text will only teach you to make errors faster.
Use hard mode as a weekly check rather than a daily drill: it is diagnostic, not a routine. The daily work stays on the specific weakness it reveals - digits, capitals, or punctuation. Run the same hard passage twice a month: the score that matters is the second one, because it is the only one you have practised for.
## Hard Typing Test FAQ
A test using text with mixed capitals, digits, punctuation and long or unfamiliar words, so the score reflects accuracy and control rather than speed on easy sentences.
45-55 WPM net with 97% accuracy is strong. Expect 10-20% below your easy-text score; the gap is the measure of how much your speed depends on predictable words.
Each capital needs Shift pressed with the opposite hand plus a quick return to the home row. Untrained typists use one hand for both, which breaks the hand position.
No. Use it weekly as a diagnostic, then spend the daily sessions on the specific weakness it exposes - digits, capitals or punctuation.
Yes. An omitted capital or full stop is an error on every mainstream typing test, and in real documents it is worse than being slow.

## Advanced Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/advanced-typing-test.html

For people who already type well: a demanding passage and honest scoring to see whether you belong in the top percentile.

Advanced starts around 70 WPM net on a five-minute test, which is roughly the 82nd percentile of the largest published sample (mean 51.56, SD 20.2). At 80 WPM you are in the top decile; at 100 WPM, the top 1%.
This page uses longer passages, mixed vocabulary and heavier punctuation so the score reflects sustained control rather than a lucky burst. A one-minute round on easy words will read 8-12 WPM higher than this test, and that difference is the point.
Look-ahead. At 70 WPM you read the word you are typing; at 90 you are two to four words ahead and the hands run on a buffer. This is the single biggest difference and the hardest to train.
Error economy. Advanced typists do not avoid errors, they avoid costly errors. They let a wrong letter go in a throwaway word and fix the ones that matter, instead of backspacing through both.
Consistency. A 90 WPM typist's ten rounds sit within a 5 WPM band; a 70 WPM typist's swing by 15. Narrowing the spread raises the average faster than sprinting raises the peak.
Short maximum-speed bursts: ten rounds of 15 seconds, three times a week. Long rounds teach endurance you already have; bursts train the top end you cannot currently reach.
Hard-text rounds: quotes with punctuation, pangrams, numbers. Speed on plain sentences does not transfer to a document with full stops and capitals, and most real work is the second kind.
One ten-minute round per week, scored on the lowest of three attempts. That number is what an employer would see on a tired afternoon.
Quote net WPM, the test length and the accuracy together: "78 WPM net, 98.5%, ten minutes". A bare number invites the assumption that it came from a fifteen-second sprint on easy words.
Compare like with like. Published averages are five-minute net scores on sentences; a one-minute gross score on random words is not comparable, and neither is a code-typing score, which runs 10-20 WPM lower for the same typist.
Above about 80 WPM, no clerical job asks for more. The returns are personal - competitive typing, live captioning, heavy code work - rather than employability. If your goal is a job, the next 20 WPM are worth less than a certificate and a clean CV line.
If your goal is the score itself, accept the timeline: 70 to 80 is months, 80 to 100 is usually years, and the last ten points are mostly consistency rather than technique.
## Advanced Typing Test FAQ
Around 70 WPM net and above, which is roughly the 82nd percentile. 80 WPM is the top decile and 100 WPM is about the top 1% of measured typists.
The passages are longer with heavier punctuation and mixed vocabulary. A one-minute test on easy words typically reads 8-12 WPM higher for the same typist.
Look-ahead reading, 15-second maximum-speed bursts, and hard-text rounds. Progress is measured by narrowing the spread across ten rounds, not by the best single round.
Yes. No clerical role requires more than about 75-80 WPM. Above that, extra speed matters only for transcription, captioning, competitive typing or heavy coding.
Net, with the test length and accuracy. Gross scores without a stated method read as the flattering version and invite a live re-test that reads lower.

## How Fast Can I Type?
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/how-fast-can-i-type.html

One minute is all it takes to answer the question. Type the passage and get your words per minute and accuracy instantly.

Take the 60-second test on this page and read net WPM from the results panel. That number is your current speed on this text at this length - not a permanent trait, and not directly comparable to a five-minute score.
If you need a number to quote to an employer or on a form, run a five-minute test instead. It reads 5-10 WPM lower and it is the figure that can be reproduced.
Your WPM | Percentile (approx.) | Reading
under 26 | bottom 10% | Hunting for keys; typing is the bottleneck
26-40 | 10th-28th | Two-finger or untrained touch typing
40-52 | 28th-50% | Average adult; enough for most office work
52-65 | 50th-75th | Comfortable all-day typing
65-78 | 75th-90th | Above almost every job requirement
78+ | top 10% | Professional typists, transcribers, developers
Percentiles come from the CHI 2018 sample of 168,960 volunteers (mean 51.56 WPM, SD 20.2), approximated as a normal distribution. The percentile page converts any score exactly.
Length. A 15-second burst reads 5-10 WPM above a five-minute run.
Text. Random words score lower than sentences; code and digits lower again.
Scoring. Gross WPM counts every character; net subtracts errors.
Keyboard. A laptop chiclet board is slower than a mechanical one for most people, and a phone is about 15 WPM slower again.
If you are under 40 WPM, the fastest gain is stopping the look-at-keyboard habit: one covered round a day for two weeks typically adds 5-8 WPM. If you are between 40 and 60, work on accuracy at speed - 30-second sprints at 90% of your maximum, checked every round. Above 60, the limiting factor becomes consistency and look-ahead reading rather than force.
Then re-test at the same length and time of day. Comparing a 9am five-minute score with a midnight one-minute score tells you nothing except that you were tired.
## How Fast Can I Type FAQ
Take the 60-second test on this page and read net WPM. For a number to quote, use a five-minute test - it reads 5-10 WPM lower and is reproducible.
51.56 WPM from the CHI 2018 study of 168,960 volunteers, with a standard deviation of 20.2. Older sources quoting 40 WPM describe office-worker samples instead.
Test length, text type and scoring method all move the result by 5-10 WPM. A 15-second gross score and a five-minute net score are not the same measurement.
You can reach about 35-40 WPM, then it plateaus. Two-finger typing needs a visual target for every keystroke, which caps the speed regardless of practice.
5-8 WPM in two weeks is typical at the start, mostly from removing bad habits. Gains slow above 60 WPM, where months of consistency work replace quick fixes.

## Typing Test for Interview
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-interview.html

Employers often ask you to sit a typing test before or during an interview. Rehearse the exact format here so there are no surprises on the day.

Three formats cover most cases: a short online test sent before the interview (one to three minutes, often automated), a timed exercise on the employer's machine during the visit, and a work sample where typing is incidental to a task such as entering records or drafting a reply.
The first two measure speed and accuracy under a clock. The third measures whether the output is usable, which is why candidates who type fast but sloppily fail work samples even with a good score.
Day | Drill | Goal
1-2 | Three five-minute rounds, same conditions | A baseline you can reproduce
3-4 | Two rounds on an unfamiliar keyboard | Remove the hardware surprise
5 | One timed round with punctuation and capitals | Accuracy under realistic text
6 | One work-sample rehearsal: enter ten records cleanly | Field accuracy, not speed
7 | Rest; one short warm-up only | Fresh hands on the day
Ask which scoring method and length the test uses before you start. Then type at 90% of your best pace for the first thirty seconds - almost everyone loses more in corrections than they gain in the opening sprint.
If the test allows a practice sentence, take it. That is where you discover whether the keyboard has a different layout or a stiff spacebar, and it costs ten seconds.
Quote net WPM, the test length and accuracy: "58 WPM net, 98%, five-minute test". If the interviewer's test then reads 52, the number is consistent; if you had quoted a 15-second burst of 70, it looks like a discrepancy.
For the preparation plans behind those numbers, see the 40 WPM and 60 WPM pages, and the jobs page for role thresholds.
## Interview Typing Test FAQ
It depends on the role: 40 WPM for clerical and reception, 45-55 for data entry and dispatch, 60+ for legal and medical support. The posting usually states the floor.
Net, in almost every case - errors are deducted. Ask before you start if the format is not stated.
Rarely. Most tests run on employer equipment, which is why rehearsing on an unfamiliar keyboard matters more than one more practice round.
Correct it if the correction is quick, otherwise keep going. A single error costs less than thirty seconds of backspacing.
Net WPM, accuracy and test length - "58 WPM net, 98%, five-minute test". It is reproducible, and a live test that reads slightly lower is normal.

## Bank Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/bank-typing-test.html

Banking and clerical exams often include a typing round with a strict accuracy cut-off. Practise the format and the pace here.

Indian bank clerical recruitment commonly quotes 30 words per minute in English or 25 words per minute in Hindi, tested on a standard keyboard for a fixed period, with a small error allowance. Probationary officer and specialist officer posts generally do not include a typing test; clerical and some office-assistant posts do.
These figures appear in recruitment notifications rather than in a single national standard, so the notice for your cycle is the authority. Read it before you practise: the language, layout and error allowance all change between years.
Element | Typical form
Mode | Copy typing from a printed or on-screen passage
Language | English or Hindi, chosen at application
Duration | A fixed period, often around ten minutes
Scoring | Words per minute with an error allowance
Outcome | Qualifying - it does not add marks to the merit list
Because it is qualifying, the strategy is accuracy at a comfortable pace, not maximum speed. A clean 32 WPM passes; a 45 WPM run with 10% errors does not.
Use full-length rounds, not one-minute bursts. The error rate at minute eight is what decides the result, and it is invisible in a short round. Type passages with punctuation and capitals, since the actual passage includes them.
Add a Hindi round if you are taking the Hindi option, on the layout named in your notice - Krutidev, Remington or InScript are not interchangeable, and learning the wrong one creates conflicting reflexes.
Bank clerical requirements are close to SSC CHSL: both ask around 30-35 WPM and both are qualifying. The SSC CHSL page covers the 35/30 WPM and 8000 key-depression split in detail, and the government typing test page covers the general civil-service format.
## Bank Typing Test FAQ
Commonly 30 words per minute in English or 25 in Hindi for clerical posts, with a small error allowance. The recruitment notice for your cycle states the exact figure.
Generally no. Clerical and some office-assistant posts include a qualifying typing test; probationary officer and specialist officer posts usually do not.
Qualifying. It does not add marks to your total, which is why accuracy at a comfortable pace beats a fast, error-heavy run.
Whichever you type faster and more accurately. Hindi requires 25 WPM against 30 for English, but only if you are fluent in the layout your notice specifies.
Full-length rounds of about ten minutes, three times a week, plus five minutes of accuracy work daily. Short bursts do not reveal the errors that appear late in a real test.

## SSC Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/ssc-typing-test.html

SSC typing rounds are a qualifying stage with a strict speed and accuracy bar. Practise the format here before the real thing.

On this page
What the SSC typing test is
The usual requirement
Training for the format
Reaching the pass mark
What typing speed do SSC-type exams require?
Beyond the exam: test-day craft
Several SSC recruitment exams include a typing test as a qualifying round, typically typing a passage in a set time to prove a minimum speed and accuracy. It is often held at a test centre and must be cleared to be considered for the post, no matter how well you did in the written exam.
SSC typing rounds commonly ask for around 35 words per minute in English, or roughly 30 words per minute in Hindi, with high accuracy. Some exams set the bar in a mix of speed and error count, so you must meet both to pass.
The passage is delivered on screen and the clock does not stop, so the goal is steady, error-free typing rather than bursts of speed. Practise with light punctuation and everyday vocabulary — the passages are ordinary prose rather than technical text.
Build your baseline with short daily sessions until you clear the required speed at 95%+ accuracy, then add a minute at a time to build stamina. Our government and bank typing pages cover the same clerical-test family; use them together for a rounded practice routine.
Most SSC-type government exams set a qualifying bar around 30–35 WPM (or the KPH equivalent) with a cap on mistakes, tested as a short timed passage. For the full comparison across data entry, clerk, transcription and office roles — plus the WPM↔CPM↔KPH conversions — see typing speed requirements by job and exam.
Exam-day skills transfer everywhere: how to pass a typing test and typing test tips apply the same accuracy-first strategy.

## Typing Test for Teachers
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-teachers.html

Teachers type constantly — lesson plans, reports, marking, emails. See where your speed sits against what the job demands.

On this page
Why teachers end up typing more than they expected
What speed is actually expected
Running a class typing test without accounts
Grade bands, and why they should not become a test
Ten-minute routines that fit a school day
The admin tasks worth automating first
A teacher's day produces text constantly: lesson plans, differentiated worksheets, parent emails, marking comments, reports. None of it is billed as typing work, and all of it competes for the same hours as preparation and feedback.
That is why the useful question is not "do teachers need to type fast" but "which of these tasks can be made cheap". Marking comments and parent emails are repetitive; lesson plans and feedback are not. Speed helps the first category, templates and text expansion help it more.
No teaching qualification specifies a typing speed. The bands below come from the clerical and administrative side of education - school office, exams office, cover coordination - where postings do quote numbers.
Role | Typical advertised band | What it is based on
Classroom teacher (no formal requirement) | 40+ WPM comfortable | Lesson planning, marking comments, emails
School administrator / exams officer | 45-55 WPM | Clerical postings, data entry of results
Teaching assistant with admin duties | 40-50 WPM | Records, reports, correspondence
Online tutoring (written feedback) | 50+ WPM | Written feedback volume per session
If you are already at 45-50 WPM, typing is not your bottleneck and further speed work will not buy back time. The bigger wins are templates, text expansion and a marking comment bank.
Any tool that requires student accounts creates a data-protection question, which is why this site stores results only in the browser and never server-side. For classroom use that has two practical consequences: no pupil data leaves the device, and results are not visible to you remotely.
The workaround is simple. Pupils take a one-minute test and report the number; you record it on paper or in your own sheet. It takes about three minutes of a lesson and gives you a baseline you can compare in six weeks.
If you want a shared record, the on-screen result can be photographed on the device rather than uploaded anywhere.
Published classroom benchmarks put grade 3 at roughly 10-20 WPM, grade 5 at 25-35 and grade 8 at 35-45, with wide variation by school and by how much keyboarding instruction pupils actually receive.
The risk of quoting these bands to children is that speed becomes the goal. A pupil pushed to 35 WPM with two fingers has hit a ceiling that costs years later; a pupil at 22 WPM with the home row habit will pass them inside a year. Score accuracy first, and only mention speed once the fingers are right.
Starter (3 min): one timed round, accuracy reported before speed.
Drill (5 min): one row or one punctuation set, typed slowly enough to be correct.
Record (2 min): pupil writes the number down. Visible progress is the motivation; a leaderboard is not needed.
Three sessions a week for a term is enough for most classes to move a full grade band, and it costs less curriculum time than a single extended project.
Before chasing speed, look at what you type most often. Parent emails about the same three issues, marking comments that repeat, report phrases that differ by one clause - those are template work, and a template removes the typing entirely rather than making it faster.
Keep the speed work for the genuinely new text: feedback that has to be specific, and plans that have to fit this class. That is where a higher WPM actually converts into time.
## Typing Test for Teachers FAQ

Around 40-50 WPM covers lesson planning, marking comments and parent emails. Above that, the limit is usually thinking and templates rather than keyboard speed.
Yes. Nothing is stored server-side and results stay in the browser on the device, which is why there is no teacher dashboard and no pupil data to protect.
Roughly 15-25 WPM at grade 4-5, with 90%+ accuracy, though bands vary widely by school. Accuracy and home-row habit matter more than the number at that age.
