## Keyboard Practice
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/keyboard-practice.html

Before speed comes familiarity. Practise finding every key without looking and build the habits that make fast typing possible.

On this page
Practice that targets the keyboard, not the text
What to look at, and what not to
Layouts and the keys that move
A ten-minute keyboard session
The keyboard itself changes the exercise
Reading your error report
Most typing practice gives you text and hopes the keyboard sorts itself out. This page inverts it: the on-screen keyboard highlights the next key and the finger that owns it, so the drill is about where the keys are rather than what the sentence says.
That is the right order for a beginner. Learn the map first, then the words. A typist who knows the map can type any text; a typist who has memorised sentences cannot type an unfamiliar word.
Look at the on-screen keyboard for the first few rounds, then at the text, then - eventually - neither. The progression matters: watching the on-screen guide builds the map, watching your hands builds a dependency.
One rule that does most of the work: cover your hands for one round per session. It is uncomfortable for three days and then it stops being an issue, and it is the difference between a ceiling at 40 WPM and no ceiling.
QWERTY - the default on most machines; the layout this page uses.
QWERTZ - German-speaking countries; Y and Z swap, umlauts get their own keys.
AZERTY - France and Belgium; A/Q and Z/W swap, M moves next to L.
Dvorak and Colemak - alternative English layouts that reduce finger travel; see Dvorak vs QWERTY before switching.
If you work across layouts, practise each one separately. Alternating within a session creates interference that slows both.
Two minutes on the home row with the guide visible, two minutes on the row you miss most, three minutes on normal text, and three minutes covered. Log one number at the end - the accuracy figure, not the speed.
That is the whole session. It is short enough to repeat daily, which is the only variable that reliably matters.
A laptop chiclet keyboard has about 1.5 mm of travel and keys 19 mm apart; a mechanical board usually has 3-4 mm and the same spacing. The spacing matters for accuracy - your fingers reach the same distance - while the travel matters for speed and for how forgiving a mistyped key is.
Three practical consequences for practice: on a laptop, your wrists sit lower and the temptation to rest them on the palm rest is stronger; on a full-size board the number pad pushes the mouse further away, which changes shoulder position; and on a compact board without a number pad, the digit row is the only way to type numbers, so the drill is different.
If you practise on one keyboard and are tested on another, spend one session a week on the other one. Key travel and keycap shape change your error rate more than a week of extra drills.
After a session, look at which keys appear most often in the miss list rather than at the score. A cluster on the right hand usually means the reaches to the bracket and apostrophe area; a cluster on the left hand usually means the pinky is not returning to A.
Then drill the cluster, not the whole alphabet. Thirty seconds on five keys beats ten minutes on all of them, because the failure is local and so is the fix.
## Keyboard Practice FAQ
Ten minutes a day: home row with the on-screen guide, then your weakest row, then normal text, then one covered round. Log accuracy rather than speed.
The middle row of letters - A S D F on the left, J K L ; on the right - where your fingers rest between keystrokes. The bumps on F and J let you find it without looking.
At first at the on-screen guide, not your hands. Cover your hands for one round per session so the mental map forms rather than a visual dependency.
Yes, with no account. Results stay in your browser.
For learning, yes - practise the layout you actually use. QWERTY, QWERTZ, AZERTY and alternative layouts move different keys, and mixing them in one session creates interference.
Ten minutes a day: home row with the on-screen guide, then your weakest row, then normal text, then one round with your hands covered. Log accuracy, not speed.
Learn the home row first and cover your hands for one round a day. The look-at-keyboard habit is what caps speed, and preventing it is easier than breaking it later.
Slightly, for most people - shorter travel and clearer feedback are worth roughly 3-8 WPM at best. It will not fix the look-at-keyboard habit, which is the larger constraint.
Yes, and you should if that is what you will be tested on. Laptops have less key travel and a lower wrist position, both of which change your error pattern.

## Japanese Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/japanese-typing-test.html

Test your Japanese typing speed with real Japanese sentences mixing kanji, hiragana and katakana. Instant speed and accuracy results. Free, no sign up.

You type romaji, the input method converts it to kana, and a second conversion turns kana into kanji. So a single word can require typing, converting, and choosing from a candidate list - three decisions per word where English requires none.
That is why Japanese typing speed depends heavily on conversion accuracy rather than raw keystrokes. A typist who converts correctly on the first try is faster than one who types faster but re-converts twice.
Romaji input maps Latin letters to kana (ka → か) and is what most learners use, because it works on any keyboard. Kana input maps each kana to a single key on a Japanese keyboard; it has a higher ceiling because each kana is one keystroke instead of two or three.
For most people romaji is the right choice: the keyboard is standard, the learning curve is shorter, and the ceiling is high enough for office work. Switch to kana input only if you type Japanese for hours a day.
Kanji selection - homophones are common (こうしょう has dozens of kanji readings), so candidate lists matter.
Katakana words - loanwords are long and the conversion is rarely the first candidate.
Names - place and person names often need manual conversion.
Punctuation - the Japanese comma 、 and full stop 。 are separate keys from their Latin counterparts.
This page reports WPM and CPM from the committed text. For Japanese, characters per minute is the meaningful figure, and it is typically much lower than an English WPM for the same typist - a reflection of the conversion work, not of slower fingers.
Compare within Japanese over time rather than against English scores. For the general benchmarks, see average typing speed.
## Japanese typing test FAQ
You type romaji, the input method converts it to kana, then a second conversion selects kanji from a candidate list. Each word can involve typing, converting and choosing.
Kana input has a higher ceiling because each kana is one keystroke, but it requires a Japanese keyboard or layout and a longer learning curve. Romaji is the practical choice for most people.
Conversion decisions cost time that keystroke speed cannot recover. Japanese characters per minute are typically far below an equivalent English WPM - compare within Japanese over time.
Kanji selection for homophones, katakana loanwords, and names. All three require candidate-list navigation rather than faster typing.
Yes, no account, and the practice pool uses real Japanese sentences mixing kanji, hiragana and katakana.

## Korean Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/korean-typing-test.html

Test your Korean typing speed with real Korean sentences in Hangul. Measure your speed and accuracy instantly with live results. Free, no sign up.

Korean is written in syllable blocks, and each block is composed from 2-4 jamo (consonant and vowel letters). You type the jamo in sequence and the input method assembles them into a block as you go: ㄱ + ㅏ = 가, and adding a final consonant changes the block again.
That has two consequences for typing speed. First, your keystroke count is per jamo, not per visible character, so characters per minute and keystrokes per minute diverge sharply. Second, a wrong jamo does not produce a wrong letter - it produces a different block, which is harder to spot when proofreading.
Most Korean typists use the 2-beolsik (두벌식) layout, which maps consonants to the left hand and vowels to the right. That division is why Korean touch typing can be fast: the hands alternate rather than competing for the same keys.
The 3-beolsik layouts assign final consonants to the right hand and have a higher theoretical ceiling, but they are rare and not worth learning unless you already type Korean professionally. If you are learning, use 2-beolsik because it is what every Korean keyboard ships with.
Batchim (final consonants) - the third or fourth jamo in a block, which moves the hand back to the consonant side.
Block boundaries - knowing when a syllable ends is a language skill, not a typing skill, and it is where learners hesitate.
Homophone selection - less severe than Chinese IMEs, but still present for Sino-Korean words.
Practise on real sentences rather than jamo lists. The jamo are easy; the block assembly under time pressure is not.
This page reports WPM and CPM from the committed text. For Korean, CPM is the more meaningful number because it counts visible characters, while the keystroke count behind it is roughly 2-3 times higher.
For comparison across languages, use CPM: the five-characters-per-word convention was designed for alphabetic scripts and understates the work in a block-based one. The general benchmarks are on average typing speed.
## Korean typing test FAQ
You type jamo (consonant and vowel letters) and the input method assembles them into syllable blocks. Two to four keystrokes produce one visible character.
2-beolsik (두벌식). It ships with every Korean keyboard, splits consonants and vowels between hands, and has a high enough ceiling for professional work.
Each visible character needs two to four keystrokes, so characters per minute and words per minute diverge. Compare CPM across languages rather than WPM.
Batchim is the final consonant in a syllable block. Typing it moves the hand back to the consonant side, which breaks the alternation that makes Korean typing fast.
Yes, with no account. Results stay in your browser, and the practice pool is real Korean sentences rather than random jamo.

## Urdu Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/urdu-typing-test.html

Test your Urdu typing speed with real Urdu sentences in the Perso-Arabic script, typed right to left. Instant speed and accuracy results. Free, no sign up.

Urdu is written right to left in Nastaliq, where most letters change shape depending on what joins them on either side. You still press one key per letter - the shaping is the font's job - but the visual result is not one glyph per keystroke, which makes proofreading harder than in Latin script.
Four characters decide accuracy: ڑ (retroflex r), ں (noon ghunna), ے (bari ye) and the difference between ہ and ھ. These are the pairs that show up in error reports, and they are the ones worth drilling.
The standard Urdu layout keeps Latin letters on the same physical keys and adds Urdu legends, so a touch typist can switch languages without moving hands. That is the good news: your existing muscle memory transfers.
The complication is direction. In a right-to-left field the cursor moves left as you type, and mixing Urdu with Latin words or digits reverses the visual order of that run. If accuracy collapses when a sentence contains a number, that is bidirectional text handling rather than typing speed.
Pakistani government and clerical posts commonly ask for a typing certificate or a timed sample, with speeds quoted in words per minute and, for some posts, in keystrokes. Because requirements are set per employer, read the notice rather than assuming a national standard.
If the test is proctored, rehearse on a different keyboard at least twice: legend placement and key travel change your error rate more than practice volume does.
Use real sentences rather than letter lists, and drill the four confusable characters in isolation for thirty seconds before each session. Then run a full-length round and check accuracy on those characters specifically.
For the English side of the same skill, see English typing test; for the general benchmark, average typing speed.
## Urdu typing test FAQ
Letters - one keystroke per letter. The joined Nastaliq shapes you see are produced by the font, not by extra keystrokes.
ڑ, ں, ے and the ہ/ھ pair. They are visually similar in context and appear less often than common letters, so they stay less practised.
Mixing right-to-left Urdu with left-to-right digits reverses the visual order of that run. It is a bidirectional text issue rather than a typing-speed problem.
200-250 characters per minute (40-50 words per minute) is comfortable office speed. Government and clerical tests commonly ask 20-30 words per minute for entry-level posts.
No. The Urdu layout keeps Latin letters on the same keys, so you add it in your operating system and switch with a shortcut.

In almost every language, a few hundred words cover most of what people actually write. English is no exception: these 200 words appear again and again in messages, documents, subtitles and web pages. If your fingers can produce them without thinking, your real-world English typing speed rises immediately — long before you memorise any larger vocabulary.
English high-frequency words are mostly short function words (the, of, and) mixed with everyday verbs and nouns. They are the words where touch-typing muscle memory pays off fastest, because you type them thousands of times a day.
Start the test above — it draws words from this very list, so every round drills the words that matter. Type a short round every day, aim for accuracy first (97%+), and only then push for speed. Hindi subtitles lean on a small set of function words — है, और, का, में, नहीं — and those same forms recur in WhatsApp messages, news captions and everyday documents. Once your fingers can produce them without hunting for a key, every sentence you type speeds up, because you stop breaking rhythm on the words that appear in almost every line.
Hindi high-frequency words are rich in matras and the conjunct consonants (क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ) that slow most typists down. Drilling these 200 words builds automaticity exactly where Hindi typing needs it.
Ten to fifteen minutes a day, all of it on this list, beats an hour of random Devanagari text. Type a round, then read the weak-key report and spend the next two minutes on the matras and conjuncts it names — क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ and the vowel signs that pull your fingers apart. Accuracy above 97% first; only add speed once the conjuncts stop breaking your rhythm.

Japanese frequency lists are dominated by particles and auxiliaries — の, は, に, を, が — plus a small set of very common verbs and sentence-final forms. Since Japanese is typed through romaji-to-kana conversion with no spaces between words, knowing these fragments by reflex is what lets you convert long strings without checking the candidate list every few characters.
Japanese high-frequency words are dominated by particles (は, が, を, に) and the most common verbs and auxiliaries. Because Japanese has no spaces between words, learning to type these fragments instantly is what makes full-sentence typing feel fluent.
Because romaji input converts to kana in bursts, practise in short rounds of single words rather than long passages. After each round check the weak-key report: if the same kana pair keeps misfiring, retype the words containing it slowly until conversion needs no correction. Keep accuracy above 97% while you learn, then add time pressure with the longer durations above.
When you want full sentences instead of single words, switch to the Japanese typing test, or benchmark yourself against the classic 1 minute typing test.

Korean subtitles repeat a compact set of pronouns, particles and verb stems — 내가, 그, 그리고, 있어 — all built from the same 24 jamo. Because Hangul is composed block by block, the bottleneck is usually one or two vowel-consonant combinations, not vocabulary. Drilling the top words isolates those blocks until syllable assembly becomes one motion instead of several.
Korean high-frequency words are short, particle-heavy forms (내가, 그리고, 있어) built from a small set of jamo. Drilling them trains the even syllable-block rhythm that real Korean typing speed is made of.
Two 5-minute rounds a day, each followed by a look at the weak-key report, is the whole programme. If a particular syllable block keeps slowing you, retype that word slowly five times before continuing — accuracy in the block comes first, and speed in Hangul follows almost by itself once the block is automatic. Push for pace only when a round lands above 97%.
When you want full sentences instead of single words, switch to the Korean typing test, or benchmark yourself against the classic 1 minute typing test.

Urdu frequency data is dominated by particles and verb endings — ہے, کی, میں, کا, نہیں — written in Nastaliq, where letters change shape depending on what joins them. That shaping is exactly what makes Urdu typing feel slow at first: drilling the top 200 words trains the joining forms you meet in nearly every sentence, so context switches stop costing you keystrokes.
Urdu high-frequency words use the special letters (ٹ ڈ ڑ ں ہ ے) that distinguish Urdu from Arabic script. Drilling these 200 words builds speed exactly where Urdu typists lose it.
Short daily rounds on this exact list work better than long occasional sessions, because Nastaliq typing is a joining-shape skill: repetition is what makes ڑ, ں, ے and their neighbours come out without a pause. After each round, use the weak-key report to find which joining forms cost you time, then drill just those for two minutes before your next round.
When you want full sentences instead of single words, switch to the Urdu typing test, or benchmark yourself against the classic 1 minute typing test.
The same top-200 frequency list is available for: English · Spanish · Hindi · Japanese · Korean. Each list is built from the same open subtitle-frequency dataset, so the lists are directly comparable across languages.

## Quotes Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/quotes-typing-test.html

Test your typing speed with famous quotes from history's greatest minds. Real sentences with natural punctuation and capitals. Free, instant results, no sign up.

A word-list test removes everything except letter-finding: no capitals, no punctuation, no sentence structure. A quotes test keeps all three, which is what a document actually contains.
The difference shows up in the score. Most typists read 5-10% lower on quotes than on plain sentences at the same effort, because every capital needs Shift with the opposite hand and every comma pulls the right little finger off the home row. That gap is not a weakness in the typist; it is the cost of real text, and it is the number that transfers to work.
Thirty-five public-domain quotations, between roughly 40 and 140 characters each, chosen so the punctuation is natural rather than decorative. They include attributions (a dash and a name), which is exactly the kind of trailing detail that gets dropped under time pressure.
The quotes are short by design. A quote round is usually 60-120 seconds, so a passage you can finish is better than a paragraph you abandon - and finishing gives you an accuracy figure over a complete unit of text.
WPM counts five characters as a word, including the space. That convention does not care whether the characters are letters or punctuation, so a comma costs exactly as much as a letter - which is why quote scores feel harsh.
Errors are counted per character: a missing apostrophe, a straight quote typed where a curly one appears, or a capital typed as lowercase all count. If you want a score that reflects real writing, that is the right behaviour.
Exam passages and workplace documents include capitals, punctuation and names. Practising on quotes builds the three habits those passages punish: Shift discipline, the comma reach, and reading ahead enough to know a capital is coming.
Run one quote round and one plain-sentence round back to back. If the gap is more than 8%, punctuation is your weak link and the punctuation test is the drill. If the gap is small and both scores are low, the problem is speed, not punctuation.
For the exam-shaped requirements themselves, see typing tests for jobs and the WPM chart.
No song lyrics, no film dialogue, no modern quotations. Everything in the pool is public domain, so there is nothing here that cannot be reproduced, and nothing that will quietly disappear from the site when someone asserts a copyright claim.

A test using real quotations as the text, so capitals, commas, semicolons and quotation marks are part of the exercise - which plain word lists remove.
Punctuation and capitals add keystrokes that a word list does not have. A 5-10% drop is normal; more than that means punctuation is a specific weakness worth drilling.
No. Every quotation in the pool is public domain, and each includes its attribution where one is traditionally given.
Sixty to 120 seconds. The quotes are short enough to finish, which gives you an accuracy figure over a complete piece of text rather than a fragment.

## Pangram Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/pangram-typing-test.html

Practice typing with pangrams — sentences that contain every letter of the alphabet. From the famous quick brown fox to fifteen harder variations. Free, instant results.

A pangram contains every letter of the alphabet at least once. That makes it the shortest text that touches every key you own, which is exactly what a warm-up should do: no letter gets skipped because the passage happened not to contain it.
It also exposes weak keys honestly. On ordinary prose you can drift for a minute without pressing Q, X or Z; on a pangram you press all of them, and the error report has something to say.
Pangram | Why use it
The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog | The classic - short, all 26 letters, quick to finish
Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow | Shorter, punctuation included, good for a 15-second round
Pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs | Letter-dense with unusual letters in the home-row reach
How vexingly quick daft zebras jump | Modern, all 26 letters, tests the Z and X reaches
Waltz, bad nymph, for quick jigs vex | Short and punctuation-heavy
Use two or three rather than all sixteen. Repetition of the same pangram is what builds the reflex; variety only prevents boredom.
A pangram round is short, so it reads high - typically 5-10 WPM above your five-minute score. Use it as a warm-up and a key check, never as the number you quote.
Best routine: one pangram at maximum speed to wake up, one at 80% pace with zero errors, then normal text for the actual measurement.
The quick brown fox dates from the late nineteenth century and was used to test typewriters and telegraphs; the shorter ones are modern inventions written to be typed. All of them are public domain and safe to reproduce.
## Pangram typing test FAQ
A test using sentences that contain every letter of the alphabet, so one short round touches every key and exposes weak ones.
The shortest commonly used ones are around 30 letters, such as "Waltz, bad nymph, for quick jigs vex". The classic quick brown fox is 35 letters plus spaces.
Short rounds avoid fatigue and drift, and a memorised sentence is easier to type than unfamiliar prose. Expect 5-10 WPM above a five-minute score.
Two or three. Repeating the same one builds the reflex; cycling through many mainly prevents boredom.
Yes, no account needed, and the pool includes sixteen pangrams from the classic quick brown fox to modern short ones.

## Python Code Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/python-code-typing.html

Practice typing real Python code — keywords, brackets, colons, underscores and f-strings. Build the symbol speed that coding actually demands. Free, instant results.

A Python code typing test measures how fast and accurately you type real Python syntax — def, return, lambda, list comprehensions, f-strings and decorators. Coding speed is a different skill from prose speed: it is dominated by symbols ({ } [ ] ( ) : ; _ =), mixed case, and indentation, which is exactly what this drill trains.
Prose typing lives on the home row; code typing lives everywhere else. Brackets sit on the top row, the underscore and colon need the shift key, and every line mixes letters with symbols in patterns your prose muscle memory never rehearses. Developers who never drill symbols stay slow at them — and symbols are half of every line of code you write.
Fifty realistic Python lines built from the official keyword list and everyday standard-library patterns: control flow, comprehensions, f-strings, pathlib, json handling, async functions, classes and dunder methods. You will type real constructs like for i in range(len(items)): and sorted(users, key=lambda u: u.score, reverse=True) — not random characters.
The pool is drawn from the Python 3 keyword set (python.org documentation) plus the standard-library calls that appear most in real codebases, so the practice transfers directly to your editor.
Run one minute a day and read the weak-key report carefully — for most developers it flags the bracket keys, the underscore or the colon. Drill those in isolation until they vanish, then retest. For prose-side speed and general developer ergonomics, see typing practice for programmers, and for JavaScript syntax try the JavaScript code typing test.

## JavaScript Code Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/javascript-code-typing.html

Practice typing real JavaScript code — arrow functions, template literals, destructuring, braces and semicolons. Build the symbol speed modern JS demands. Free, instant results.

A JavaScript code typing test measures how fast and accurately you type real JavaScript — const and let, arrow functions, async/await, template literals and destructuring. Modern JS is one of the most symbol-dense languages in everyday use: braces, brackets, backticks, dollar signs, arrows and semicolons fill every line.
JavaScript stacks more symbol types per line than almost any other popular language: ( ) for calls, { } for blocks and objects, [ ] for arrays, ` ` for template literals with ${ } inside, => for arrows, and ?. plus ?? for safety. Every one of those is a shift key or an awkward reach, and every one appears dozens of times in a normal workday. Drilling them directly is the only way they stop being friction.
Fifty realistic lines built from the MDN JavaScript reference and everyday patterns in modern codebases: array methods, destructuring, spread, async/await, DOM calls, fetch with AbortController, classes, getters, and React-flavoured hooks like useState and useEffect. You will type constructs like const users = list.filter(u => u.active); and const merged = { ...defaults, ...options };
The lines follow the MDN documented language syntax (developer.mozilla.org) plus patterns that dominate real repositories, so the practice transfers to your daily editor work.
Run one minute a day and study the weak-key report — JS developers typically discover the curly brace, backtick or dollar-sign keys as their bottlenecks. Drill those until they disappear, then retest. For the Python side of the stack see the Python code typing test, and for general developer typing ergonomics see typing practice for programmers.
