## Best Free Typing Tests Online (2026)
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/best-typing-test-online.html

An honest comparison of the best free typing tests online — monkeytype, 10fastfingers, typing.com, keybr, TypingTest.com and Typing.Rerivo — by features, languages and what each is actually best for.

On this page
The quick comparison table
monkeytype: the minimalist's favourite
10fastfingers: the global multiplayer giant
typing.com: the classroom standard
keybr and TypingTest.com: the two extremes
Typing.Rerivo: multilingual practice with measurement built in
How to choose in ten seconds
How this comparison was made
What this comparison does not measure
Site | Sign-up | Ads in the test | Languages | Lessons | Certificate | Best for
monkeytype | Not required | None | Many (community packs) | No | No | Repeat testing, customisation, no ads
10fastfingers | Optional (for rankings) | Yes on free tier | Many | Basic | No | Competing against other people
typing.com | Required for progress | Yes on free tier | English-focused | Yes, graded | No | Classrooms, structured curriculum
keybr | Not required | None | Several | Algorithmic drills | No | Fixing weak keys with generated text
TypingTest.com | Not required | Yes | English-focused | Limited | Paid | A formal-looking certificate
Typing.Rerivo | Not required | None in the typing area | 12 practice pools | Guides and a 12-lesson course | Free, self-issued | Multilingual practice with the measurement explained
Six typing tests dominate the free tier, and they are genuinely different tools, not copies. This table compares what matters in daily use: whether you need an account, how many languages the practice text covers, whether the tool tells you which keys to fix, and extras like certificates and word lists.
monkeytype is the design darling of the typing world: a clean, fast, endlessly customizable test with themes, modes and a huge community. It needs no account for the core test, supports many test languages and modes, and its smooth interface is genuinely the best-feeling in the category.
Its trade-offs: weak-key analysis is basic compared to dedicated trainers, there are no structured word lists or lessons, and the sheer number of options can overwhelm a beginner who just wants to know if they're getting faster. Pick monkeytype if you already know how to type and want the most polished daily driver.
10fastfingers quietly became the biggest typing site outside the English-speaking world by doing two things brilliantly: a multiplayer race mode that turns practice into competition, and a staggering language matrix — 45+ interface languages crossed with 50+ test languages. In Indonesia, Vietnam and Turkey it is the default typing test.
Its trade-offs: the interface feels dated, per-key weakness analysis is limited, and content beyond the test (guides, word lists) is thin. Pick 10fastfingers if you want competitive racing or practice in a language other than the big five.
typing.com is built for schools: complete curricula, teacher dashboards, student management, and standards-aligned lessons from kindergarten to adult. For structured learning with accountability, nothing else in the free tier comes close.
Its trade-offs: most of the good stuff sits behind a free-but-required account, the site is heavy (ad-supported), and casual users who just want a quick speed check will find it overkill. Pick typing.com for a child learning properly, a classroom, or if you want a guided course rather than a test.
keybr is the algorithmic coach: it generates practice from your own error patterns, letter by letter, with a clean no-account interface. It's excellent for building touch-typing fundamentals, though it offers no languages beyond practice variants and no real-text passages early on.
TypingTest.com is the opposite extreme: the internet's original quick check — one page, one test, zero clutter, zero account. It's English-only with no analysis, but as a ten-second 'how fast am I today' it has worked since 1999. For anything beyond the quick check, look at the others above.
Full disclosure: this is our site, so read this row with appropriate skepticism — but here's what it does differently. The test runs in 12 languages with real practice text per language (not translated English), every round ends with a per-key weak-key report, and it ships with 200-word frequency lists per language, a printable certificate, and 30+ guides on speed, exams and technique. No sign up, no install, works offline in your browser.
Its trade-offs: it's the newest site here, so there's no community or multiplayer yet, and the design is functional rather than flashy. Pick it if you type in more than one language, you're preparing for an employment typing test, or you want your practice to come with a measurement plan attached. Start with the 1 minute typing test or browse typing tests in other languages.
Want the prettiest daily test? monkeytype. Want to race people? 10fastfingers. Teaching a class or a child? typing.com. Learning finger placement from zero? keybr. A ten-second speed check? TypingTest.com. Multilingual practice, exam prep, or measured improvement with weak-key data? Typing.Rerivo.
The honest meta-answer: all of them are free, so use two. A daily measurement on one site and practice on another keeps both scores honest — and if you ever need to prove your speed, a typing certificate from a timed, dated test beats any screenshot.
Checked in October 2026 by opening each site and using its free tier: whether a test starts without an account, whether ads appear inside the typing area, which languages the practice pool offers, whether lessons exist, and whether a certificate is offered and at what cost.
Where a feature sat behind a sign-up, that is recorded as "required" rather than missing. Nothing here is based on traffic estimates, backlink counts or revenue - those are not observable, so they are not claimed.
It does not measure speed or reliability under load, accessibility for screen readers, data retention policies beyond what the public pages state, or how many people use each site. Those matter, and they are not visible from outside.
It also does not rank the sites. "Best" depends on the job: a classroom needs accounts and reports, a job seeker needs a repeatable score and a certificate, and someone fixing a weak left hand needs generated drills.
## Best typing test FAQ
It depends on your goal: monkeytype for design and daily use, 10fastfingers for multiplayer and non-English languages, typing.com for classrooms and courses, keybr for learning finger placement, TypingTest.com for a zero-clutter quick check, and Typing.Rerivo for multilingual practice with per-key weakness analysis.
Typing.Rerivo, monkeytype, 10fastfingers, keybr and TypingTest.com all work with no account. typing.com requires a free account for its lessons and courses, though its basic test is open.
10fastfingers has the broadest matrix — 45+ interface languages crossed with 50+ test languages. Typing.Rerivo offers 12 test languages with real practice text per language plus top-200 word lists for each.
Look for per-key weakness analysis and structured practice: keybr adapts to your errors letter by letter, typing.com has full courses, and Typing.Rerivo gives a weak-key report after every round plus word lists and drills targeting exactly those keys.
Yes, all six have usable free tiers. typing.com and monkeytype offer paid tiers (ad-free/premium features); Typing.Rerivo, keybr and TypingTest.com are free with no account and no paywall.
For repeat measurement with no ads, monkeytype. For classrooms and graded lessons, typing.com. For a printable certificate, this site or a paid one. For fixing weak keys, keybr. There is no single best.
Yes - the measurement is characters against a clock. Paid tiers sell certificates, accounts and reporting, not a better stopwatch.

## Online Typing Practice
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/online-typing-practice.html

Free online typing practice with structure built in: timed rounds, per-key weakness analysis, practice in 12 languages, and a daily 10-minute plan. No account, no install.

On this page
Online typing practice
Why browser-based practice beats installed software
A practice structure that actually improves you
Practice in your own language
When practice stops working
Setting up your first practice week
Common practice mistakes to avoid
Making practice a habit that survives busy weeks
Online typing practice is structured, timed repetition in the browser — not just 'typing more'. The difference between practice and testing is intent: a test measures where you are; practice deliberately attacks one measured weakness at a time until it moves. Done right, ten minutes of structured online practice outperforms an hour of unstructured typing.
This page gives you the practice itself plus the structure around it: timed rounds with live WPM and accuracy, a per-key weakness report after every round, practice text in 12 languages, and a daily plan built from those measurements. Everything runs in your browser — no account, no download, and your history stays on your device.
Installed typing software made sense in 2005. Today the browser wins for four reasons: zero install and zero account (you are practising ten seconds after opening the page), your progress history stays private on your device instead of a company's server, the tool works identically on any computer you sit down at, and updates arrive without downloads.
Desktop software still has one niche — locked-down enterprise environments with no browser access. For everyone else, browser practice is strictly more convenient and exactly as effective. The typing practice page here is the working example: full practice suite, nothing to install.
The daily ten minutes, in order: two 15-second sprints to wake your fingers, one full measured minute, five minutes drilling the two weakest keys from your last result, and two minutes on a text type you find hard — numbers, quotes, or a new language. That is the whole routine, and it covers every bottleneck a typist has.
The weekly piece matters as much: one honest measurement under the same conditions, compared against last week. Daily scores wander; weekly trends tell the truth. The table below maps the routine to your specific goal.
Goal | Daily 10 minutes | Weekly check
Raw speed | 2 sprints + 1 measured round + 5 min weak keys | Net WPM trend
Accuracy | 3 controlled rounds at 98% accuracy floor | Accuracy + net-raw gap
Exam preparation | 1 full simulation at the test's duration | Simulation score vs the gate
New language | 1 round in the target language's word pool | Language round WPM + accuracy
Endurance | 1 long round (3-10 minutes) | Decay in final third
Most online typing practice is English-only, which is useless if your daily writing is in another language. This site runs practice in 12 languages — English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Arabic, Japanese, Korean, Urdu, Indonesian, Vietnamese, Turkish and Thai — each with real practice text, not translated English, and a top-200 word list per language.
The skills transfer: accuracy habits built in one script carry to every other script you type. Multilingual practice also breaks rhythm monotony, which is the hidden cause of most plateaus.
Every practitioner hits the wall: two or more weeks of flat scores despite daily practice. The wall is always one of three things — a bottleneck you have not measured (check the weak-key report), a drill that has gone stale (change text type or duration), or accumulated fatigue (take two rest days; adaptation happens on rest).
What never works is more volume of the same practice. Ten measured minutes with a changed stimulus beats every marathon. For the full drill library, see typing speed exercises, and for the theory behind the plan, how to get better at typing walks the 4-week system.
Day one is measurement day, not practice day: take a 1 minute typing test three times, record the middle net WPM and accuracy, and read the weak-key report carefully. Those three numbers are your baseline — everything you do for the next month gets measured against them.
Days two to seven follow the daily ten-minute structure from the table above, chosen for your goal. Day seven: retest under the same conditions and compare. Most people see the first measurable movement inside two weeks — and almost all of it comes from accuracy, not raw speed. From there it is the same weekly cycle: measure, drill the bottleneck, repeat.
The biggest one is practising for speed from day one. Speed built on sloppy foundations has a hard ceiling, and every hour of it deepens the errors you will later pay weeks to unlearn. Start at ninety percent of your comfortable pace and hold a 97-98% accuracy line; speed follows automatically once the base is clean.
Second: marathon sessions on weekends. Motor memory consolidates overnight between sessions, so ten minutes daily outperforms seventy minutes on Sunday by a wide margin. Third: measuring yourself every day. Daily scores wander by several points for no meaningful reason, and watching them is discouraging without being informative. Measure weekly, under the same conditions, and act on the trend.
Fourth: ignoring the weak-key report after each round. It is the single most useful piece of practice data you have — the difference between knowing your speed and knowing what is slowing it down. Every practice session should end with one glance at that report and one decision about what to drill next.
The routine that fails is the one that depends on motivation. Anchor your ten minutes to an existing daily event — the first coffee, the start of a work block, the end of lunch — so the practice happens at the same cue every day without negotiation. Habit piggybacking beats willpower every time.
Have a minimum viable day too: on your worst day, do one single measured minute and stop. One minute keeps the chain unbroken and takes less time than finding an excuse. The people who improve are not the ones with perfect weeks; they are the ones whose bad weeks still contain a minute a day.
## Online Typing Practice FAQ
Yes — this practice suite is free with no sign up, no install and no account. Your practice history stays privately on your own device.
Ten focused minutes daily beats an occasional hour. Motor memory consolidates between sessions, so frequency matters more than session length.
Yes, if it is structured: measurement, weak-key targeting and weekly review. Unstructured 'typing more' just rehearses your current ceiling, errors included.
Yes — 12 languages with real practice text per language, from Spanish and Hindi to Vietnamese and Thai. See the typing tests in other languages page for the full list.
Change the stimulus, not the volume: new text type, different duration, or targeted weak-key drills. Plateaus are technique signals, and more of the same practice only deepens them.

English follows a steep frequency curve: a few hundred words account for the overwhelming majority of everything written and spoken, and the first thousand take that coverage further still. That is why learners are told to master high-frequency words before anything else — and why typists should drill them too. These are the words your fingers will type thousands of times, so making them automatic pays back on every sentence you ever write.
The practical version: if you can type these thousand words without thinking, ordinary English prose stops being a typing challenge. Unusual words are rare by definition — when one appears, you have time to handle it.
Start the test above — it draws from this exact frequency list, so every round drills the words that matter. Type a short round daily, accuracy first (97%+), and only then push for speed. The weak-key report after each round tells you which letters are actually slowing you down; drill those, not the words you already know.
For a shorter daily set, the top 200 English words page covers the highest-value core. When you want full sentences instead of single words, switch to the English typing test.
The FrequencyWords dataset counts word occurrences across millions of subtitle lines, which makes it a good proxy for everyday spoken-style English. We filtered the raw ranking to plain alphabetic words (dropping numbers, punctuation fragments and proper-noun noise) and kept the top thousand in order.
Frequency lists differ slightly by source — a news corpus will over-rank formal vocabulary, a subtitle corpus over-ranks conversational words. For typing practice, the conversational bias is a feature: these are the words you actually type.
Once these words are automatic, progress comes from three places: longer texts for stamina (the 5 minute typing test), symbol-heavy text for punctuation speed (numbers and quotes modes), and your own real writing — emails, documents, notes — typed with deliberate accuracy.
And if you type in more than one language, the same frequency-first method works there: see the typing tests in other languages for word lists and practice pools in eleven more languages.

## Typing Games for Kids
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-games-for-kids.html

Typing games for kids work best as short, game-feeling sessions — five to ten minutes, instant feedback, always stopping before boredom hits. Here is the method and why it beats formal drills.

On this page
Why games beat drills for kids
Letter-hunt games: the fastest way to the keyboard map
Word-collection and mini-challenges
The right duration and cadence
How to keep kids practising without nagging
Games that help with specific skills
A sample 5-minute session
Games that help with specific skills
A sample 5-minute session
Children learn typing fastest through play, not repetition. A five-minute game with instant feedback trains the same letter-location habit a worksheet drills over twenty minutes — but the child finishes the game wanting more, and coming back tomorrow is how motor memory actually forms. Boredom is the killer, and games are the antidote; drudgery is the reason most learn-to-type programs lose kids by week three.
The rule that makes it work: stop while it is fun. A child who quits a game asking for one more round will come back; a child who is forced through a full drill session will find reasons not to. Five to ten minutes, always, is the ceiling for young children.
Letter-hunt games — spot the word, find the key, type it — build spatial memory, which is the foundation of touch typing. The child learns where the letters live without it feeling like work. Two rounds of letter-hunt a day beats a week of staring at a finger chart.
Start with the home row (A-S-D-F / J-K-L-;) and the child's own name — names are the highest-motivation text there is. Then expand to short familiar words, then the words they read in daily life.
Once letter locations are automatic, game-style word tasks take over: type the word to collect it, spell the sight word to burst it, type a whole short sentence to earn a badge. The key is the reward timing — instant, visual, and one round long. Kids respond to 'got it' feedback every five seconds far more than to a prize at the end of a month.
Keep the words at reading level. A six-year-old should type the words they read, not the words they are learning to spell — reading and typing develop together, and the text should stay comfortably easy.
Five minutes a day for young children, up to ten for older ones, and always before fatigue or frustration. Short daily sessions out-teach long weekly ones, because typing is motor memory and motor memory forms in the gaps between practices. The cadence that works: two short rounds most days, a longer challenge on the weekend, and immediate stop when accuracy collapses.
Watch the error rate as your signal: accuracy slipping below 90% mid-round means the material is too hard, not that the child is failing. Drop the difficulty, not the motivation.
The single best motivator is visible progress. A small chart of words-per-minute rising over weeks — or in this case, a personal-best saved in the browser the child can beat — turns practice into a game they run themselves. Framing it as 'beat your last score' rather than 'type faster' converts external pressure into a self-run challenge.
The second motivator is control: let the child pick the text (their favourite words, a story they like, their own name). Owning the choice is the difference between practice and homework, and it is the difference between a child who persists and one who quits.
Keyboard-familiarity games (letter hunt, name typing) build the map. Accuracy games (type the word perfectly to collect it) build clean habits — the thing that actually predicts real-world speed. Speed games (beat your last time) build confidence once accuracy is solid. Introduce speed only after accuracy holds, exactly like adult training.
Punctuation and capitals come later and are best learned last for kids; start with lowercase words and short sentences. The typing test for kids on this site is tuned for exactly these short, friendly, game-like rounds.
Minute one: letter-hunt on the child's name. Minute two: home-row words. Minute three: the sight words they are learning at school. Minute four: a 'beat your last score' round. Minute five: one short, easy sentence to finish on a win. Five minutes, five wins, and the child asks for another round tomorrow.
The whole session runs on the free test above — short durations, instant results, no account, and for a longer library of classic finger-drill games there is typing games and the keyboard practice page.

Speed games (beat your last time) build confidence once accuracy is solid. Introduce speed only after accuracy holds, exactly like adult training.

The whole session runs on the free test above — short durations, instant results, no account, and for a longer library of classic finger-drill games there is typing games and the keyboard practice page.
## Typing Games for Kids FAQ
Yes — short game-style sessions train the same letter-location habits as drills, but children stay engaged and come back. Five to ten minutes, with instant feedback and always stopping before boredom, beats longer forced sessions every time.

## Bigram Typing Practice
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/bigram-typing-practice.html

A bigram typing practice drill targeting the most common English letter combinations.

On this page
What is bigram typing practice?
Common vs rare bigrams
The most common English bigrams
How to use this page
Bigram practice for exam preparation
Rare bigrams that break rhythm
How bigram practice translates to real text
Practising bigrams for exam typing
Two difficulty levels
How bigram fluency compounds
A bigram is a pair of consecutive letters that appears very often in English: th, he, in, er, on, ed, nd, ti, es, re, ou, ar and st. These thirteen pairs dominate English text, so a bigram typing practice drill that repeats them builds the exact finger coordination that real-world typing demands.
When the letters th appear in a word, your two fingers must coordinate - one strikes t while the other prepares h. If this transition is hesitant, every word containing th is slowed. Drill the bigram and every matching word speeds up.
There are two drill modes. Common bigrams (th, he, in, er, on) train the transitions you use every minute. Rare bigrams (wh, kn, gh, qu, ch, ght, ugh, ought) train the combinations that break rhythm even in skilled typists. Start with common until they feel automatic, then switch to rare for a challenge.
Alternating between the two keeps each round fresh while covering the full range of English letter combinations.
These thirteen pairs dominate English text. Practice each until the combination feels like a single keystroke.
# | Bigram | Example words
1 | th | the, that, this, three
2 | he | the, he, her, here
3 | in | in, into, thing
4 | er | her, here, there
5 | on | on, only, one
6 | ed | ended, typed, looked
7 | nd | and, end, under
8 | ti | time, this, until
9 | es | best, test, these
10 | re | are, more, there
11 | ou | you, our, about
12 | ar | are, card, hard
13 | st | best, most, start
Take a 15-second round on common bigrams, note your weak-key report, then a 15-second round on rare bigrams. The keys in both reports are your true weak keys. Drill them until they stop appearing, then retest with the 1 minute typing test.
For more drills see typing speed exercises. For symbols try quotes typing test.
Government and clerk typing tests in India test accuracy and speed on timed passages. Bigram fluency directly improves passage typing because common letter combinations no longer cause hesitation. Practice common bigrams until automatic, then hard bigrams until comfortable, and finally full sentences to tie them together. Punctuation symbols carry more CPM weight than people expect, because they break letter rhythm: practise them with quotes mode or the punctuation test on this site to keep every keystroke type at the same automatic level.
While common bigrams build your baseline, rare bigrams are what hold elite typists back from the next level. The combinations wh, kn, gh, qu, ch and the clusters ght, ugh, ought appear in words like though, knight, bought, through and thought. These are high-frequency in real text but rare in typical practice, so your fingers never build the automatic reach for them.
The rare bigram mode on this page packs every round with these combinations at high density. A few 15-second sessions daily will train these alternate reaches until they feel as natural as the home row.
The most common objection to bigram practice is that real text is full sentences, not random pairs. This has a clear answer: when you type a sentence like 'the thing that made them start', your fingers fire a chain of bigrams: th, em, ad, ar, rt. Each pair has been drilled individually. The sentence becomes a smooth sequence of known patterns rather than a series of new decisions.
Research on motor learning calls this chunking: the brain groups repeated movements into single units. Bigram typing practice is chunking at the letter-pair level.
Government and clerk typing exams test WPM, CPM and accuracy on timed passages. Bigram fluency directly improves passage typing because exam texts are built from common English words whose letter pairs match the table above. If your bigram speed is automatic, the passage feels like chaining known blocks.
For more preparation context, see the 1 minute typing test or the typing speed requirements page.
This page has two drill levels. The common drill packs every sentence with th, he, in, er, on and st words: the backbone of English typing. The rare drill challenges you with wh, kn, gh, qu, ch and ght clusters: the reaches that separate fast typists from very fast typists.
Switch between them to keep each round fresh. For symbols instead of letters, try the quotes typing test.
Every English word is built from letter combinations, and the same combinations repeat across related words. When you drill th in the words the, that, this and three, you are also training the th in their, them, other and weather. Bigram practice compounds across vocabulary because the alphabet only has 26 letters and English only has a handful of high-frequency pairs.
This is what makes bigram typing practice more efficient than whole-word practice: one drill covers dozens of words. See the typing finger chart for the finger-to-key mapping that underlies every reach, and typing speed exercises for the full drill library.

## Best Free Typing Lessons for Adults

The best free typing lessons for adults are not a course you buy - they are a daily 10-minute structure you follow for four weeks. Adults learning touch typing face one challenge that children do not: decades of hunt-and-peck muscle memory to unlearn. The fix is a hard three-week boundary (touch type everything, including real work), then a permanent improvement phase built on measurement and weak-key drilling.
Most adults reach 40-50 WPM within one month, 60 WPM within three months, and 80 WPM within a year of this structure. The paid courses package the same free drills with a login screen.
Week one: home row only. A-S-D-F / J-K-L-;, eyes up no matter what. One 1 minute typing test daily to record your baseline. Week two: add numbers and capitals with opposite-side shift. Accuracy floor 98%. Week three: full-sentence practice with punctuation and real email text. Use the typing trainer for structured drills.
Week four: speed work. Two 15-second sprints before every measured round. Retest on the 1 minute typing test and compare against week one. Most people gain 10-15 WPM in four weeks - enough to clear every office benchmark in the typing speed requirements table.
Week | Focus | Daily routine | Metric
1 | Home row + accuracy 98% | 1 min + 5 min drills | Accuracy %
2 | Numbers + capitals | 2 sprints + 1 min + symbols | Accuracy 98%
3 | Full sentences | 1 min + trainer drills | Net WPM
4 | Sprint + speed work | 2 sprints + 1 min + weak keys | Net WPM vs baseline
A browser is the only requirement. This site provides the timed test, the practice text in 12 languages, the word lists, the trainer, the lessons and the certificate - all free with no account. The learn to type page has the full beginner course. The typing lessons page structures the drills as progressive lessons.
Weekly measurement on the same test under the same conditions is the entire tracking system. Record net WPM, accuracy and weak keys. Compare the weekly trend, not daily scores. If the number rises, keep going. If it flattens for two weeks, change the drill, not the volume. The browser history saves every result automatically for you to compare.
Adults who learn touch typing report two categories of improvement beyond raw speed. First: less fatigue, because hunt-and-peck fingers travel six times farther than touch typing for the same sentence, which over eight hours of work causes evening pain. Second: faster thought-to-text flow, because when letter reaches are automatic the bottleneck shifts from the fingers to the brain. Third: professional credibility from a dated typing speed certificate attached to your resume.
Mistake one: mixing touch typing in practice with hunt-and-peck in real work, which prevents consolidation. Fix: a three-week no-mixing boundary. Mistake two: no accuracy floor, which at 95% builds error habits faster than speed. Fix: always 90% pace with 98% floor. Mistake three: re-typing comfortable texts instead of rotating text types to train the full keyboard surface.
Anchor the ten minutes to an existing daily event: first coffee, morning stand-up, end of lunch. Use a fixed test format, and have a one-minute minimum for crowded days; one minute is better than zero and keeps the chain unbroken. After four weeks of daily practice, the weekly measurement becomes self-correcting: the number rises when drills are right and flattens when the bottleneck has moved.
Adults bring vocabulary and context to typing practice that younger learners lack: you already know every word you type, so look-ahead reading is free instead of a skill to develop. Adults also know exactly which days matter for an exam, which text types their work requires, and how to think through a timed test under pressure.
Weekly measurement under identical conditions is the entire tracking system. Record net WPM, accuracy and weak keys in any note-taking app. A simple table with twelve weeks of numbers is more motivating than a gamified dashboard.
Three self-inflicted mistakes keep adult learners from improving. The first: practising without cancelling the old hunt-and-peck habit, which happens when touch typing is used only for practice sessions while pecking continues for real work. The fix: a three-week hard boundary where touch typing is used exclusively, no matter how slow it feels. The brain cannot consolidate two motor patterns simultaneously; it must be forced to choose one before it can automate it.
The second: setting no accuracy floor. Typing at 95% accuracy or below builds error habits faster than speed. The fix: always practise at 90% of comfortable pace with an explicit 98% accuracy floor. The third: re-typing the same comfortable sentences instead of rotating text types. A rotation between prose, numbers, quotes and code text ensures every key on the keyboard is trained equally.
The time question is the most common barrier for adult learners. The answer is not to find a new block of time; it is to attach the practice to an existing daily event. The first coffee becomes the trigger for one measured round. The end of lunch becomes the second practice slot. The commute (on a phone or tablet) becomes a reading-ahead exercise. Ten minutes exists in every adult's day, fragmented across multiple small gaps.
The other answer is to make the practice itself shorter rather than longer. One measured minute is better than zero minutes. One minute keeps the chain alive, maintains the habit, and produces a data point for the weekly trend. The days when you can only do one minute are the days that keep the habit from dying.

## Typing Speed Test for Government Jobs
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-government-jobs.html

The typing speed test for government jobs typically requires 25-35 WPM with a mistake cap, tested as a short timed passage.

Government typing exams test speed and accuracy on timed passages in English or Hindi. The most common bar is 30-35 WPM with a mistake cap, assessed over a five-minute passage. The SSC typing test and bank clerk typing test pages have role-specific details.
Converting to the standard metric: 30 WPM is 150 CPM or 9,000 KPH. The accuracy cap means one error in a hundred characters is the maximum acceptable rate.
Most government typing exams follow a fixed format: a passage of 2,000-4,000 characters typed over five to ten minutes. The scoring deducts one mark per mistake. Practising with the exact format removes the pacing anxiety on test day.
The data entry typing test and keystrokes per hour test provide the closest simulation for KPH-based roles.
Week one: accuracy base. Daily rounds at 90% of comfortable speed with a hard 98% accuracy line. Practise in the exam language, with the same punctuation marks. Week two: pace and simulation. Lift speed 5% a day, hold the accuracy floor, run a full simulation daily.
Speed beyond the requirement does not earn extra marks in most government exams. Consistent accuracy over the full duration does. The typing speed requirements table marks these exams as accuracy-critical.
There are three data-entry test formats to practise: format one is a straight KPH test with mixed text and digits in a fixed duration; format two is form-filling with fields on screen and source beside them; format three is audio data entry where numbers are read aloud. Find out which format your specific exam uses and practise that exact format in a timed one-take simulation twice per week.
Field analysis of data-entry and clerk typing test results shows that the accuracy gate fails more candidates than the speed floor. Candidates who pass at exactly the minimum speed with 99% accuracy consistently outperform those who exceed the speed requirement but drop below the accuracy line by one or two points.
Many Indian government exams accept either English or Hindi typing. English is more standardised across posts and simpler on standard keyboards. Hindi uses a Devanagari layout (Kedmanee or Remington) that requires dedicated practice. Choose the language you can type most accurately on test day.
Full-time government clerk roles: stable, formal testing, slow hiring. Part-time and remote task work: fast entry, flexible, rating-driven. Seasonal volume (tax season, enrollment period, retail peak): hires fast with lower speed gates. Seasonal work is the underrated entry point for one good season of a track record worth a year of applications.
For SSC CHSL and court clerk exams, both English and Hindi typing layouts are accepted depending on the post. Hindi uses either the Kedmanee or Remington layout. Practising in the language you will use on test day builds the exact letter patterns and pacing habits that the exam measures.
The most valuable practice session is one that replicates the test conditions exactly: the same duration, the same language, the same punctuation style, and a single take with no re-dos. Practising with a simulation once a week teaches you how to pace over the full duration, how to handle errors without breaking rhythm, and how to maintain accuracy when fatigue starts to appear in the final minutes of a long test.
The variables to match in each simulation: the text length (2,000-4,000 characters or the KPH equivalent), the language (English or Hindi, depending on the post and state), the punctuation style (full punctuation or exam abbreviation), and the one-take rule. Each of these is testable at home with a browser and a timer, and the feedback from each simulation guides the next week of practice.
Many Indian government posts accept both English and Hindi typing. Hindi typing exams test accuracy and speed on Devanagari script passages, where the layout is either Kedmanee (the standard Hindi layout) or Remington (the older typewriter convention, still used in some state exams). Both layouts place the most common Hindi consonants on the home row and the vowels on the top row.
For Hindi typing practice, consistent daily rounds on real Hindi sentences build both script familiarity and the mental toggling between English QWERTY and Devanagari layouts that many bilingual typists need for exams. The key is to practise the full passage length in one sitting, matching the exam format rather than practising in short fragments that never build endurance.
Beyond government exams, typing speed matters in every role that involves writing on a computer: email, documentation, code, chat support, content writing and project management. The same accuracy-first practice that prepares for government exams also prepares for these roles, because the keyboard skills are the same even when the application differs.
For developers specifically, the Python code typing test and JavaScript code typing test serve real code lines with symbol-heavy syntax. For general office skills, the typing speed requirements page has the comparison table across all job types, and the data entry practice page has the numeric keypad drills for KPH-quoted roles.

## Programmer Typing Speed
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/programmer-typing-speed.html

Why do programmers need faster typing? Code is the most symbol-dense language you write: brackets, semicolons, underscores, backticks.

On this page
Programmer typing speed
Code typing is a separate skill from prose typing
A developer's typing workout
Three code-heavy reaches that slow every developer
What senior developers know about typing that juniors do not
How to choose which language code drill to start with
IDE autocomplete does not make typing speed irrelevant
The developer week of typing practice
Symbol density as the real bottleneck in coding speed
Three levels of code typing practice that build on each other
Compounding returns: faster typing means more practice, which means faster typing
A programmer's typing speed matters more than most people think, because code is the most symbol-dense text you can write. A single JavaScript line contains brackets, braces, dots, commas, arrows, quotes and semicolons - each one a separate keystroke with a different finger and reach.
Fast coders are not fast because they think faster; they are fast because the symbols and keywords are automatic. The keyboard stops being a barrier and becomes an extension of thought.
Prose lives on the home row; code lives everywhere. Brackets sit on the top row, underscores and colons need the shift key, and every line mixes letters with symbols in patterns prose typing never rehearses. Developers who never drill symbols stay slow at them.
The fix: practise typing code text in controlled timed rounds. The Python code typing test and JavaScript code typing test serve real code lines that drill exactly these reaches.
The most valuable typing routine targets three code-heavy reaches: brackets and braces on the top row, underscore and hyphen on the bottom row, and the quote-backtick pair used in every string. Run a 60-second code typing round daily, then a 30-second round on your weakest code symbol from the weak-key report. The code-typing pages here are built for this pattern.
See typing practice for programmers for the full technique guide.
First: brackets and braces on the shift row. These appear in nearly every line of code and require either a shift hold or a dedicated finger from home row. Second: underscore and hyphen on the bottom row, which is the least accessible key group. Third: backtick-shift and dollar-sign-brace combinations in template strings.
Symbol | Keypress | Frequency in code
() | Shift+9/0 | Every function call
{} | Shift+[ / Shift+] | Every block and object
_ | Shift+- | Python naming
: | Shift+; | Python blocks
= | Direct | Assignment every line
> | Shift+. | Arrow functions
Senior developers who are fast coders share this specific belief: typing is a tool they have made invisible so the keyboard never competes with the thought. The focus is not how fast they type but whether every symbol reaches the screen without conscious thought about fingers or keys.
Start with the language you spend the most hours in. Python developers should drill the underscore and colon patterns. JavaScript developers should drill brackets, template literals and arrow function reaches. Use the code typing test that matches your language and switch only after automaticity is achieved in one.
Autocomplete saves you from remembering API calls and parameter names, but it does not save you from typing the code structure around those calls. Array methods, control flow patterns and variable declarations are still typed character by character. Typing speed determines how fast you reach the autocomplete trigger.
Monday: code typing round in your primary language, 60 seconds. Tuesday: prose accuracy round at 98% floor. Wednesday: code typing in your secondary language, 60 seconds. Thursday: prose speed round with sprints. Friday: code typing round plus weak-key drill. Weekend: rest or one long round for stamina.
A typical line of JavaScript code contains seven to twelve characters that are not letters: brackets, braces, dots, commas, arrows, colons and semicolons. In Python, the ratio is similar, with underscores, colons, square brackets and function call parentheses dominating. When these symbols require a conscious finger reach, every line costs more time than the same line of prose.
The solution is not to type faster in general but to bring the specific symbol reaches up to the same automatic level as the letter reaches. A developer who types every bracket, colon and underscore with the same confidence as A and S has removed the keyboard as a barrier to writing code. That automaticity is built with daily rounds on code-specific typing tests that serve real code lines rather than random characters.
Level one: language-specific typing tests serving real code lines in Python, JavaScript or another language. These drill the keywords, operators and symbol patterns that the framework demands. Level two: symbol-focused practice isolating the hardest reaches for targeted work. Level three: mixed-mode practice alternating between code and prose, building the switching speed that daily development requires.
The free code typing tests on this site cover level one for Python and JavaScript with top word lists and full sentence practice. The weak-key report after each round identifies exactly which symbol reaches need work, and the accuracy tracking shows whether you are building the precision that production code demands.
The gap between typing practice and real coding is bridged by consistency and the right feedback loop. Code-specific typing practice at typing.rerivo.com serves real Python and JavaScript lines with symbol-rich syntax, so what you practise is what you write. After two weeks of daily rounds, developers report that common code patterns flow without conscious thought about individual characters.
The compounding effect is real: faster typing makes practice feel less tedious, which means more rounds are completed, which builds more automaticity, which makes subsequent rounds faster. This positive feedback loop is the same one that drives elite typists and elite musicians. The skill feeds the practice, and the practice feeds the skill, and the cycle compounds over months into a skill that most people never develop because they stop at the first plateau.

## 10,000 Keystrokes per Hour Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/10000-keystrokes-per-hour-test.html

Data-entry job ads ask for 10,000 keystrokes per hour and never explain what that is in WPM. It is 166.7 characters per minute, or about 33 words per minute. This page runs the test and does the arithmetic.

A keystroke is one character: a letter, a digit, a space or a punctuation mark. Keystrokes per hour (KPH) is therefore a characters-per-minute figure multiplied by 60. Ten thousand KPH is 10,000 ÷ 60 = 166.7 CPM. Divide by five, the standard characters-per-word convention, and you get roughly 33 WPM.
Recruiters use KPH instead of WPM because data-entry work is judged on characters: account numbers, postcodes, invoice references and part numbers have no word boundaries. KPH measures the same keyboard output without pretending the text is prose.
Keystrokes per hour | Characters per minute | Words per minute (÷5) | Typical use
5,000 | 83 | 17 | Entry-level alphanumeric, slow but accurate
6,000 | 100 | 20 | Common minimum in general office ads
8,000 | 133 | 27 | Data entry with checking, most clerical roles
9,000 | 150 | 30 | Medical billing, insurance claims
10,000 | 167 | 33 | The number most data-entry postings quote
12,000 | 200 | 40 | Numeric keypad work, ten-key operators
15,000 | 250 | 50 | Fast numeric entry, transcription from clean audio
Set the timer to five minutes. One-minute runs measure your best burst; five minutes measures the pace you can hold, which is what a shift actually requires. Choose the Words text mode for alphanumeric work and the Numbers mode if your job is keypad-heavy, because digits are typed by a different hand position and score differently.
Type the text as it appears, including capitals and punctuation, without correcting every slip. The score panel reports WPM and CPM after the round; multiply CPM by 60 for KPH. A five-minute round gives a stable number because a single slow sentence cannot dominate the result.
The two numbers only agree when your text averages five characters per word including the space. Sentences with long words produce fewer WPM for the same KPH; number strings produce far higher KPH for a low WPM because every keystroke counts but there are no words.
Accuracy matters more in KPH work than in prose typing. An uncorrected digit error in an account number is a failed record, not a typo. If your raw and net scores differ by more than about 5%, practise accuracy before pushing speed: the arithmetic of corrections costs more time than typing slightly slower.
It sits in the middle of office typing. It is above the ~20 WPM that untrained typists manage and below the ~50 WPM average reported for people who type daily, so it is reachable in a few weeks of deliberate practice rather than years.
If you are at 6,000–8,000 KPH, the gap to 10,000 is a pace problem, not a knowledge problem. Daily five-minute rounds plus one accuracy drill will usually close it faster than longer sessions, because fatigue at minute eight teaches you nothing about minute one.
## Frequently asked questions
About 33 WPM. 10,000 ÷ 60 = 166.7 characters per minute, and 166.7 ÷ 5 = 33.3 words per minute using the standard five-characters-per-word convention.
It is the number most data-entry job postings quote as a minimum, and it corresponds to roughly 33 WPM, which is a solid office speed. Faster roles such as medical billing often ask for 9,000–12,000 KPH with high accuracy.
It counts the characters you typed correctly against the elapsed time. CPM × 60 gives keystrokes per hour, and the panel shows both CPM and WPM after each round so you can convert without a calculator.
Use Words for alphanumeric data entry and Numbers if the job is keypad-heavy. Digits use a different finger pattern, so a words score will flatter or penalise you inaccurately for numeric work.

## WPM to KPH Converter
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/wpm-to-kph-converter.html

Keystrokes per hour is characters per minute × 60. Because one word is counted as five characters, the shortcut is KPH = WPM × 300. The chart below covers every speed you are likely to be asked for.

Both directions work: type in either box. The conversion uses five characters per word and sixty minutes per hour, so KPH = WPM × 300 exactly. CPM = WPM × 5.
One word is counted as five characters, the convention every typing test uses because it makes speeds comparable across languages and text styles. One minute of typing at W WPM is therefore 5W characters, and an hour is 60 × 5W keystrokes.
KPH = WPM × 300. The reverse is WPM = KPH ÷ 300. If you prefer to work from CPM, KPH = CPM × 60, and CPM = WPM × 5.
WPM | CPM | KPH | Where you see this number
20 | 100 | 6,000 | Minimum in general clerical ads
30 | 150 | 9,000 | Insurance and billing support
33 | 167 | 10,000 | The standard data-entry requirement
40 | 200 | 12,000 | Ten-key and order processing
50 | 250 | 15,000 | Fast data entry, transcription
60 | 300 | 18,000 | Above most clerical requirements
80 | 400 | 24,000 | Professional typing, court reporting support
100 | 500 | 30,000 | Top decile of typists
WPM × 60 converts minutes to hours but keeps the unit: 50 WPM × 60 is 3,000, and 3,000 is words per hour, not keystrokes. The missing factor of five is the characters-per-word convention. A 50 WPM typist produces 15,000 keystrokes in an hour, not 3,000.
The second mistake is comparing KPH across text types. A page of digits produces a much higher KPH than a page of long English words at the same effort, because every digit is one keystroke and every long word is eight. KPH requirements are usually quoting alphanumeric data, so test with numbers if the job is numeric.
Run a five-minute round and read the CPM figure from the results panel, then multiply by 60. The page reports CPM as well as WPM on every run precisely so that conversion does not need a separate tool.
If you want the number an employer will see, use net rather than raw: subtract the characters you typed wrong before dividing. A run of 250 CPM with twelve uncorrected errors is 238 net CPM, which is 14,280 KPH, not 15,000.
## Frequently asked questions
Multiply WPM by 300. Five characters make one word and sixty minutes make an hour, so 5 × 60 = 300. A 45 WPM score is 13,500 KPH.

## Gross WPM vs Net WPM
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/gross-wpm-vs-net-wpm.html

Two typing tests can score the same run ten words apart. The difference is gross (all characters typed) versus net (errors subtracted). Here are both formulas and one worked example.

Gross WPM: every character you produced, including wrong ones, divided by five and by the minutes elapsed. Net WPM: the same calculation after the incorrect characters are removed. Some tests subtract a fixed penalty per error instead of the characters themselves; both arrive at a lower number, they just describe the penalty differently.
Method | Formula | What it rewards
Gross (raw) WPM | characters ÷ 5 ÷ minutes | Speed alone
Net WPM | (characters − errors) ÷ 5 ÷ minutes | Speed that survives accuracy
Adjusted WPM (AWPM) | all characters ÷ 5 ÷ minutes, errors counted as typed | School and exam scoring, where every keystroke is credited
Suppose you type 300 characters in 60 seconds and 12 of them are wrong. Gross is 300 ÷ 5 ÷ 1 = 60 WPM. Net is (300 − 12) ÷ 5 ÷ 1 = 57.6 WPM. Adjusted WPM stays at 60, because the method credits what you typed and reports accuracy separately.
That is a 2.4 WPM spread on a single minute at 96% accuracy. At 90% accuracy the spread widens to 6 WPM, and at 85% it is 9 WPM — which is why the same typist can look fast on one site and average on another.
Quote net WPM, and quote the accuracy beside it: "62 WPM net, 98.5% accuracy, 5-minute test". Anyone who screens typists knows the difference between the methods, and an unqualified number invites the assumption that you picked the flattering one.
If a job ad specifies a method — some government and court tests do — report that method and say so. Never mix: a gross 70 next to someone's net 65 is not a like-for-like comparison, and it makes the higher number look inflated.
Gross and net both fall as the clock runs, because the first thirty seconds are warm-up pace you cannot hold. A 15-second score is a burst; a 10-minute score is a shift. When you compare yourself to a published average, check how long the test was before you conclude anything about your speed.
The practical rule: train on one-minute rounds, verify on five, and quote the five-minute number. It is the only one an employer can reproduce.
## Frequently asked questions
Gross WPM counts every character you typed, right or wrong. Net WPM subtracts the incorrect characters first, so it reflects usable output. Net is always equal to or lower than gross.
Take the characters typed, subtract the errors, divide by five, then divide by the minutes elapsed. 300 characters with 12 errors over one minute is (300 − 12) ÷ 5 ÷ 1 = 57.6 net WPM.
Adjusted WPM (AWPM) is used in school and exam scoring. It credits all characters typed including errors and reports accuracy separately, so it matches gross WPM rather than net.
Usually the scoring method and the test length. A 15-second gross score can be 10 WPM higher than a 5-minute net score for the same typist. Compare like with like before deciding you got slower.
Net WPM with the accuracy and the test length, for example "62 WPM net, 98.5% accuracy, 5-minute test". That is reproducible and it answers the follow-up question before it is asked.

## Typing Test for Receptionist Jobs
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-receptionist.html

Front-desk work is typing while a phone rings. Employers screen at 40–50 WPM with high accuracy, not at headline speeds. This page covers what each employer type asks for and how to rehearse it.

A receptionist types names, phone numbers, appointment notes and short emails, usually while listening to someone. That means the skill being tested is accurate short-burst typing, not sustained prose speed. Recruiters typically quote 40–50 WPM and an accuracy floor around 95–98%.
The accuracy floor matters more than the speed number: a misspelt surname in a client record is a real cost, whereas 45 WPM instead of 50 is invisible in the day-to-day.
Employer | Typical requirement | What the test adds
Medical or dental front desk | 45–55 WPM, 98% accuracy | Patient names, dates of birth, procedure codes
Hotel or hospitality | 40–45 WPM | Booking references, email addresses
Corporate office | 50 WPM, 97%+ | Minutes, meeting notes, calendar entries
Legal reception | 50–60 WPM, 98%+ | Client names, case references, punctuation
Call centre with reception duties | 35–45 WPM | Typing while talking, call notes
These are the ranges that appear in public job ads and in recruitment guides; treat them as a target band, not a legal threshold. A posting that says 40 WPM rarely rejects a 42 that is clean.
Days 1–5: one 60-second sentence round, three times a day. Type at the speed where you make almost no errors and let the score climb on its own. Most people gain 5–8 WPM in a week at this stage simply by stopping the backspace habit.
Days 6–10: switch to two- and three-minute rounds so you meet the length most screening tests use. Add one Numbers round a day, because phone numbers and reference codes are where front-desk accuracy actually breaks.
Days 11–14: rehearse the real task — read a short message out loud and type it without looking at the keyboard, then check it character by character. That is the job. Then take one five-minute test and record net WPM plus accuracy as the number you quote.
Ask which scoring method the test uses, gross or net, and how long it runs. Then type at 90% of your best pace for the first thirty seconds; almost everyone loses more in corrections than they gain in the opening sprint.
If the test includes punctuation and capitals, do not skip them to save time. Uncorrected omissions are counted as errors on every mainstream test, and they are the most common reason a fast typist fails a receptionist screening.
## Frequently asked questions
Most postings ask for 40–50 WPM with 95–98% accuracy. Medical and legal front desks sit at the top of that band because names and reference codes must be exact.
Yes for most office, hotel and clinic roles. 45 WPM with clean accuracy clears the common 40 WPM floor; only legal and specialist desks routinely ask for 50–60.
Often. Phone numbers, appointment times and booking references are the realistic content, so practise the Numbers mode as well as sentences. Digits use a different finger pattern.
One to three minutes in most screening tools, sometimes five. Train at three minutes so a one-minute test feels short rather than tight.
For this role, yes. Records with wrong digits or misspelt names are rework. A 42 WPM run at 99% is a better signal to an employer than 55 WPM at 92%.

## Typing Test for Call Center Jobs
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-call-center.html

Call centre work is typing while listening. The requirement is lower than office typing — usually 30–45 WPM — but accuracy on names and reference numbers is what separates the shortlist from the reject pile.

Role | Typing target | Why
Inbound voice support | 30–40 WPM | Short call notes, CRM fields, reference numbers
Outbound sales | 30–40 WPM | Disposition codes and call-back notes
Chat and email support | 40–55 WPM | The conversation itself is typed, often two at once
Technical support | 40–50 WPM | Ticket text, error codes, device identifiers
Back-office and escalations | 45–55 WPM | Case notes and customer correspondence
Voice roles are deliberately lenient on speed: nobody types a paragraph while a customer is mid-sentence. What the test is really checking is that you can capture a name, a postcode and a reference without asking the caller to repeat themselves.
Reading and copying is a different task from hearing and recording. In the second, your eyes are free but your buffer is short — people drop the last two digits of a phone number because they were still typing the previous word.
Rehearse it directly: play a podcast or read a sentence aloud, then type it from memory in one pass and check it. Do five of these a day for a week. Accuracy on heard digits improves faster than raw speed, and it is the part the job actually punishes.
A transcription error on a card number, an order reference or a callback number turns into a second call, and second calls are the metric every contact centre tracks. Practise the Numbers mode for two minutes a day and check your error count rather than your speed.
If your accuracy on digits is below 97%, stop chasing speed for a week. The arithmetic is unforgiving: at 40 WPM with 94% accuracy you are generating about two and a half errors a minute, most of them in exactly the fields that matter.
Ask whether the test is scored gross or net, and whether the timer is visible. If it is, do not watch it — the countdown costs more accuracy than it buys speed.
Type in short bursts and release the keys between words. Call-centre typing rewards a steady rhythm over a fast start, because the test is usually one to three minutes and the notes you will type in the job are never longer than a sentence or two.
## Frequently asked questions
Usually 30–45 WPM for voice roles and 40–55 WPM for chat and email support, with accuracy above 95%. The numbers are lower than general office typing because most notes are short.
For inbound voice support, often yes, provided your accuracy on names and numbers is high. Chat support and technical roles ask for more because the conversation itself is typed.
Play audio or read a sentence aloud once, then type it from memory in a single pass and check it. Five repetitions a day for a week improves captured-digit accuracy noticeably.
Frequently. Reference numbers, postcodes and callback numbers are the realistic content. Practise the Numbers mode as well as sentences so the digit row is not a surprise.
95% is the usual floor and 98% is comfortable. Errors in customer identifiers create repeat calls, so screening tools often weight accuracy more heavily than speed for these roles.

## Typing Speed Percentile Calculator
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-speed-percentile.html

A WPM number means little without a distribution. This page converts your score into a percentile using the largest published sample of real typing — 136 million keystrokes from 168,960 volunteers.

The reference distribution comes from Dhakal, Feit, Kristensson and Oulasvirta, "Observations on Typing from 136 Million Keystrokes" (CHI 2018), which recorded 136,857,600 keystrokes from 168,960 volunteers. It reports a mean speed of 51.56 WPM with a standard deviation of 20.2, an average uncorrected error rate of 1.17%, and 1.173 keystrokes per character. The paper is open at doi.org/10.1145/3173574.3174220.
Percentiles below are computed from a normal distribution with that mean and standard deviation. It is an approximation: real typing speed is mildly left-skewed, so the approximation is slightly generous in the middle and slightly conservative in the far tail. It reproduces the study's reported deciles — top 10% above about 78 WPM, bottom 10% below about 26 WPM — to within about one percentile point, which is the check that matters.
WPM | Percentile (approx.) | CPM | Keystrokes per hour
20 | 6th | 100 | 6,000
26 | 10th | 130 | 7,800
30 | 14th | 150 | 9,000
40 | 28th | 200 | 12,000
50 | 47th | 250 | 15,000
60 | 66th | 300 | 18,000
70 | 82nd | 350 | 21,000
78 | 90th | 390 | 23,400
80 | 92nd | 400 | 24,000
90 | 97th | 450 | 27,000
100 | 99th | 500 | 30,000
120 | 99.9th | 600 | 36,000
The population behind the distribution - who was measured, on what device, and why the numbers differ between sources - is on the average typing speed page.
The sample is self-selected: people who choose to take an online typing test are not a random sample of the population, and they are disproportionately young, educated and comfortable in English. A 60 WPM score being the 66th percentile here does not mean it is the 66th percentile of all office workers.
The study also measures transcription typing — copying displayed text — on a desktop keyboard in English. Phone typing, dictation, code and non-Latin scripts are different tasks with different distributions, so a percentile from this table describes one specific skill.
For job applications, percentiles are persuasive but not what screeners check: they check against a fixed threshold such as 40 or 50 WPM. Use the percentile to decide whether you are in the band, and the raw net WPM to report it.
For practice targets, aim at the next decile rather than the mean. Moving from the 50th to the 66th is roughly 10 WPM and takes weeks; moving from the 90th to the 99th is 22 WPM and takes months of deliberate practice on specific key sequences.
Every figure on this page, with its source and a downloadable CSV, is collected on the typing speed benchmarks page.
## Frequently asked questions
About the 66th percentile, using the CHI 2018 distribution with mean 51.56 and standard deviation 20.2. In other words, faster than roughly two thirds of the volunteers in that study.
About the 99th. The study's fastest decile exceeded roughly 78 WPM, so 100 WPM sits well inside the top 1% of that sample.
51.56 WPM, from 136,857,600 keystrokes recorded from 168,960 volunteers (Dhakal et al., CHI 2018). Older sources often quote 40 WPM, which reflects office workers rather than self-selected test takers.
Within about one point across the middle of the distribution, and it reproduces the study's reported 10th and 90th percentile thresholds (about 26 and 78 WPM). Extreme tails above 130 WPM are less reliable.
It is based on speed as the study measured it, with errors reported separately at 1.17% uncorrected. A net score with heavy corrections would rank lower than the raw WPM suggests.
No. A percentile describes position in a sample; a ranking in a job test compares you to that employer's applicants. The thresholds employers use — 40, 50, 60 WPM — are usually fixed, not percentile-based.

## Typing Test for Nurses
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-nurse.html

Nurses do not type fast for a living; they type accurately under interruption. Charting notes, medication names and dosages are short, frequent and unforgiving. Practise at 35–45 WPM with accuracy above 98%.

A shift note is a few hundred characters typed between tasks: assessment findings, interventions, a time, a signature. The volume is modest. What breaks is the detail — a dose written as 10 instead of 100, a drug name auto-corrected into a different drug, an identifier attached to the wrong patient.
That is why nursing informatics training emphasises verification over velocity, and why the typing requirement in job ads is usually a modest 35–45 WPM. Speed matters because charting happens at the end of a twelve-hour shift when everyone wants to go home; accuracy matters because the error is clinical.
Digits. Dosages, vitals, weights and times are numeric. The number row is typed with a different reach than the home row and it is where most slips happen.
Look-alike drug names. Hydralazine and hydroxyzine, prednisone and prednisolone. Autocomplete is not your friend here; type the name rather than accepting a suggestion.
Interruption. You type half a sentence, answer a call bell, come back and continue in the wrong field. The typing skill is resuming without losing the thread.
Five minutes, twice a day. One 60-second sentence round for rhythm, one Numbers round for digits, then stop. Short daily rounds beat a weekly marathon because the skill you are training is availability under fatigue, not peak output.
Once a week, take one five-minute test and record net WPM and accuracy. Five minutes is roughly the length of a focused charting session, so it is the honest number to compare month to month.
Level | Net WPM | Accuracy | What it supports
Minimum for most postings | 35 | 97% | Short shift notes, care plans
Comfortable | 45 | 98.5% | Full assessment charting, discharge summaries
Fast | 55+ | 99% | Admissions, triage notes, telephone orders
These bands come from the ranges printed in nursing and medical-administration job advertisements; they are a target, not a licensure standard. No nursing board certifies a typing speed.
The people who struggle most are usually experienced clinicians, not new typists. Twenty years of handwriting produces efficient note language and a hunt-and-peck relationship with the keyboard. The fix is not a typing course; it is ten minutes a day of copying your own note style, not textbook sentences.
Type the phrases you actually write — "alert and oriented", "denies chest pain", "afebrile" — until they are automatic. Domain vocabulary is where speed comes from once the keys stop needing attention.
## Frequently asked questions
Most nursing and medical-administration postings ask for 35–45 WPM with high accuracy. The number is modest because notes are short; the accuracy expectation is high because dosages and identifiers are clinical data.
Sometimes, especially for roles with heavy electronic documentation such as triage, admissions or telehealth. More often it is assumed rather than tested, which is why a low speed shows up later as unpaid overtime.
A wrong digit in a dose or a wrong patient identifier is a clinical incident, not a typo. Corrections also cost more time than typing slightly slower, so a 45 WPM run at 99% finishes a shift ahead of 60 WPM at 94%.
Use the Numbers mode for two minutes a day and grade yourself on errors rather than speed. Dosages, vitals and times are the content that matters, so numeric accuracy is the skill to build first.
Five minutes once a week for the benchmark, plus 60-second bursts daily for rhythm. A five-minute round approximates a charting session; a 15-second round measures a sprint you will never use on a ward.

## Typing Test for Court Reporters
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-court-reporter.html

Court reporting certification is 225 words per minute — on a stenotype machine, not a QWERTY keyboard. The two numbers are not comparable, and confusing them is the most common mistake applicants make.

A stenotype writes syllables, not letters: multiple keys are pressed together and a chord resolves into a word or phrase. That is how 225 WPM is reachable at all. A QWERTY keyboard writes letter by letter, and the fastest competitive typists in the world top out around 200 WPM in short bursts on text they can see.
So the 225 WPM requirement is not a claim that court reporters can type 225 WPM on a laptop. It is a test of realtime dictation capture through a machine built for it.
Speed | Machine | Typical meaning
180 WPM | Stenotype | Often the floor for graduation from a reporting program
200 WPM | Stenotype | Entry-level freelance work in many markets
225 WPM | Stenotype | The certified reporter standard, tested on live dictation
260 WPM | Voice or stenotype | Higher-tier certification for fast proceedings
60–90 WPM | QWERTY | Transcript editing, scoping, proofreading support roles
The lower bands are programme requirements rather than universal law: schools and states vary. Check the specific certification body before planning a timeline around one number.
Most working hours are not spent on the machine. They are spent editing: correcting names, fixing speaker attribution, verifying exhibit numbers and formatting the transcript. That work happens on a keyboard, and it is where a reporter's day actually goes.
Scoping and proofreading roles, which are the usual entry point while certification is pending, are keyboard jobs outright. A 60–80 WPM editing speed with clean accuracy is the practical requirement.
Dictation practice, not typing practice, moves the stenotype number: five minutes at a speed where you can write every word, then a speed where you cannot. The second set is where the growth happens, provided you review the strokes you fumbled.
Use a keyboard test for the editing half of the job. Ten minutes of 10-minute rounds at 98% accuracy will make transcript cleanup painless, and it is the part candidates neglect because it is not the number they are chasing.
## Frequently asked questions
No. 225 WPM is a stenotype standard, achieved by chording syllables on a purpose-built machine. Keyboard typing at that speed is not what the certification measures.
60–90 WPM is comfortable for transcript editing, scoping and proofreading, which is where most keyboard time goes. Accuracy matters more than speed because transcript corrections are billable work.
Reporting programmes typically run two to four years, and speed is the usual reason people take longer. The machine skill is built by daily dictation practice at the edge of your current speed.
There are voice-writing and digital reporting routes, and some jurisdictions accept them. They have their own certification requirements, so confirm with the body that governs your state or country.
For the editing side, yes — it measures sustained keyboard accuracy rather than a burst. It will not predict your steno speed, which is a different motor skill.

## Typing Test for 911 Dispatchers
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-dispatch.html

Dispatch is typing while talking, under a clock. Agencies commonly ask for 35–45 WPM, but the deciding factor is whether a plate number, an address or a callback number survives contact with a stressed caller.

A dispatcher enters an address, a name, a phone number and a plate while the caller is still explaining. The typing is short, numeric and immediately consequential. Public postings typically list 35–45 WPM, and the assessment usually adds a multitasking or call-taking simulation on top of the typing score.
No single national typing standard applies to dispatch; requirements are set per agency. Treat published ranges as the target band and check the specific posting, because a state police dispatch centre and a small municipal one often differ by ten WPM.
Prose typing rewards rhythm. Dispatch typing rewards the number row, the ten-key area and the ability to spell an unfamiliar street name correctly the first time. That is a different practice target.
Numbers mode for two minutes a day, graded on errors not speed.
Listen to a podcast and type the numbers you hear — times, prices, years — in one pass.
Type addresses from a map app, including postcodes, without looking down.
Role | Typical WPM floor | Added assessment
Call taker | 35–40 | Structured call interview, data capture
Dispatcher | 40–45 | Radio simulation, multitasking test
Supervisor or trainer | 45+ | Quality assurance, report writing
The typing test is rarely the only gate. Agencies also test hearing, memory, prioritisation and stress tolerance, and a 60 WPM score will not offset a failed call simulation.
Two-minute rounds are the right length: long enough to feel the pressure of a call, short enough to repeat. Two minutes at 45 WPM net with 99% accuracy on digits is a stronger signal than five minutes of prose at 55.
Then rehearse the split-attention part. Read a sentence aloud, type it from memory in one pass, and check character by character. Five repetitions a day for two weeks is enough to feel the difference in how you hold digits in working memory.
## Frequently asked questions
Usually 35–45 WPM, with accuracy weighted heavily. Requirements are set per agency rather than nationally, so the posting is the authority.
No. The call-taking simulation and multitasking assessment usually eliminate more candidates. Typing is a floor you clear so the rest of the assessment can be scored.
Both, but lead with numbers. Plate numbers, addresses and callback numbers are the content that fails in real calls, and the number row is where untrained typists lose the most accuracy.
Aim for 99% on digits. A transposed digit in an address sends responders to the wrong place, which is the failure mode agencies screen hardest for.
Often the assessment includes a simulated call where you must enter data as it is spoken. Rehearse that directly: audio in, one-pass typing out, then verify.

## SSC CHSL Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/ssc-chsl-typing-test.html

Two different skill tests sit inside SSC CHSL: 35 WPM English or 30 WPM Hindi for LDC and JSA posts, and 8000 key depressions per hour for DEO posts. They are scored differently and rehearsed differently.

Post | Standard | Duration | Scoring
LDC / JSA | 35 WPM English or 30 WPM Hindi | 10 minutes | Words per minute with an error allowance
DEO / DEO Grade A | 8000 key depressions per hour | 15 minutes | Total key depressions against an 8000/hour rate
8000 key depressions per hour is about 26.7 WPM under the five-character convention, but it is measured as raw keystrokes including corrections you make, so a typist who backspaces constantly loses ground even at a good words-per-minute rate.
The typing test is qualifying: you either clear the standard or you do not, and the score does not add to your merit total. That changes the strategy completely. A candidate chasing 45 WPM with 12% errors fails; a candidate at 37 WPM with 3% errors passes.
Practise with the error budget in view: type at a pace where you can hold mistakes under the allowance, and never let a correction spree eat the clock. On the 10-minute LDC test, thirty seconds lost to backspacing is roughly 18 words you never typed.
The test is taken on a standard QWERTY keyboard provided at the centre. Hindi candidates may opt for Krutidev or Remington layout depending on the notice in force, and the layout is usually chosen at the application stage — check your admit card and the current notice rather than assuming.
Because the machine is not yours, rehearse on something other than your laptop at least twice before the exam. Key travel and spacing change your error rate more than practice volume does.
Week 1: ten-minute rounds at a comfortable pace, recording accuracy only. Week 2: same length, push until errors cross the allowance, then back off 3 WPM — that is your exam pace. Week 3: alternate sentences and passages with punctuation, because the actual passage includes capitals and full stops. Week 4: full-length simulations at the same time of day as your shift, with no pause button.
The DEO candidate should add a daily 15-minute numbers round, since key depressions include digits and the numeric reach is the slowest part of the keyboard for most people.
## Frequently asked questions
35 words per minute in English or 30 words per minute in Hindi for LDC and JSA posts, and 8000 key depressions per hour for DEO posts. Both are qualifying tests.
Qualifying. It does not add marks to your total; you either meet the standard or you do not. That is why accuracy matters more than a high raw speed.
Ten minutes for LDC and JSA, fifteen minutes for DEO. Practise at the full length rather than in one-minute bursts, because the error rate at minute nine is what decides the result.
A small error allowance applies, commonly around 5% of the words typed, and it is specified in the notice for that cycle. Check the current notice: the allowance and the passage length change between years.
No. The test is conducted on centre equipment. Rehearse on a different keyboard at least twice so key travel and spacing are not a surprise on the day.

## Typing Test for 5th Graders
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-5th-graders.html

By fifth grade most children can type 25–35 WPM if they have had regular practice, and accuracy matters far more than the number. Here is what the grade bands look like and how to practise without tears.

Classroom benchmarks vary by district and by how much keyboarding time a school actually provides, so treat any table as a rough band rather than a standard. The pattern that holds across published curricula is steady growth of roughly 5 WPM per grade once formal instruction begins.
Grade | Typical range | What to focus on
3rd | 10–20 WPM | Home row, not looking down
4th | 15–25 WPM | All letters, capitals with Shift
5th | 25–35 WPM | Accuracy above 90%, punctuation
6th–8th | 30–45 WPM | Sustained paragraphs, editing
A child who types 35 WPM by hunting for keys with two fingers has hit a ceiling that will cost years later. A child at 22 WPM with all ten fingers on the home row is on a curve that reaches 50 by secondary school with no extra lessons.
So score the round on errors, not words per minute. If accuracy is below 90%, the speed number is fiction — it is measuring how fast the child can produce text that has to be retyped.
Ten minutes, three times a week, is enough. One minute of warm-up, five minutes of the actual test, then two minutes of the child's own choice — quotes, pangrams, numbers. Stop while it is still fun; the failure mode is a forty-minute session that ends in an argument and no practice for a month.
