Use the on-screen keyboard and finger guide on this site so the child can see which finger owns which key without an adult narrating it. Cover the hands with a light cloth for one round a week if looking down has become a habit — it is uncomfortable for two days and then it works.
Games are legitimate practice if the child is typing rather than watching. The test that matters: are the fingers moving on the home row, or is one finger stabbing at the keyboard while the other hand rests? If it is the second, the game is entertainment and the drill still has to happen separately.
A reasonable split for a fifth grader is one game session for every two test sessions. The test gives the number; the game gives the motivation.
## Frequently asked questions
Roughly 25–35 WPM with 90% or better accuracy if they have practised regularly. Bands vary by school and by how much keyboarding instruction the child has actually had.
No. It is normal for a child who has not had formal keyboarding instruction. What matters is whether the fingers are on the home row and whether accuracy is climbing.
Ten minutes, three times a week. Short and frequent beats a long weekly session, and it keeps practice from becoming a punishment.
Not while testing. Looking down is the habit that caps speed. Cover the hands for one round a week so the child is forced to build a mental map of the keys.
Yes when the child is genuinely typing with correct fingers. If the game rewards speed with two fingers, it teaches a habit that has to be undone later.

## Typing Test for Legal Secretaries
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-legal-secretary.html

Legal support is the top of the clerical typing band: 60–70 WPM with accuracy high enough for citations, party names and numbered paragraphs. Speed alone will not pass the formatting half.

A legal document is read by people who will quote it back. Party names must be exact, citations must be punctuated correctly, and a paragraph number that shifts breaks every cross-reference after it. That combination pushes the requirement to 60–70 WPM in job advertisements, above the 40–50 WPM typical of general clerical roles.
The speed figure exists because documents are long. A 40-page agreement at 45 WPM is two days of typing; at 65 WPM it is a day and a half with time left for checking.
Numbered paragraphs. Auto-numbering that renumbers on paste is the single most common formatting failure.
Capitalisation of defined terms. "the Company" is not "the company", and a find-and-replace will not fix it safely.
Citations. Italics, full stops and abbreviations follow a house style; consistency is the whole job.
Track changes. Typing inside a tracked document is slower and less forgiving than typing into a blank page.
Setting | Typical WPM | Accuracy | Notes
Small general practice | 55–65 | 98% | Letters, forms, correspondence
Corporate legal department | 60–70 | 98.5% | Contracts, board papers
Litigation support | 65–75 | 99% | Court filings, exhibits, indexes
Transcription-heavy role | 70+ | 99% | Dictation, hearing notes
Ranges reflect what appears in legal recruitment advertising; a firm that tests will usually set its own floor and tell you before the test.
Stop practising plain sentences after the first week. Type a real contract clause, complete with defined terms and numbered sub-paragraphs, and check it against the source line by line. That is a slower exercise and a far better predictor.
Then add the time pressure: five-minute rounds of dense text with punctuation, targeting 98.5% accuracy. If your accuracy falls below that at 70 WPM, work at 60 until it holds — a legal document with two errors per page costs more to check than it saved to type.
## Frequently asked questions
Commonly 60–70 WPM with accuracy near 98.5%, which is above the 40–50 WPM typical of general clerical roles. Firms that test usually state their own floor.
For a small general practice handling letters and forms, often yes. Corporate and litigation roles usually screen at 60 and above because documents are long and reference-heavy.
A plain typing test does not, but the job is mostly formatting. Rehearse numbered paragraphs, defined terms and citations separately, because those are the errors that get noticed.
Type real clauses rather than random sentences, then proof against the source. Capitals, full stops and italics are pattern work, and patterns only build on realistic text.
Yes. At 60+ WPM sustained over long documents, looking at the keyboard is the limiting factor. Two weeks of home-row drills typically adds more than months of hunt-and-peck speed work.

## Federal Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/federal-typing-test.html

The US federal clerical standard is 40 words per minute on a five-minute sample with no more than three errors. It is a pass or fail gate, not a score to maximise, and it is easier than most commercial tests if you rehearse the exact format.

Federal clerical and office-automation positions are commonly advertised with a typing requirement of 40 words per minute, demonstrated on a five-minute sample, with no more than three errors. Some agencies accept a self-certification on the application; others ask for a certificate from a testing centre or an approved online test.
The arithmetic is simple: 40 WPM for five minutes is 200 words, or about 1,000 correct characters at five characters per word. Three errors in that sample is 1.5% - so the real requirement is roughly 98.5% accuracy at a moderate speed, not a fast run.
They practise one-minute bursts. A five-minute sample has a different error profile: fatigue, drifting attention, and the temptation to speed up when the end is in sight.
They correct too much. Three errors are allowed; twelve corrections in a panic can push you under 40 WPM even though your accuracy was fine.
They have never seen the format. Some tests show the passage continuously and scroll; others replace line by line. Rehearse both.
Run a five-minute sentence test with the passage visible and no pause. Then count: net WPM must exceed 40 and uncorrected errors must stay at or below three. Do this three times in a week; if all three pass, the format is not going to surprise you.
If you are failing on errors rather than speed, slow to about 45 WPM indicated and hold it. The extra five WPM of headroom is what absorbs a bad sentence.
A self-certification is the fastest route: you state your speed on the application and the agency may verify later. A proctored certificate costs money and takes a visit, but it never expires in the middle of a hiring cycle and some postings require it outright.
Read the announcement carefully. If it says "must submit a typing test with your name and date", a self-certification will be rejected, and a certificate older than a year is often refused as well.
Once you clear 40 WPM, stop optimising it. Federal screening is qualifying: a 70 WPM score does not add points that a 45 WPM score misses. Put the remaining effort into the rest of the application, where the competition actually is.
Keep one dated record of a passing five-minute run so you can attach it to future applications without re-testing.
## Frequently asked questions
Commonly 40 words per minute from a five-minute sample with no more than three errors for clerical and office-automation roles. Individual announcements state their own version, so read the posting.
No. 40 WPM is around the 28th percentile of measured typists, and most people reach it within a few weeks of daily practice. The error limit is the part that catches people.
Three in a five-minute sample at the 40 WPM standard. That is about 1.5% of the characters, so the practical target is 98.5% accuracy or better.
Only if the announcement says so. Many federal postings accept self-certification at application and verify later; some require a dated test result with your name on it.
Sometimes, if the result shows your name, the date and the test length. Check the specific announcement first, because agencies differ on which providers they accept.

## Civil Service Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/civil-service-typing-test.html

State and county civil service exams typically require 40 net WPM on a five-minute proctored sample, and they issue a certificate with an expiry date. The rules vary by jurisdiction, so the notice is the authority.

You apply for a clerical title, the agency tells you whether a typing certificate is required at application or after a conditional offer, and you book a proctored test. The result is filed against your name and often carries an expiry - commonly between one and four years depending on the state.
Some jurisdictions accept a certificate from a commercial testing centre, some run their own at a workforce office, and a few allow remote proctoring. The one constant is that the sample is timed, five minutes in most cases, and scored on net words per minute.
Score | What it usually clears | What it does not
30-35 net WPM | Some entry clerk and typist titles | Office assistant and secretary titles
40 net WPM | The most common civil service floor | Senior clerical, legal and medical support
50 net WPM | Senior reception, HR support, court clerk | Transcription and court reporting
60+ net WPM | Legal secretary, word processing operator | Stenographic titles, which need machine skills
These are the bands that appear across published county and state postings; a specific notice will name one figure, and that figure is the one that matters.
Civil service scoring almost always deducts errors before reporting the score. That means a cautious 44 net is worth more than a reckless 55 gross that nets 38 after a dozen mistakes.
Rehearse accordingly: type at the pace where errors stay under about 2%, then check the net figure rather than the raw one. If your net and gross differ by more than 5%, accuracy is the whole project for the next two weeks.
Bring photo identification, arrive early, and expect the keyboard to be unfamiliar - usually a basic membrane board rather than the laptop you practise on. Type one warm-up sentence before the clock starts if the proctor allows it.
Keep a copy of the certificate. Replacing a lost one usually means re-testing, and a lapsed certificate takes you off the eligible list until you rebook.
## Frequently asked questions
40 net WPM is the most common floor for clerical titles, taken from a five-minute sample. Senior clerical, legal and court roles often ask 50 to 60 net WPM.
Usually one to four years depending on the jurisdiction. The notice states the validity period; an expired certificate generally takes you off the eligible list until you re-test.
Net, in almost all cases - errors are deducted before the score is reported. Practise to a 2% error rate so the deduction cannot change your result.
Some jurisdictions allow remote proctoring and some require an in-person session at a workforce or testing centre. Check the notice for the title you are applying to.
Rarely for typing itself - it is usually a qualifying gate. Your rank on the list comes from the written examination and any experience credits, not from typing faster than the minimum.

## CritiCall Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/criticall-typing-test.html

CritiCall is not a typing test with extra steps - it is a battery of dispatcher simulations, and keyboarding is one module among many. Here is what the typing modules actually measure and how to prepare for the ones you cannot see on a typing site.

CritiCall is a computer-based pre-employment testing battery for public-safety telecommunicators. Agencies configure which modules they use, so two candidates for two different agencies can sit substantially different tests. The keyboarding module is usually a short, time-limited data-entry task rather than a prose passage.
That is why practising prose typing alone does not prepare you. If you have been told your agency uses CritiCall, the typing component is the easiest part; the modules that fail candidates are the ones involving simultaneous listening and recording.
Keyboarding / data entry: short timed entry of names, addresses and numbers, scored on accuracy and speed.
Call summarisation: read or hear a call and produce a short structured summary within a time limit.
Memory recall: reproduce details - a plate, a street, a name - after a delay.
Cross-referencing and prioritisation: match records, decide which incident outranks which.
Map reading and spatial judgement: pick the closest unit or the correct jurisdiction.
Basic arithmetic and spelling: small, time-limited question sets.
The exact list is agency-configurable, and the vendor does not publish a universal pass mark. Your agency sets the cut score, and it is not disclosed to candidates in advance.
Use the Numbers mode for two minutes at a time and grade on errors. The content in the module is alphanumeric - addresses, dates, codes - so digits and capitals matter more than prose rhythm.
Then rehearse the split-attention skill separately: play a recorded voice giving an address and a callback number, type both in one pass, and verify character by character. That is closer to the job than any prose typing test.
Expect to move between modules quickly, with instructions read aloud under time pressure. The common failure is not slowness; it is losing the instruction because you were still finishing the previous screen.
Read the instruction line before touching the keyboard, then work at a pace you can sustain for the whole module. Timed batteries punish the candidate who sprints the first screen and runs out of attention on the fifth.
## Frequently asked questions
No. It is a multi-module pre-employment battery for dispatchers. Keyboarding and data entry are modules inside it, alongside call summarisation, memory recall, map reading and prioritisation.
There is no universal published figure - agencies set their own cut scores. The keyboarding module is typically short and time-limited, in the 35-45 WPM range that dispatch postings quote.
It varies by agency because each one selects its own module set. Expect a session of roughly one to two hours rather than a five-minute typing sample.
You can practise the component skills - timed alphanumeric entry, listening and recording, memory recall - but the actual battery is administered by the agency. Practise the skills, not the interface.
Numbers and addresses, then listening while typing. Those two cover the keyboarding module and the module most candidates find hardest.

## Alphanumeric Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/alphanumeric-typing-test.html

Most typing tests use prose. Real data entry is alphanumeric: reference codes, postcodes, part numbers, invoice IDs. Mixed content is slower and less forgiving, and it is what employers actually screen.

On a QWERTY keyboard the letters sit under your fingers and the digits sit on the row above, reached with an extended finger and no tactile landmark. Every transition from a name to a number costs a reach, a visual check and a return.
The result is that someone who types prose at 60 WPM often manages 35-40 WPM on mixed alphanumeric content. That is not a regression; it is a different task, and it is the task data-entry employers test.
Number row reaches - 1 to 0 with the correct finger, without looking down. Two minutes a day.
Alternating patterns - strings like AB12CD34, which force a shift between letter and digit clusters.
Numeric keypad - if the job is invoice or order entry, the ten-key pad is faster than the number row and worth learning separately.
Verification - read your own output against the source, character by character, once per round. This is the step that separates 97% from 99.5%.
Unit | Formula | Typical requirement
Keystrokes per hour (KPH) | characters per minute × 60 | 8,000-12,000
Key depressions per hour (KDPH) | all keys pressed, corrections included | 8,000 (SSC DEO)
Fields per hour | completed records, not characters | role-specific
Accuracy | correct fields ÷ total fields | 97-98%
Field accuracy is the metric that matters in practice. A record with one wrong digit is a failed record regardless of how fast the other nineteen fields were typed.
Week one: two minutes of Numbers mode, twice a day, graded on errors. Add one round of alternating letter-digit strings. Week two: move to five-minute blocks and score fields, not characters - type a real form layout (name, reference, date, amount) repeatedly and count how many records come out clean.
Stop when a five-minute block produces three consecutive clean records. At that point your accuracy is job-ready and further gains come from speed work, which is the easier half.
## Frequently asked questions
A typing test using mixed letters and digits rather than prose - reference codes, postcodes, part numbers and IDs. It measures the skill data-entry roles actually use.
Digits sit on the number row, which needs an extended reach with no tactile landmark. Switching between letters and numbers costs time, so 35-40 WPM on mixed content is normal for a 60 WPM prose typist.
97-98% on fields, and often 99% for medical or financial records. One wrong digit makes the whole record invalid, so field accuracy matters more than character speed.
Use the keypad for numeric-heavy work such as invoices and order entry, and the number row when digits are mixed into text. Learning ten-key properly is usually worth a week of practice.
Usually in keystrokes per hour or key depressions per hour, sometimes in completed fields per hour. 8,000-12,000 KPH is the common data-entry band.

## Typing Test for Virtual Assistants
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-virtual-assistant.html

Virtual assistant work is mostly written: inboxes, calendars, CRM notes, research summaries. Clients commonly look for 55–65 WPM with clean accuracy, and many screen with a paid trial task rather than a typing test.

A VA's output is measured in completed tasks, and most tasks are typed: replies, notes, data cleanup, scheduling messages. At 45 WPM a morning of inbox work takes three hours; at 65 WPM it takes two, which is the entire margin a client is paying for.
That is why VA postings cluster at 50-65 WPM rather than the 40 WPM typical of in-office clerical roles. The work is not harder, it is simply a bigger share of the job.
Clean written English. Typos in a client-facing email cost more than a slow reply. Accuracy is the first filter.
Formatting discipline. Bullets, dates, time zones, signatures - the same output every time.
Tool fluency. Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, a CRM, a scheduling tool, and increasingly an AI assistant used to draft rather than to replace judgement.
Turnaround. A trial task with a deadline is the most common screen, and it tests all four at once.
Keep a dated five-minute result with a visible WPM and accuracy, and mention the test length. "62 WPM net, 99% accuracy, five-minute test" is credible; "fast typist" is not.
If a client asks for a trial, deliver it in the format you would actually use - correct file naming, a short cover note, no stray formatting from a copy-paste. Half of VA trials fail on presentation rather than content.
Dictation and editing. Drafting by voice and cleaning up by keyboard is how experienced VAs double throughput on long-form work, and it is a different skill from typing tests: you need fast, accurate editing rather than fast transcription.
Practise by dictating a paragraph, then editing it to publishable quality in under two minutes. If the edited version reads better than your typed draft, you have the workflow.
## Frequently asked questions
Most postings ask for 50-65 WPM with high accuracy. The upper end reflects that nearly all VA output is typed, so speed converts directly into completed tasks.
Some ask for a score, but many use a paid trial task instead. A trial tests speed, accuracy, formatting and reliability at the same time, which a typing test cannot.
Yes for general admin support, provided your written accuracy is high. Specialist work such as transcription, bookkeeping support or medical admin usually expects 60 WPM or more.
Keep a dated five-minute result showing WPM and accuracy, and offer to re-test live on a call. That is usually accepted because it is verifiable in the moment.
Yes. Drafting by voice and editing by keyboard is faster than typing long documents, and it is a selling point for clients with heavy written output.

## Typing Test for Medical Billing
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-medical-billing.html

Billing and coding work is numeric and exact: CPT and ICD codes, dates of service, amounts, member IDs. Employers typically look for 45–55 WPM, but a single transposed digit is a denied claim.

A claim has a fixed shape: patient, payer, codes, dates, amounts. Every field is typed rather than composed, so throughput is a direct function of keyboard accuracy and speed. Postings commonly ask 45-55 WPM, and the accuracy expectation is high because a rejected claim costs the practice money and time.
The number is lower than transcription because the text is short. The consequence of an error is higher, which is why billing tests weight accuracy far more heavily than speed.
ICD-10 codes mix letters and digits in patterns like M54.5 or E11.9; CPT codes are five digits, sometimes with modifiers. The digits are frequently the same key reached with the same finger in sequence, which is where transpositions happen.
That is a typing problem, not a knowledge problem: 99213 becoming 99123 is a motor slip. Practise numeric strings and alternating letter-digit patterns until the sequence errors fall, then add the code vocabulary.
Two minutes of Numbers mode daily, graded on errors rather than speed.
One round of alphanumeric entry - the alphanumeric test is closer to claims work than a prose passage.
Five-minute blocks scoring clean records: type a mock claim line (code, date, amount) ten times and count how many are perfect.
Target three consecutive clean five-minute blocks before you claim the skill on a CV. That is roughly the accuracy a billing manager is buying.
Quote net WPM, accuracy and test length, and add the numeric result separately if you have one - for example "52 WPM net, 99% accuracy on alphanumeric entry". Billing managers read the second number first.
If you have coding certification but a modest typing score, say so plainly and offer a timed sample. A 45 WPM coder with clean output is employable; a 65 WPM coder generating denials is not.
## Frequently asked questions
Usually 45-55 WPM with 98% or better accuracy. Speed matters less than error-free entry of codes, dates and amounts, because a rejected claim costs more than a slow one.
No. Both sit in the same band. Coding adds judgement and code lookup rather than more keystrokes, so speed is rarely the limiting factor.
98% is the usual expectation and 99% is comfortable. Field-level accuracy matters most: one wrong digit in a code or an amount is a denied claim, not a typo.
Both, but lead with numbers and alphanumeric strings. Claims are mostly codes, dates and amounts, and the number row is where untrained typists lose accuracy.
Often yes, if your accuracy is clean and you know the code sets. Employers will usually prefer a careful 45 over a careless 65 because denials are expensive.

## 30 WPM Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/30-wpm-typing-test.html

Thirty words per minute is 150 characters a minute, or 9,000 keystrokes an hour. It is the floor most clerical and dispatch postings quote, and roughly the 14th percentile of measured typists — close enough to reach in weeks, not months.

30 WPM is 150 characters per minute, 9,000 keystrokes per hour (KPH), and 9,000 key depressions per hour if you make no corrections. It is 0.5 words per second.
For context: 30 WPM is faster than roughly 86% of people are slower than — that is, about the 14th percentile of the 168,960-person sample behind the CHI 2018 typing study, whose mean was 51.56 WPM.
Requirement | At 30 WPM
Some dispatch and call-centre floors (30-35 WPM) | Clears
County clerk postings at 35-40 net WPM | Short by 5-10
US federal clerical standard (40 WPM) | Short by 10
Data entry at 8,000 KPH (26.7 WPM) | Clears on speed, accuracy decides
Receptionist at 40-50 WPM | Short
So 30 WPM is a starting point rather than a qualification for most office work. The gap to 40 is the single most valuable 10 WPM you will ever add, because it moves you across the most common screening line.
Almost nobody is stuck at 30 because their fingers are slow. They are stuck because they look at the keyboard, which forces a look-down-look-up cycle on every word, and because they correct with the backspace key instead of slowing down.
The two fixes, in order: cover your hands for one round a day so the looking habit breaks, then set a rule that you do not backspace during a test round. Your raw score will climb by 4-6 WPM within two weeks of holding both rules, before you have practised any speed work at all.
Days 1-7: three one-minute rounds a day, hands covered for one of them, no backspace. Record accuracy only. Days 8-14: switch to two-minute rounds, still no backspace, and add one Numbers round because digits are where beginners lose the most.
At the end, take one five-minute test and record net WPM. If you are above 35, continue with the 40 WPM plan. If you are still at 30, the constraint is the looking habit, not effort — keep the covered round daily for another two weeks.
## Frequently asked questions
It is about the 14th percentile, so it is below average but far from hopeless. It clears a few dispatch and data-entry floors; most office postings ask for 40 WPM or more.
Usually two to six weeks of daily ten-minute practice, mostly by fixing the look-at-keyboard habit and cutting corrections. Progress is faster at this level than at 60 WPM.
9,000 KPH. Thirty words per minute is 150 characters per minute, and 150 × 60 = 9,000.
Accuracy. At this level most lost time is corrections, so holding 97% accuracy while typing steadily raises the score faster than a deliberate speed push.
Yes, and that is the trap. Two-finger typing plateaus around 35-40 WPM. Learning the home row costs two uncomfortable weeks and removes that ceiling.

## 40 WPM Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/40-wpm-typing-test.html

Forty words per minute is the number that appears in more job postings than any other: 40 WPM, five minutes, few errors. It is roughly the 28th percentile — the threshold that separates 'can type' from 'can be employed to type'.

40 WPM is 200 characters per minute, 12,000 keystrokes per hour, and 200 words over a five-minute test. On a standard error rule of one error per ten words, you are allowed about twenty errors across the five minutes — which sounds generous until you watch your score after a bad paragraph.
The US federal clerical standard is published as 40 WPM over five minutes with no more than three errors, which is far stricter: 98.5% accuracy. Most private employers quote the speed and leave the accuracy floor at 95%.
Role | Stated requirement | At 40 WPM
Receptionist | 40-50 net WPM | Bottom of the band
General office / admin | 40-55 WPM | Bottom of the band
County clerk-typist | 35-45 net WPM | Comfortable
US federal clerk | 40 WPM, ≤3 errors | Exactly at the line
Data entry clerk | 45-65 WPM or 13,500+ KPH | Short
Being exactly at the line is risky on a five-minute test, because one bad sentence can drop you under it. Aim for 44-45 before you apply, which gives you the margin that 40 alone does not.
Week 1 — measure and stop the bleeding. Three five-minute rounds, no backspace rule, accuracy recorded. Most candidates at 40 WPM are correcting 8-12 times a minute; removing that habit alone buys 3-5 WPM.
Week 2 — cover the keyboard. One round a day with hands covered. This is uncomfortable for three days and then stops being an issue, and it is the difference between a ceiling at 45 and no ceiling.
Week 3 — length and mode. Five-minute sentence rounds three times a week, one numbers round a week. Add capitals and punctuation deliberately: real tests include them and untrained typists drop them under time pressure.
Week 4 — simulate. Full-length, time of day matching your interview, unfamiliar keyboard. Then test once and use that number on applications.
Stop training for 40 and move to the 60 WPM plan; the skill work is the same but the drills change. At 55 you are already above the requirement for almost every clerical role, so further gains are for transcription, legal and medical work rather than for clearing a gate.
## Frequently asked questions
For most clerical, receptionist and county government roles, yes — 40 WPM is the figure those postings quote. Aim for 44-45 so a bad sentence on a five-minute test cannot drop you below the line.
About the 28th percentile of the CHI 2018 sample (mean 51.56 WPM, standard deviation 20.2). Roughly seven in ten measured typists are faster.
12,000 KPH. Forty words per minute is 200 characters per minute, and 200 × 60 = 12,000.
Five minutes, with no more than three errors in most published announcements. That is 98.5% accuracy, stricter than the 95% floor private employers usually apply.
Two to six weeks of daily ten-minute practice for most people, mostly from removing the look-at-keyboard habit and reducing corrections rather than from raw speed drills.

## 50 WPM Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/50-wpm-typing-test.html

Fifty words per minute is the median: half of measured typists are faster, half slower. It clears almost every office requirement and it is where most people plateau — which is why the useful work here is about breaking a ceiling, not clearing a gate.

Fifty words per minute is 250 characters per minute, 15,000 keystrokes per hour, and about the 47th percentile of the 168,960-person CHI 2018 sample. It is the middle of the distribution, not a fast score — but it is above the 40 WPM line that most clerical postings quote, which is what matters for employment.
It is also the exact point where most self-taught typists stop improving. The reason is not finger speed: it is that they read one word at a time, so their eyes and hands take turns instead of working together.
At 50 WPM you are typing roughly four characters per second. That is fast enough that the read-type-read cycle becomes the bottleneck rather than the keystrokes themselves. Fast typists read one to three words ahead and let the hands work on a buffer; plateaued typists read the word they are about to type.
The second cause is uniform speed. Typing every word at the same pace means slowing down for easy words and losing time on hard ones. Skilled typists accelerate through familiar sequences and slow slightly on unfamiliar ones, which averages out higher.
Look-ahead drill: before you start, read the first line aloud in your head. Then type it without re-reading. Do this for five rounds; it feels wrong for three of them.
Burst drill: 15-second rounds, maximum speed, twice a day. This trains the top end you cannot reach in a one-minute test.
Bigram drill: the twenty most common letter pairs in English (th, he, in, er, an, re, on, at, en, nd...). Practising transitions rather than words is what moves you from 50 to 65.
Accuracy floor: never let a session end below 96%. Speed built on errors does not survive a five-minute test.
It clears general office, admin, receptionist, county clerk and most customer-service requirements. It does not clear data entry quoted at 13,500+ KPH (45 WPM is 13,500, so you are at the entry edge), legal secretary at 60-75, or medical transcription at 65-80.
If your goal is a specific posting, read the number in the posting and train to that plus five. If your goal is general employability, 50 is enough and the next ten points are optional.
## Frequently asked questions
It is about the 47th percentile — essentially the median adult score — and it clears almost every office, admin and receptionist requirement. It is a solid, employable speed rather than a fast one.
Read ahead by one to three words, drill 15-second bursts for top-end speed, and practise common letter pairs rather than whole words. Most people need four to eight weeks of short daily sessions.
15,000 KPH. Fifty words per minute is 250 characters per minute, and 250 × 60 = 15,000.
Almost always because you read one word at a time, so your eyes and hands take turns. Look-ahead practice and bigram drills address that directly, where more of the same typing does not.
At the entry edge. 50 WPM is 15,000 KPH, above the 8,000-12,000 KPH most postings quote, but below the 13,500-19,500 band used for senior data-entry roles.

## 60 WPM Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/60-wpm-typing-test.html

Sixty words per minute is the 66th percentile and the point where job descriptions stop saying 'typing required' and start saying 'fast, accurate typing'. It is also the floor for legal, medical and transcription roles.

Sixty words per minute is 300 characters per minute, five characters per second, 18,000 keystrokes per hour, and about the 66th percentile of measured typists. Two thirds of people are slower; one third are faster.
In employment terms it is a threshold: clerical adverts quote 40-50, whereas legal, medical and transcription adverts start at 60 and go up. Crossing 60 changes which jobs are open to you, which is why it is worth more effort than crossing 50.
At 60 WPM a 2% error rate means about one error every 8 seconds — roughly seven or eight errors in a five-minute test. On a net-scored test that costs you 5-6 WPM, dropping you back to the mid-50s. That is the arithmetic that keeps people at 55.
So the last stretch is not 'type faster'. It is 'hold 98% while typing at 60', which is a different drill: shorter rounds, stricter error budget, and stopping a round the moment accuracy falls below the floor rather than pushing to the timer.
30-second accuracy sprints: type at 90% of maximum for 30 seconds, stop, check errors. Repeat five times. This builds the accuracy-at-speed habit that longer rounds cannot.
Punctuation and capitals: most people lose 3-5 WPM here. Run rounds with quotes and sentence case deliberately until the Shift press stops breaking rhythm.
Numbers once a week: the number row is a separate motor skill and it is where a 60 WPM typist becomes a 52 WPM typist on real work.
One long round per week: ten minutes, to confirm the speed survives fatigue.
Medical transcription commonly asks 65-80 WPM with 98-99% accuracy, and it is measured over audio, which is harder than copying visible text. Court reporting is 225 WPM on a stenotype and is a different skill entirely.
For legal secretary work, 60-75 WPM is the advertised band, so 60 is the entry edge — aim for 65 before applying to a firm that tests.
## Frequently asked questions
It is about the 66th percentile and the point where job adverts start calling typing 'fast'. Top 10% is 78 WPM and above, so 60 is comfortably above average but not exceptional.
Legal secretary roles (60-75), transcription entry points (65+), medical admin and word-processing operator titles. Most general office roles stop at 50.
18,000 KPH. Sixty words per minute is 300 characters per minute, and 300 × 60 = 18,000.
Four to eight weeks of short daily sessions for most people, provided the practice targets accuracy at speed rather than raw output.
Net scores subtract them. A 60 WPM gross score at 94% accuracy nets about 56, which is why the accuracy floor matters as much as the speed target.

## 70 WPM Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/70-wpm-typing-test.html

Seventy words per minute is the 82nd percentile — faster than four out of five measured typists, and the entry band for general transcription. At this level the limiting factor stops being your fingers and becomes your rhythm.

Seventy words per minute is 350 characters per minute, 21,000 keystrokes per hour, and roughly the 82nd percentile of the CHI 2018 sample. It is faster than the top-quintile boundary and still 8 WPM short of the top decile at 78.
That last stretch is the hardest in typing: the 70-to-80 range typically takes months rather than weeks, because the easy inefficiencies are already gone.
Below 60 WPM most gains come from removing bad habits — looking down, backspacing, two-finger reaches. Above 70 there are no bad habits left to remove; the work is consistency. A 70 WPM typist's speed varies by 15-20% between rounds, and the variance itself is what holds the average down.
So the metric to watch changes from peak WPM to the spread between your best and worst round. Narrowing that spread raises the average faster than trying to sprint.
Ten consecutive one-minute rounds, once a week. Record all ten. The number that matters is the lowest, not the highest.
Hard-text rounds: quotes with punctuation, code, or pangrams. Speed on easy sentences is not transferable; speed on awkward text is.
Audio transcription practice: transcribe two minutes of speech and time it. Spoken English runs at 130-160 WPM, so 70 WPM typing leaves you well behind real-time — which is why transcriptionists use foot pedals and text expanders.
Text expansion: learn five short forms for phrases you type constantly. At this level, tooling beats training.
Transcription is advertised at 65-80 WPM, but the measurement is over audio with playback control, not over visible text. The skill gap is short-term memory: you hear a phrase, hold it, and type it, which is harder than copying.
If transcription is the goal, test yourself on audio rather than on this page. If it is not, 70 WPM already clears every clerical requirement and further speed is a hobby.
## Frequently asked questions
Yes — about the 82nd percentile, faster than four in five measured typists. It is the entry band for general transcription and well above every clerical requirement.
21,000 KPH. Seventy words per minute is 350 characters per minute, and 350 × 60 = 21,000.
Usually months, not weeks. The easy inefficiencies are gone by 70; remaining gains come from consistency, hard-text practice and tooling such as text expansion.
It is the entry band for general transcription, which advertises 65-80 WPM. Medical and legal transcription often expect the upper end plus domain vocabulary.
Variance is normal and grows with speed. Track your lowest of ten rounds rather than your best; narrowing the spread is what raises a 70 WPM average toward 80.

## 100 WPM Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/100-wpm-typing-test.html

One hundred words per minute is roughly the 99th percentile of measured typists. It is not a faster version of 70 WPM — the technique is different, the practice is different, and for most jobs it is not required at all.

One hundred words per minute is 500 characters per minute, about 8.3 characters per second, and 30,000 keystrokes per hour. In the CHI 2018 distribution with mean 51.56 and standard deviation 20.2, it sits near the 99th percentile — roughly one typist in a hundred.
For comparison: the fastest decile starts around 78 WPM, so 100 is not the edge of the distribution but well inside its tail. World-record competition typing exceeds 200 WPM on short bursts of known text, which is a different activity again.
At 70 WPM you are typing words. At 100 WPM you are typing letter sequences with almost no conscious word recognition — the buffer is two to four words deep and the hands run ahead of attention. Typists at this level typically cannot tell you what they just typed.
That is why deliberate practice at 100 WPM looks strange: it is mostly very short maximum-speed bursts on familiar text, plus accuracy work on unfamiliar text, plus keyboard and layout optimisation. Long slow practice rounds stop helping.
For employment, no. The highest clerical requirement you will meet is 75-80 WPM (legal, medical transcription) and court reporting uses a stenotype, not a keyboard. Above 80, extra speed adds no job options.
For work where you think in text — programming, live captioning, competitive typing, writing to a deadline — it removes the keyboard as a bottleneck entirely. That is a real but narrow benefit, and it costs months of practice to reach.
Keyboard: a mechanical board with short-travel switches is measurably faster for most people than a laptop chiclet keyboard. Try before buying.
Layout: some typists gain 5-10% from Colemak or Dvorak after a month of pain. Most do not; measure before committing.
Bursts: 15-second maximum rounds, ten per session, three sessions a week. Long rounds teach endurance you already have.
Accuracy gate: never accept below 97%. A 100 WPM score at 94% nets 94 and fails any real test.
## Frequently asked questions
Yes — roughly the 99th percentile of measured typists. About one in a hundred people in the CHI 2018 sample typed at or above that speed.
30,000 KPH. One hundred words per minute is 500 characters per minute, and 500 × 60 = 30,000.
No standard clerical role does. Legal and medical transcription top out around 80 WPM, and court reporting uses a stenotype at 225 WPM rather than a keyboard.
Usually years from a standing start, and months from 80. The gains come from short maximum-speed bursts, hard-text accuracy work and keyboard optimisation rather than more of the same practice.
Effectively no. Two-finger typing plateaus around 35-40 WPM because each keystroke needs a visual target. Reaching 100 requires all ten fingers and no looking.

## WPM Chart: Is Your Typing Speed Good?
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/wpm-chart.html

Find your score in the table, read the verdict. Percentiles come from the 168,960-person sample behind the CHI 2018 typing study (mean 51.56 WPM, SD 20.2), and the job bands come from advertised requirements.

WPM | Percentile | Verdict | What it opens
20 | 6th | Slow — hunting for keys | Nothing that screens; fine for personal use
26 | 10th | Below average | Entry data entry at 7,000-8,000 KPH if accuracy is high
30 | 14th | Below average but workable | Some dispatch and call-centre floors
40 | 28th | Good enough — the standard floor | Most clerical, receptionist and county government roles
50 | 47th | Average adult | Office, admin and customer service bands
60 | 66th | Fast | Legal secretary entry, transcription entry
70 | 82nd | Very fast | General transcription, medical admin
80 | 92nd | Top decile | Medical transcription upper band, competitive typing
100 | 99th | Top 1% | No job requires it; it removes typing as a bottleneck
120 | 99.9th | Exceptional | Competition level on short bursts
Percentiles are a normal approximation of the study distribution; it reproduces the paper's reported deciles (about 26 and 78 WPM) to within a point. The percentile page computes any score exactly.
Background on how those figures were measured, and why a 40 WPM figure and a 51.56 WPM figure can both be right, is on the average typing speed page.
The verdict is relative to the measured population, not to a job you want. A 45 WPM score is genuinely average and genuinely enough for a receptionist posting; both statements are true at once. Employers do not rank candidates by percentile, they compare against a fixed number in the advert.
So use the percentile to know where you stand and the job column to know what to aim at. If the posting says 50 and you are at 44, the gap is a fortnight of accuracy work, not a personality problem.
Five-minute net WPM with the accuracy beside it. A 15-second run reads 5-10 WPM higher, random word lists read lower than sentences, and gross reads higher than net. Any of those will flatter or penalise you relative to this chart.
If you only have a one-minute score, subtract 5 before reading the table. It is a rough correction, but it is closer than treating a burst as your real speed.
20 to 30: stop looking at the keyboard. One covered round a day for two weeks. This is the largest single gain available to anyone.
30 to 40: stop backspacing during tests. Most people at 30 lose 5-6 WPM to corrections.
40 to 50: accuracy at speed. Thirty-second sprints at 90% of maximum, checked every round.
50 to 60: read ahead. The bottleneck moves from the fingers to the eyes, and look-ahead practice fixes it.
60 to 80: consistency. Type ten one-minute rounds and track your worst, not your best.
Each band has a different cause, which is why generic advice stops working after the first twenty points.
The underlying study figures, the phone-versus-keyboard comparison and a CSV of this curve are on the benchmarks page.
How the count is made - five characters per word, errors subtracted - is set out on the words per minute test page, which reports both raw and net.
If you have characters and time rather than a test score, the typing speed calculator converts them into gross WPM, net WPM, CPM, KPH and a percentile.
## Frequently asked questions
Yes — about the 66th percentile, faster than two thirds of measured typists, and the point where job adverts start calling typing fast. It is the entry band for legal secretary and transcription work.
It is the standard floor: around the 28th percentile and the number most clerical, receptionist and county government postings quote. Aim for 44-45 so a bad sentence cannot drop you under it.
51.56 WPM from the CHI 2018 study of 168,960 volunteers, with a standard deviation of 20.2. Older sources quoting 40 WPM describe office-worker samples instead.
Yes, about the 99th percentile. No standard clerical job requires it; it matters for competitive typing, live captioning and heavy code work.
Test length, text type and scoring method all move the number by 5-10 WPM. A five-minute net score on sentences is the figure this chart refers to; a 15-second gross score is not comparable.

## Typing Speed: Phone vs Keyboard
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-speed-phone-vs-keyboard.html

Two large studies measured the same task on different devices: 36.2 WPM on a phone (37,370 volunteers) and 51.6 WPM on a desktop keyboard (168,960 volunteers). The 15 WPM gap is real, measured, and mostly mechanical.

Measure | Phone (touchscreen) | Desktop keyboard
Average speed | 36.17 WPM (SD 13.22) | 51.56 WPM (SD 20.2)
Uncorrected error rate | 2.34% | 1.17%
Keystrokes per character | 1.18 | 1.173
Volunteers | 37,370 | 168,960
Source | Palin, Feit, Kim, Kristensson & Oulasvirta, MobileHCI 2019, doi.org/10.1145/3338286.3340120 | Dhakal, Feit, Kristensson & Oulasvirta, CHI 2018, doi.org/10.1145/3173574.3174220
Both studies used the same method - transcribe a displayed English sentence - so the comparison is unusually clean. The mobile study explicitly compares itself to the desktop one and reports that average performance is about 15 WPM slower on a phone.
Fewer fingers. Over 74% of phone typists use both thumbs, and two thumbs are faster than one thumb or one index finger - but still nowhere near ten fingers on a physical keyboard.
No tactile feedback. You cannot feel the key boundary, so every press carries a small positional uncertainty that a keyboard removes.
Correction cost. Fixing a mistake on glass takes more gestures, which is why phone typists leave more errors uncorrected (2.34% versus 1.17%) rather than fixing them.
Layout. A QWERTY touchscreen is a compromise; physical keyboards can be swapped for whatever suits your hands.
Using the mobile distribution (mean 36.2, SD 13.2), a normal approximation gives a rough position:
Phone WPM | Approx. percentile | Reading
20 | 11th | Slow thumb typing
30 | 32nd | Below the phone average
36 | 50th | Exactly average for phone users
45 | 75th | Fast for a phone
60 | 97th | Exceptional on glass
The approximation is labelled as such: the mobile distribution is right-skewed, so the far tail is less reliable than the middle.
Most online typing tests and every job screening test assume a physical keyboard. A 36 WPM phone score is not evidence that you would score 36 WPM at a desk - the desk number is usually higher, often by 10-15 WPM if you touch type.
The reverse is also true and less convenient: a good desktop score does not transfer to mobile work. If your job involves replying from a phone, practise separately, because the two skills share vocabulary but not motor memory.
Only if the work happens on a phone. Practising phone typing to raise a desktop score is wasted effort; the mechanics do not transfer. If you want the desktop number to rise, use a keyboard and work on accuracy and look-ahead.
Where phone practice does pay: switching to two thumbs if you currently use one finger, and enabling autocorrect, which the mobile study found correlates with faster entry. Word prediction, by contrast, correlated with slower entry in that dataset.
## Frequently asked questions
36.17 words per minute, from a study of 37,370 volunteers (Palin et al., MobileHCI 2019), with 2.34% of errors left uncorrected. The fastest participants exceeded 80 WPM.
About 15 WPM on average: 36.2 on a phone versus 51.6 on a desktop keyboard, measured with the same transcription task in two large studies.
Yes. Over 74% of participants used both thumbs, and that was significantly faster than one thumb or a single index finger, though still about 70% of desktop speed.
Correcting on a touchscreen costs more gestures than pressing backspace on a keyboard, so phone typists accept more errors instead of fixing them - 2.34% uncorrected versus 1.17% on desktop.
You can, but do not. Screening tests assume a physical keyboard and the same skill typically scores 10-15 WPM higher on one. Use a desktop or laptop for any test that counts.

## Typing Speed by Grade
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-speed-by-grade.html

Grade-level typing expectations are bands, not standards: schools differ enormously in how much keyboarding time they provide. Here is what the published classroom ranges look like, and what to actually teach at each stage.

Grade | Typical WPM band | Priority
1st-2nd | 5-11 WPM | Finding letters; keyboard familiarity, not speed
3rd | 10-20 WPM | Home row and correct fingers
4th | 15-25 WPM | All letters without looking down
5th | 25-35 WPM | Accuracy above 90%, capitals with Shift
6th | 30-40 WPM | Punctuation, sustained paragraphs
7th-8th | 35-45 WPM | Editing, formatting, real documents
These are the ranges that appear across classroom keyboarding curricula and district technology plans; treat them as a guide to whether a child is roughly on track, never as a pass or fail line. A child who has had no formal instruction can be two grades behind the band and still catch up in a term.
Two things are still developing before about age ten: hand size relative to the keyboard, and the fine motor control needed for independent finger movement. A seven-year-old reaching across a full-size keyboard is doing a different physical task from a twelve-year-old.
That is why early keyboarding instruction focuses on letter location and posture rather than words per minute. Pushing speed before the hands are ready produces the two-finger hunt-and-peck style that later caps out around 35-40 WPM.
For the adult benchmarks those grade bands are heading towards, see average typing speed.
Grades 1-2: letter games, five minutes at a time, no timer. The goal is knowing where the keys are.
Grades 3-4: home row drills and short un-timed copying. Cover the hands for one round a week once the home row is secure.
Grade 5: timed one-minute tests, but score accuracy first. A child at 90% accuracy will overtake a faster child who types sloppily.
Grades 6-8: full-length tests, real documents, editing practice. This is when speed starts to matter for schoolwork volume.
One test a week, one minute long, and read out the accuracy before the speed. Children optimise for whatever the adult reacts to - if the number that gets attention is WPM, they will type faster and sloppier within a fortnight.
Keep a simple record of the weekly score so progress is visible when it feels slow. Children improve in steps: three flat weeks and then five WPM in one.
First check the physical setup: feet supported, elbows near 90 degrees, screen at eye level, a keyboard that is not oversized. A child typing on an adult keyboard at the wrong height will underperform regardless of practice.
Then check the method: are they using all fingers and not looking? If not, that is the whole project for the next month, and grade-level speed will follow. If both are fine and the score is flat, the issue is usually practice frequency, not ability - five minutes four times a week beats thirty minutes once.
## Frequently asked questions
Roughly 25-35 WPM with 90%+ accuracy if they have had regular keyboarding practice. Bands vary widely by school and by how much instruction the child has actually received.
Usually 10-20 WPM. At this age letter location and home-row habit matter far more than speed, and timed tests should not be the main activity.
35-45 WPM is a reasonable band by the end of middle school, with accuracy above 95%. Students who reach it usually had formal instruction around grade 4 or 5.
No. It is normal for a child without formal keyboarding instruction, and it is well within the grade 4-5 band. What matters is whether the fingers are on the home row.
Ten minutes, three to four times a week. Short frequent sessions build the motor pattern; a long weekly session mostly builds frustration.

## How to Put WPM on a Résumé
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/how-to-put-wpm-on-resume.html

A typing speed belongs on a résumé only when the job screens for it, and it should be written so it can be verified: method, length and accuracy, not a bare number.

Put it in the skills section, not the summary. A recruiter scanning for a 50 WPM requirement looks at skills, certifications and the line under the job title - not at a paragraph about your professional philosophy.
Skills line: Typing: 62 WPM net, 98.5% accuracy (5-minute test)
Within a role bullet: "Typed 60+ WPM net while handling 40+ client records daily" - only when the job actually required it.
Certification line: Typing certificate, 55 WPM, proctored at [testing centre], [date] - when a formal certificate is required.
Net WPM subtracts errors, so it is the number a screening test will reproduce. Gross WPM without a length is unverifiable and reads as the flattering version - recruiters who hire typists know the difference.
Adding the test length does two things: it signals that you know a 15-second burst is not a working speed, and it pre-answers the follow-up question. "62 WPM net (5-minute)" is more credible than "70 WPM" even though the number is lower.
Leave it off when the role does not screen for typing: management, sales, design, engineering, research. A speed listed against a job that never asked for it looks like filler, and an average number can create a doubt that would not otherwise exist.
The exception is when typing is an explicit part of the posting - a project manager who writes documentation all day can reasonably list 60 WPM if the advert mentions documentation volume.
If you list a number, expect to be tested. Most employers use a short online test, and a handful ask for a certificate. If your listed score came from a one-minute burst on a good day, the live test will read 5-8 WPM lower and the discrepancy is what they will notice.
So list the score you can reproduce on a bad day, at the test length the employer uses. If you do not know the length, assume five minutes and quote that.
Take a five-minute test now, screenshot the result, and use that number - it is current and reproducible. Re-test every six months or after a role change, because typing speed drifts with how much you type.
Keep the screenshot. It costs nothing and it settles the occasional "can you prove that" question without a re-test.
## Frequently asked questions
Yes for clerical, data entry, transcription, dispatch, legal support and customer service roles that screen for typing. No for roles where typing is not part of the job description.
"Typing: 62 WPM net, 98.5% accuracy (5-minute test)". Net, with accuracy and test length, so the number is reproducible rather than flattering.
Yes. 60 WPM net is about the 66th percentile and above almost every clerical requirement. Below 40 WPM, only list the number if the posting explicitly asks for a lower threshold.
Net. Screening tests deduct errors, so a net figure is what they will measure. Gross WPM without a stated method reads as inflated.
Often yes, with a short online test or a certificate. List a score you can reproduce at the same test length, because a live test that reads lower than your résumé is a credibility problem.

## Will Employers Accept a Free Typing Certificate?
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-certificate-acceptance.html

A free certificate printed from a website is self-reported evidence, not a credential. Some employers accept it, some require a proctored test, and knowing which is which saves you a wasted application - or a wasted fee.

Type | What it proves | Who accepts it
Self-issued certificate (printed from a website) | That you used the site and got a score | Some private employers, as a screening signal
Third-party timed result (dated, named, unproctored) | A specific score on a specific date | Many private employers; occasionally agencies
Proctored certificate (testing centre or remote proctor) | That someone observed the test | Government, courts, staffing agencies, some hospitals
The difference that matters is observation. A certificate nobody watched you earn establishes intent and baseline skill; it does not establish that the score is yours.
Private-sector applications where the recruiter just wants a rough number before scheduling an interview.
Freelance profiles - showing a dated result is better than claiming "fast typist".
Your own tracking - a monthly certificate is a simple progress record.
In all three cases the certificate is a convenience, not proof. Do not pay for one believing it changes the category.
Public-sector postings frequently state the requirement in a way that excludes self-issued documents: "must submit a typing test with your name and date", "proctored within the last twelve months", "issued by an approved testing centre". If the wording includes any of those, a website certificate is not the document they want.
Court and legal roles, dispatch centres and hospital transcription departments are the most consistent about requiring a proctored result. The cost is usually modest; the inconvenience is the appointment.
No stated proctoring. If nobody observes the test, you are buying a PDF.
No verification ID or lookup page. An employer cannot check it, so it carries no more weight than your own screenshot.
No expiry stated. Real credentials state validity; typing certificates typically run one to four years.
Scores that cannot be this high. A service guaranteeing 90+ WPM to anyone is selling paper.
Keep a dated, named screenshot of a five-minute result and put the number on your résumé with the test length and accuracy. Then let the employer test you - which most will, and which you will pass if the listed number is honest.
If a posting demands a proctored certificate, book one at a local testing centre or workforce office and treat the fee as part of the application cost. It is the only version that satisfies that wording.
## Frequently asked questions
Some private employers accept them as a screening signal, but they are self-reported. Government, court, dispatch and hospital roles usually require a proctored or employer-administered test instead.
Only a proctored one. A certificate printed from a website shows that you took a test, not that anyone verified the result.
Typically one to four years depending on the issuer or agency. Postings often refuse results older than twelve months, so check the wording before reusing an old certificate.
Yes, with the test length and accuracy, for example "55 WPM net, 98% accuracy, five-minute test". Expect to be re-tested, and list a score you can reproduce.
Only when a posting asks for a proctored result or a specific issuer. For private-sector applications, a dated screenshot and an honest résumé line do the same job for free.

## All Typing Tests
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-tests.html

Every test on the site in one directory: duration variants, languages, skill drills, exam and job pages, metrics and guides. Each link says what the page measures rather than repeating a keyword.

Type a word above to filter the list below - a job title, a language, a unit, a length, a format. The directory is generated from the site's own page configuration, so it always matches what exists.
Three questions decide which page you want. First: are you measuring or improving? A timed test on the home page measures; a practice page with drills improves.
Second: what length? Fifteen and thirty seconds measure a burst, one to three minutes matches most screening tests, and five to ten minutes measures the pace you can hold through a working session.
Third: what content? Sentences are the default, quotes add punctuation and capitals, numbers train the row that data entry actually uses, and code tests are for programmers. Languages switch the practice pool without changing the timer.
I have an interview or screening test — start with the five-minute test, then the role page for your job, which lists the threshold the employer is likely to use.
I want a number to quote — a five-minute net score with accuracy is the reproducible one. The certificate page explains what a self-issued certificate does and does not prove.
I am learning from scratch — home row, then beginner, then one-minute rounds. Ten minutes a day beats a weekly marathon.
I am stuck at a speed — the WPM chart names the cause for each band, from looking at the keyboard at 20 WPM to inconsistency above 70.
The footer already links every page, but a flat list of 160 links tells a reader nothing about which one to open. This directory groups them by the question they answer, and it is generated from the same configuration that builds the pages, so it cannot drift out of date or link to something that no longer exists.
New to this? The free typing test gives you a sixty-second baseline before you choose a longer test; come back here once you know roughly where you stand.
Choosing between sites rather than tests? The comparison of six free typing tests covers sign-up, ads, languages and certificates.
For the length most screening tools use, start with the three-minute test.
