## SQL Typing Practice
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/sql-typing-practice.html

SQL is punctuation with words attached. Every query needs quotes, semicolons, parentheses and usually a pipe, and those keys are where analysts lose their speed. This drill types 36 real queries, not prose.

Plain English uses 26 letters and a space. A single SELECT statement uses quotes, a semicolon, parentheses, an underscore, a dot and often a pipe or a cast operator. None of those sit under the home row, so a typist who is comfortable at 70 WPM on prose will typically drop to 40-50 WPM here.
The second factor is structure. You are not copying a sentence, you are reproducing a syntax tree, and the eye has to jump between keywords and symbols instead of flowing left to right. That is a trainable skill and it is separate from general typing speed.
Single quotes on the pinky, doubled in SQL because strings are delimited - the most common source of a broken query.
Parentheses and underscores on the right pinky, which is already the weakest finger for most typists.
Semicolons and colons, one key apart, typed in sequence in casts and labels.
Pipes and arrows for concatenation and JSON access, which pull the right hand off the home row entirely.
If your error log concentrates on the pinky keys, that is not a knowledge gap - it is a reach problem, and it responds to a few minutes of deliberate symbol drill per day.
The pool on this page is 36 real statements: a projection, a join with an alias, a grouped aggregate, a CTE, a window function, an index creation, an UPDATE with a timestamp. They are the shapes you actually type in a working day, not keyword soup.
Run one-minute rounds until the syntax stops needing thought, then move to three-minute rounds. Analysts rarely type one query at a time; they type twelve in a row while reading output, and the stamina matters more than the peak.
If you write Python or JavaScript, the Python code typing and JavaScript code typing pools use the same engine with different syntax. For spreadsheet work, the Excel formula practice page trains the same bracket-and-comma vocabulary in a different grammar.
For a general benchmark rather than a drill, take the WPM test - code typing and prose typing are not comparable numbers, so keep the two scores separate.
## Frequently asked questions
40-60 WPM on real queries is comfortable for most analysts. Prose speed is not comparable because SQL has roughly one symbol every five characters, and symbols need extended reaches.
Symbols do not sit under the home row. Quotes, parentheses, underscores, pipes and semicolons all need an extended finger, and alternating between words and symbols breaks the rhythm that prose typing relies on.
Yes - 36 statements covering SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, CTEs, window functions, UPDATE, DELETE, DDL and JSON access, written in ordinary PostgreSQL-flavoured syntax.
Indirectly. No one screens analysts on typing speed, but at 30 WPM the keyboard becomes the bottleneck when you are writing long ETL scripts or documentation.
Five to ten minutes a day, one-minute rounds, scored on errors. Symbol accuracy improves faster than raw speed, and it is the part that actually costs you time in a query.

## TypeScript Typing Practice
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typescript-typing-practice.html

TypeScript adds a second layer of punctuation to JavaScript: angle brackets, colons, question marks and arrows in every signature. This drill types 36 real lines from application code, not toy examples.

Angle brackets for generics, typed with Shift plus comma and Shift plus full stop - two reaches that pull both hands off the home row.
Colons and question marks in type annotations and optional properties, frequently adjacent.
Arrow operators in callbacks, which need the hyphen and the greater-than key in sequence.
Braces and parentheses in destructuring and object literals, often nested three deep.
A JavaScript typist at 65 WPM typically measures 50-58 WPM on the same content once types are added. That is not a regression in skill; it is more symbol work per line.
Thirty-six lines taken from ordinary application code: an interface with optional fields, a discriminated union result type, a typed reducer, a generic type guard, an error class with a constructor parameter property, a debounce hook, a fetch with an abort signal, and a schema `.safeParse` branch.
They are deliberately not one-liners from tutorials. Real files mix declarations, expressions and early returns, and switching between those shapes is what makes editor typing feel different from typing a passage.
Type the lines as written, including semicolons and trailing commas. Autocomplete does not type for you during the drill, which is the point: you are rebuilding the muscle memory that autocomplete usually hides.
Then run one round with the on-screen keyboard visible and watch which key your eye goes to before the miss. It is usually the bracket cluster on the right, and it is fixable in a week of two-minute drills.
For plain JavaScript, the JavaScript code typing page uses the same engine without the type layer. For Python, Python code typing. Spreadsheet work is on the Excel formula page.
## Frequently asked questions
Yes, typically 10-20% slower at the same accuracy, because types add angle brackets, colons, question marks and arrow operators that JavaScript does not require.
Most developers sit above 60 WPM on prose and 45-55 WPM on code. No employer screens for it, but below 40 WPM the keyboard starts to limit how much code and documentation you produce.
No. Autocomplete hides the symbol reaches, so they stay weak. Typing full lines rebuilds them, which is what you need when you write something autocomplete does not know.
Yes, 36 lines of ordinary application TypeScript: interfaces, unions, generics, hooks, async/await, error classes and schema validation branches.
Two weeks of five-minute daily drills usually shows 5-8 WPM on this content, mostly from the bracket cluster ceasing to need a visual check.

## Rust Typing Practice
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/rust-typing-practice.html

Rust is the most punctuation-dense mainstream language: lifetimes, turbofish-free generics, match arms, ? and => on nearly every line. This drill types 36 real lines from ordinary Rust code.

Three characters dominate: & for borrows, ' for lifetimes and char literals, and < > for generics. Each sits on the top row or the right pinky, and lifetimes put the apostrophe immediately after an ampersand - a two-key sequence that prose never asks for.
Then there is the shape of idiomatic Rust: `match` arms with indentation, iterator chains broken across lines, and `?` at the end of expressions. The line breaks are part of the syntax you are training, not formatting noise.
Thirty-six lines covering the constructs that appear in real files: a struct with a generic parameter, a lifetime-annotated function, a `match` with an error branch, a `HashMap` build, an iterator chain with `filter_map`, a trait implementation, a `#[derive]` attribute, an async function signature with `anyhow::Result`, and a test module.
The lines are short enough to finish inside a minute round and varied enough that you cannot memorise the sequence.
Alternate two rounds per session: one straight accuracy round at your normal pace, one where you deliberately slow to 80% and watch the right hand. The second round is where the improvement happens; the first is where you measure it.
Track the errors rather than the WPM for the first week. In symbol-dense code, error count is the leading indicator and speed follows it, not the other way round.
Same engine, different grammar: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, SQL. If you want the general number, use the programmer typing benchmarks page.
## Frequently asked questions
No one measures this formally. In practice most developers type prose at 60-90 WPM and real Rust at 40-55 WPM because of symbol density and line breaks.
A lifetime needs an apostrophe immediately followed by a letter, and borrows need ampersands. Both sit on the top row and the right pinky, so the sequence interrupts the home-row rhythm.
Yes, 36 lines of ordinary Rust: generics, lifetimes, match arms, iterator chains, trait impls, async signatures and a test module.
Not directly. It matters only when the keyboard becomes the bottleneck for long files, documentation or review comments - below about 40 WPM on code, that happens regularly.
Five minutes a day for two to three weeks. Symbol accuracy responds quickly; after that, speed follows without extra drills.

## Excel Formula Typing Practice
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/excel-formula-typing-practice.html

A formula is a chain of brackets, commas and dollar signs wrapped around a function name. XLOOKUP, SUMIFS, FILTER and LET all punish the keys you never practise. This drill types 36 real formulas.

Parentheses - every function opens one and most nest two deep; an unbalanced bracket stops Excel accepting the entry at all.
Commas - the argument separator in en-US locales, and a semicolon in many European ones. Typing a full stop instead is the single most common formula error.
Dollar signs - absolute references need Shift+4, a reach that pulls the left hand off the home row.
Double quotes - required around text criteria, and doubled inside strings.
None of these appear often in prose, which is why people who type quickly in Word still fumble a nested IF.
Thirty-six formulas at the level a real spreadsheet uses: a basic SUM range, IFERROR-wrapped VLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH, SUMIFS with two criteria, TEXTJOIN, XLOOKUP with a fallback, SUMPRODUCT, LET, FILTER, SORT(UNIQUE()), MAP with LAMBDA, CHOOSECOLS, VSTACK and a SEQUENCE date series.
They are written the way they appear in a cell, including the leading equals sign, because that keystroke is part of the habit.
Type into a plain text field first, then reproduce the best lines in a real workbook. The drill builds the keystroke sequence; the workbook confirms that the brackets balance and the separators are the ones your locale expects.
If your locale uses semicolons as argument separators, type the formulas with semicolons after the drill. Muscle memory for the wrong separator is worse than no practice.
Numeric work benefits from the 10-key typing test, and data-entry roles are covered by the keystrokes per hour test. For database syntax rather than spreadsheet syntax, see SQL typing practice.
## Frequently asked questions
For formula-heavy work, yes. Analysts who can type a nested function without looking at the keyboard build models noticeably faster, and they make fewer bracket-balance errors.
An unbalanced parenthesis, followed by a full stop typed where a comma separator belongs. Both are stopped by Excel and both cost a re-type of the whole argument list.
Whichever your locale uses. En-US uses commas; many European locales use semicolons. Practise the one your workbook expects, because the habit is hard to unlearn.
Yes, 36 formulas using current functions including XLOOKUP, XMATCH, FILTER, SORT, UNIQUE, LET, LAMBDA, MAP, CHOOSECOLS and VSTACK.
Five minutes a day for a week is enough to stop fumbling the bracket and dollar reaches; after that, use it as a warm-up before model-building sessions.

## Typing Test for Accountants
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-accountants.html

Accountants do not need prose speed. They need numeric accuracy at pace: 10-key entry, decimals in the right place, and the ability to type a figure once and have it be right.

A ledger entry is a date, an account code, a description and an amount. Three of those four are numeric or alphanumeric, and the amount has a decimal point in a position that matters more than any word you will type all day.
Firms rarely quote a words-per-minute figure in accounting adverts because prose speed is not the constraint. If they test at all, it is a numeric or 10-key exercise, or an Excel-based work sample.
Task | Target | Why
10-key numeric entry | 8,000-12,000 KPH | The band employers quote for numeric data entry
Accuracy on amounts | 99%+ | A transposed digit is a reconciliation problem
Alphanumeric codes | 97-98% | Account and tax codes mix letters and digits
Prose notes | 40-50 WPM | Enough for memos and client correspondence
In practice the accuracy column decides whether you are useful. A 12,000 KPH entry rate with 96% accuracy creates more work than it saves, because every error has to be found later.
Learn the keypad as a separate instrument: 4-5-6 on the home row, index on 4, middle on 5, ring on 6, thumb on 0. Type without looking, entering a figure and pressing Enter after each, which is how accounting software behaves.
Then add the parts that break in real work: negative signs, decimal points, and the Tab key between fields. A drill that only types clean integers trains a skill you will never use.
Use the 10-key typing test for keypad speed, the Numbers mode on this page for mixed numeric content, and the Excel formula practice page for spreadsheet syntax. Then measure prose separately with the WPM test if a posting asks for it.
Keep the three numbers distinct on a CV. "12,000 KPH 10-key, 99.2% accuracy; 48 WPM prose" tells an accounting manager far more than a single WPM figure.
## Frequently asked questions
Postings rarely quote one. Numeric entry at 8,000-12,000 keystrokes per hour with 99% accuracy on amounts matters more than prose speed, which is usually fine at 40-50 WPM.
Sometimes, especially for accounts payable, payroll and bookkeeping roles. Larger firms more often use an Excel work sample, which tests the same accuracy under realistic conditions.
About 33 words per minute equivalent, or 167 characters per minute. On a numeric keypad that is a comfortable working pace rather than a sprint.
A transposed digit in an amount becomes a reconciliation break, which takes longer to find and fix than the entry saved. Accounting work is judged on the ledger balancing, not on entry rate.
The keypad, for amounts. Use the number row only for alphanumeric strings such as account codes where your hand is already on the main keyboard.

## Typing Test for Paralegals
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-paralegal.html

Paralegal typing is document work: exhibit lists, citations, numbered paragraphs and defined terms. Firms look for 50–65 WPM, but the errors that matter are formatting errors, not slow words.

Paralegal and legal assistant adverts commonly quote 50-65 WPM, below the 60-75 band for legal secretaries because the role includes more research and drafting than pure transcription. Accuracy expectations are high in both, because a document that misnames a party is a real problem.
That is why the useful practice is not speed drills on random sentences but repeated typing of the structures you will actually produce: a caption block, a numbered list with consistent indentation, a citation with the right punctuation, a table of exhibits.
Numbering. Auto-numbering that renumbers when you paste is the most common way a filing goes out wrong.
Defined terms. "the Company" keeps its capital; the rest of the document depends on it.
Citations. Italics, full stops and abbreviations follow a house style, and consistency is the whole point.
Track changes. Typing inside a tracked document is slower and less forgiving than typing a blank page.
Take one real clause with three sub-paragraphs and a defined term, and type it three times: once for accuracy, once at pace, once with track changes on. Compare the three outputs against the source line by line. That exercise finds more problems than any typing test.
Then run five-minute rounds on dense text with punctuation, targeting 98% accuracy. If accuracy falls below that at 65 WPM, work at 58 until it holds - a legal document with two errors a page costs more to check than it saved to type.
For the transcription-heavy version of the role, see legal secretary. For dictation and audio work, audio typing. For the general benchmark that most postings quote, the WPM chart shows where 50-65 sits.
## Frequently asked questions
Usually 50-65 WPM with high accuracy. Legal secretary roles sit slightly higher at 60-75 because transcription is a larger part of the job.
For many roles, yes, provided formatting and accuracy are clean. Firms that test usually care more about whether a citation and a numbered list come out identical every time.
Sometimes. Work-sample tests use real clauses with defined terms and citations, which is why practising on legal text beats practising on random sentences.
Type the same citation ten times from the source, checking character by character, rather than typing ten different citations once. Pattern repetition is what makes punctuation automatic.
No. Typing is a threshold you clear; the role is judged on document accuracy and research quality. That is why the bar sits at 50-65 rather than 75+.

## USPS Postal Exam Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/usps-postal-exam-typing-test.html

The honest answer first: the USPS virtual entry assessments do not contain a typing test. They measure work simulation, memory and customer service judgement. Keyboard speed still matters on the job, and some roles test it locally.

USPS replaced its older paper exams with virtual entry assessments tailored to job families: 474 for mail handler, 475 for mail processing, 476 for customer service and 477 for maintenance. They present work-sample scenarios - sorting decisions, address matching, register and money-order arithmetic, customer interactions - and score judgement and speed of decision rather than keystrokes.
That is why a candidate searching for a postal typing test usually finds practice sites selling a typing drill that does not match the exam. Practising WPM will not raise a 476 score; practising the scenario format will.
Data-entry-adjacent roles - address updates, redirects and claims work move faster with clean numeric typing.
Facility-level checks - some offices still administer a basic keyboarding or data-entry exercise during onboarding.
The job itself - retail counter and processing roles type addresses, tracking numbers and short notes all day, and an unfamiliar keyboard slows that down.
The figure that appears in comparable clerical settings is 30-40 WPM with accuracy above 95%. Treat it as a sensible personal target, not a published USPS requirement.
Work on the scenario skills: reading an address quickly and spotting the mismatch, doing change-making arithmetic without a calculator, remembering a short instruction sequence, and choosing the answer that follows procedure rather than the one that feels kindest.
Then use typing practice as a background habit - five minutes a day for the job, not for the exam. The two goals are different and mixing them wastes the preparation window.
Take a five-minute sentence test and a two-minute numbers test, record net WPM and accuracy for both, and keep the screenshot. It is useful for the interview conversation and for any local keyboarding check, and it costs five minutes.
For address-style content specifically, the alphanumeric typing test is closer to the work than a prose passage, because postcodes and route numbers are mixed letter-digit strings.
## Frequently asked questions
No. The virtual entry assessments (474, 475, 476, 477) are scenario-based work simulations. They do not report a words-per-minute score.
There is no published universal WPM requirement for the entry assessments. Comparable clerical roles quote 30-40 WPM with 95% accuracy, which is a sensible target for the job rather than an exam rule.
Because people search for it. The practice is usually generic typing drill content that does not match the assessment format, so it will not raise a 474-477 score.
Address comparison, money and change arithmetic, short instruction memory, and procedure-following judgement. Those are the four skills the scenarios actually test.
Sometimes. Some offices run a basic keyboarding or data-entry exercise during onboarding. It is usually a low bar, but a clean 40 WPM with accurate digits removes the risk.

## Typing Test for Seniors
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-seniors.html

Typing speed settles with age, but accuracy and comfort do not have to. This page is about testing without strain: longer rounds, bigger text, and a realistic target instead of a leaderboard.

Two things slow down measurably: reaction time and fine motor steadiness. Both show up as more mistyped adjacent keys rather than as slower thinking, which is why older typists often report knowing the word but hitting the wrong key.
What does not change is vocabulary, sentence planning or the knowledge of where the keys are. That is why accuracy-focused practice still pays: the skill you already have is the part that carries over, and the reach is the part that needs the work.
Length: two to three minutes. A 15-second sprint measures reaction time, which is exactly what declines; a longer round measures sustainable pace.
Text: sentences rather than random words. Familiar sentence structure lets you use knowledge instead of reaction.
Display: browser zoom at 125-150% and the widened keyboard view. Reading strain produces more errors than typing strain.
Posture: feet flat, elbows near 90 degrees, screen at eye level. A laptop on a coffee table is the most common cause of shoulder fatigue in an hour of practice.
Thirty to forty words per minute with 97% accuracy covers email, forms, banking, messaging and almost every personal computing task. It is also inside the band that part-time and volunteer clerical roles quote.
Chasing 70 WPM is not useful unless you are going back into transcription or legal support. Chasing 97% accuracy is useful at any age, because it removes the corrections that make typing feel tiring.
Stop a session at the first sign of tingling or numbness in the fingers, or aching in the forearm. Those are early signs of strain and they respond to rest, not to more practice. Persistent numbness is worth a doctor's opinion rather than a typing drill.
Ten minutes, three times a week is a good ceiling to start with. If that feels easy after two weeks, extend the rounds rather than the frequency - shorter sessions recover better.
## Frequently asked questions
Most sit between 25 and 45 WPM, and the variation within the group is much larger than the average difference from younger typists. Accuracy is usually maintained even when speed settles.
No. Adults learn the key map quickly because they already read and write fluently; the slower part is building new finger habits, which takes a few weeks of short daily practice.
Two to three minutes. Short sprints measure reaction time, which declines with age, so they understate what you can actually sustain.
Yes. Reading strain causes more errors than typing strain at any age. Zoom the browser to 125-150% and use the widened keyboard view.
Stop the session, rest, and check posture and keyboard height before resuming. Persistent numbness or tingling should be reviewed by a doctor rather than worked through.

## Typing Test for Customer Service
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-customer-service.html

Written support is a typing job with a customer attached. Chat and email roles usually ask 35–50 WPM, and the thing that gets measured in probation is not speed but whether your replies are clear and typo-free.

Channel | Typical WPM | What the job really tests
Phone support with notes | 30-40 | Capturing names, references and next steps while listening
Email support | 40-50 | Clear, correct written English; template editing under time pressure
Live chat | 45-60 | Typing the conversation itself, often with two or three chats open
Social media support | 40-55 | Public tone, short replies, high visibility of mistakes
The bands come from advertised requirements and from what contact-centre training programmes assume. A posting that quotes 35 WPM for email is unusual; 45 is the common floor for written channels.
A typo in a reply is read by a customer who is already frustrated. It costs trust in a way that a slow reply does not. Support teams therefore judge written output on clarity and correctness, and they will happily keep a 45 WPM agent who writes cleanly over a 65 WPM agent who needs every message checked.
Practise accordingly: type a short reply, then proofread it. Two-thirds of the improvement in the first month comes from the proofreading habit, not from the keyboard.
Two-minute sentence rounds for the base pace, one a day.
Template editing - take a canned reply and rewrite the middle sentence for a specific customer in under 30 seconds. That is the actual task.
Numbers mode once a week for order and reference numbers, which is where written support makes its costly mistakes.
Two conversations at once - type alternate replies to two prompts without mixing them up. Chat roles test this informally within the first week.
Voice-first roles are covered on the call centre page, which includes the listening-while-typing drill. For the numeric side, see alphanumeric typing. For a general number to quote, the WPM chart shows where 45 sits.
## Frequently asked questions
Usually 35-50 WPM depending on channel: 30-40 for phone support notes, 40-50 for email, and 45-60 for live chat where you type the conversation itself.
It is marginal. Chat roles usually ask 45-60 because you type the entire interaction, often across two or three concurrent conversations.
Yes in written support. A typo in a reply reaches a frustrated customer and costs trust; a slightly slower correct reply does not. Teams keep clean 45 WPM agents over sloppy 65 WPM ones.
Practise template editing: rewrite the middle sentence of a canned reply for a specific customer in under 30 seconds, then check it for typos. That is the real task.
Often yes, usually a short typing test plus a written role-play. The role-play is the deciding part, which is why tone and clarity practice matters as much as WPM.

## 30-Day Typing Improvement Plan
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/30-day-typing-improvement-plan.html

Fifteen minutes a day for thirty days, with a checkpoint every Sunday. The plan changes what you practise each week because the cause of slow typing changes as you get faster.

On this page
The daily block (15 minutes)
Week 1 — remove the two habits that cap speed
Week 2 — make the home row automatic
Week 3 — accuracy at speed, punctuation and digits
Week 4 — full length and consistency
What to do on day 31
2 min warm-up - one 60-second round at a comfortable pace, no target.
8 min drill - whatever the week prescribes, in 60- or 120-second rounds.
3 min accuracy round - slow to 85% of your pace and aim for zero errors.
2 min log - net WPM, accuracy, and one sentence on what felt wrong.
The log is not bureaucracy. Fifteen minutes of daily data tells you whether the plan is working in week two, instead of leaving you guessing at day thirty.
Drill: covered-keyboard rounds and no-backspace rounds, alternating. One round with your hands covered, one round where a mistake is not corrected - just keep going. Both feel wrong for three days.
Checkpoint: accuracy should be above 92% by day seven, and your no-backspace score should be within 3 WPM of your normal score. If it is not, the corrections are costing you more than they are worth, which is the whole point of the week.
Drill: home-row and top-row drills, plus one round of pangrams a day (they touch every letter). Type slowly enough that you never look down - slow and correct beats fast and corrected.
Checkpoint: by day fourteen you should be able to type a full sentence without glancing at the keyboard. Speed usually rises 3-8 WPM in this week without any deliberate speed work.
Drill: 30-second sprints at maximum speed followed by a slow accuracy round, three pairs per session. Add one Numbers round and one punctuation-heavy round (quotes) every other day.
Checkpoint: your sprint peak should be 10-15 WPM above your sustainable pace. If the two are equal, you are not pushing; if accuracy collapses in the sprint, you are pushing past control.
Drill: five-minute rounds, three per session, no pause. Then one ten-minute round on the final two days. Score the lowest round of the three, not the highest - that is the number an employer would see on a bad day.
Checkpoint: compare day 30 against day 1 on the same test length. Beginners typically gain 5-15 WPM, people already above 60 typically gain 3-6. Both are real; neither is a guarantee.
Drop to maintenance: five minutes, four days a week, one full test a month. Most of what you gained stays if you keep typing daily at work or in messages; the part that fades is the deliberate accuracy habit.
If you want to keep climbing, the next project is look-ahead reading - see the 50 WPM plan for the drills that break a plateau, and the WPM chart to see which cause applies at your band.
## Frequently asked questions
Yes, by 5-15 WPM if you are starting below 50, and 3-6 WPM if you are already over 60. The gains come from removing habits, not from talent.
Fifteen minutes a day. The plan is built around 2 minutes warm-up, 8 minutes drill, 3 minutes accuracy and 2 minutes logging.
Continue where you left off rather than restarting. The weeks are ordered by cause, not by calendar; a missed day costs nothing, a missed week means repeating that week's checkpoint.
No. Timed rounds, a covered keyboard (a cloth works), and a note of your scores are enough. The drill content matters more than the tool.
At day 30, then switch to maintenance: five minutes, four days a week. Deliberate practice has diminishing returns once your habits are clean.

## Typing Test for Court Clerks
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-court-clerk.html

A court clerk types case numbers, filing codes, party names and dates into a docket system all day. The speed bar is moderate — 45 to 55 WPM — but an identifier typed wrong creates a filing that cannot be found.

A docket entry looks like this: a case number with a year and a court code, a filing type from a fixed list, the filing party, a date, and a short description. Almost every field is either a code or a proper noun, and several are checked against an existing record.
That shape matters for practice. Copying prose trains sentence rhythm; docket entry trains short alphanumeric bursts with a verification step after each field. The second is what the job actually rewards.
A misspelt word in a note is readable. A case number with a transposed digit is a filing that cannot be retrieved by the parties who need it, and fixing it usually requires a correction entry and a supervisor.
Case numbers - alphanumeric with a year and a court or division code.
Dates - filing date, hearing date, deadline; format depends on the court.
Party names - often unusual spellings, and never autocorrected.
Filing codes - short, similar-looking, and chosen from a list rather than typed freehand.
Type a case number, check it character by character, then type the next one. Ten repetitions of the same number beat one pass through ten different numbers, because the goal is a verification habit rather than exposure to variety.
Then add the field-switching behaviour: case number, Tab, filing type, Tab, date, Enter. Real docket systems move between fields, and typing a clean number followed by a wrong Tab is a lost record just the same.
Band | Clears | Notes
35-45 WPM | Entry-level clerk-typist titles | Usually paired with a data-entry exercise
45-55 WPM | Most court clerk and deputy clerk postings | The common advertised band
55+ WPM | High-volume filing desks | Accuracy floor matters more than the extra speed
Public-sector postings often state the requirement in net WPM on a five-minute sample, and some require a proctored certificate. Check the notice: the wording tells you which document they will accept.
## Frequently asked questions
Usually 45-55 WPM with high accuracy, and often on a five-minute proctored sample. The accuracy requirement is strict because a wrong case number creates an unretrievable filing.
A large part of it is docket entry and filing, which is typing in short alphanumeric bursts. The rest is checking documents, answering counter enquiries and managing records.
Some jurisdictions require a proctored typing certificate with a stated speed and date; others accept self-certification and test later. The posting states which, and the wording is usually explicit.
Type the same number ten times, checking character by character after each attempt, then move to a new one. Repetition builds the verification habit that prevents transposition errors.
Somewhat. You need to recognise filing types and party designations, but you select codes rather than compose text, so accuracy matters more than vocabulary.

## Typing Test for Medical Receptionists
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-medical-receptionist.html

Medical reception is typing with a queue: patient names, dates of birth, insurance IDs and appointment slots, entered while someone waits. Clinics commonly ask 40–50 WPM, and the failure mode is always a digit.

A registration is a form: name, date of birth, address, phone, insurance carrier, member ID, group number, reason for visit. Between six and eight of those fields are numeric or alphanumeric, and two of them (date of birth and member ID) are the ones that cause billing rejections when mistyped.
The typing is short and interrupted. That combination — many short entries, frequent interruptions — is why front-desk staff who type 50 WPM in a test can still feel slow on a Monday morning.
Letters can be inferred from context; digits cannot. A member ID with two digits swapped is rejected by the clearing house weeks later, and the correction costs the practice more than the registration did.
Dates of birth - format-sensitive, and a common source of duplicate patient records.
Insurance member IDs - alphanumeric, often 10-15 characters with no internal logic to catch an error.
Phone numbers - ten digits, typed while the patient is still talking.
Appointment times - a single digit decides whether someone arrives at 9 or 19 past the hour.
Two minutes of Numbers mode daily, graded on errors. Then a form drill: type a mock registration (name, DOB, phone, member ID) ten times and count how many are completely clean. Three clean records in a row is the realistic readiness bar.
Add the interruption: type half a record, look away for five seconds, then finish it. That is the actual working condition, and it is where the errors appear in practice rather than in a quiet test.
If asked for a speed, quote net WPM with accuracy and test length, and mention numeric entry separately if you have a figure. A clinic manager reads the accuracy number first, because they have seen what a mistyped member ID costs.
Ask which practice-management system they use. The typing skill transfers; the keyboard shortcuts do not, and knowing the system name tells you what the first week will feel like.
## Frequently asked questions
Most clinic postings ask 40-50 WPM with accuracy above 97%. Medical and dental front desks sit at the top of that band because patient identifiers must be exact.
Basic familiarity helps for reason-for-visit fields, but you select from lists more often than you compose. Accuracy on names, dates and insurance numbers matters more.
Two minutes of numeric practice daily, graded on errors rather than speed, plus a form drill where you type the same mock registration ten times and count clean records.
Sometimes, usually a short online test or a timed registration exercise. Larger practices and hospital groups are more likely to test formally.
No. Speed is a floor; knowing the practice-management system and the registration workflow is what makes someone fast in the first month.

## Typing Test for Insurance Claims
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-insurance-claims.html

Claims work is code entry under a queue: policy numbers, claim references, loss codes, reserve amounts. The advertised speed is modest — 45 to 55 WPM — and the accuracy expectation is the strictest in clerical work.

A first-notice-of-loss record is a fixed form: policy number, insured name, date of loss, loss type code, description, estimated reserve, adjuster assignment. Two of those fields are money, three are codes, one is narrative. The narrative is the only part where prose typing helps.
That ratio is why claims processors who type 50 WPM with clean digits outperform colleagues at 65 WPM who need corrections. The queue measures completed, correct records.
Reserve amounts - a misplaced decimal changes a reserve by a factor of ten.
Policy numbers - alphanumeric, no checksum you can rely on, and a wrong digit attaches the claim to the wrong policyholder.
Loss codes - similar-looking categories where a mis-selection routes the claim to the wrong team.
Dates of loss - coverage windows depend on them, so a wrong year can void a valid claim.
Two minutes of Numbers mode daily, then a record drill: type a mock claim (policy, date, code, amount) ten times, verify against the source each time, and count clean records. Target three consecutive clean records before you claim the skill.
Practise decimal placement deliberately. Type amounts with two decimal places and a thousands separator until the pattern is automatic, because that is the field where a single keystroke has the largest consequence.
Claims processing usually advertises 45-55 WPM with 98% accuracy. Related roles differ: medical billing sits at 45-55 with 98%, data entry is quoted in keystrokes per hour at 8,000-12,000, and customer service claims handling drops to 35-45 because the work is more conversation than entry.
If a posting quotes keystrokes per hour instead of WPM, convert before deciding whether you qualify — 10,000 KPH is about 33 WPM, which is a different test from a 50 WPM prose reading.
## Frequently asked questions
Usually 45-55 WPM with accuracy of 98% or better. Codes, amounts and policy numbers dominate the work, so numeric accuracy is the deciding factor.
A large part of it is data entry into a claims system, alongside document review and correspondence. The entry is short, coded and repeated, rather than long-form typing.
A wrong reserve amount, policy number or loss date can misroute a claim, delay payment or change a reserve by a factor of ten. Corrections are expensive and sometimes regulated.
Type amounts with two decimals and a thousands separator until the pattern is automatic, then add the surrounding fields (policy number, date, code) so you practise the field-switching as well.
Yes for the role, no for the screening test. Employers test the typing floor because it is cheap to measure; the job itself is judged on accuracy and turnaround.

## Typing Test for Warehouse Admin
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-warehouse-admin.html

Warehouse administration is SKUs, quantities, carrier references and addresses. The speed bar is low — 35 to 45 WPM — but a mistyped SKU or postcode sends the wrong item to the wrong place.

A goods-in entry is a purchase order reference, a SKU list with quantities, a supplier and a date. A dispatch entry is an order reference, a carrier, a tracking number, a postcode and a weight. Both are short fields typed at speed while a vehicle waits.
Because the rhythm is driven by the dock rather than the screen, the typical failure is not slow typing but a skipped field or a transposed digit in a postcode. Speed matters mainly so the queue does not build.
SKUs - often alphanumeric with similar-looking variants (0/O, 1/I, 5/S).
Postcodes - a single wrong character changes the delivery area.
Quantities - digits only, and an extra zero is a real cost.
Tracking references - long, no internal logic, and copied from a label.
Where barcode scanning exists, typing is the fallback and the audit path; where it does not, typing is the only record. Both need the same accuracy habit.
Two minutes of Numbers mode a day, plus an address drill: type ten postcodes and street lines, then check them character by character. Add a SKU drill with confusable characters (0/O, 1/I, 5/S) because that is where picking errors originate.
If you already work in a warehouse, copy real SKUs from a pick list rather than random strings. Familiarity with the format is what makes the practice transfer.
35-45 WPM clears most warehouse admin postings, and many roles never test it formally — they check whether you can use the warehouse management system without errors. If a test exists, it is usually a short alphanumeric exercise.
For adjacent roles, see data entry if the work is volume entry, or alphanumeric typing for the drill that matches SKU and postcode content.
## Frequently asked questions
Usually 35-45 WPM. Many roles do not test formally; they check whether you can enter codes and quantities into the warehouse system without errors.
Both matter. Scanning is faster where barcodes exist, but typing is the fallback and the audit path, and quantities and exceptions are usually keyed by hand.
Practise confusable characters (0/O, 1/I, 5/S) deliberately, and verify each SKU against the pick list character by character for the first weeks on the job.
No. The dock sets the pace, and accuracy determines whether the queue clears. 35-45 WPM with clean codes is enough for most admin roles.
Numbers and postcodes. They are the fields with real-world consequences, and they are where untrained typists lose accuracy first.

## Typing Speed Benchmarks
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-speed-benchmarks.html

Every number this site uses, with where it comes from. 51.56 WPM on a desktop keyboard and 36.17 WPM on a phone are the two measured averages; everything else on this page is either arithmetic or a labelled market range.

On this page
Measured averages (the only two hard numbers)
Percentile curve (derived, labelled as an approximation)
Unit conversions (arithmetic, not measurement)
Job requirement bands (market ranges, labelled)
What is not on this page, and why
How to cite this page
Measure | Desktop keyboard | Phone (touchscreen)
Mean speed | 51.56 WPM (SD 20.2) | 36.17 WPM (SD 13.22)
Uncorrected error rate | 1.17% | 2.34%
Keystrokes per character | 1.173 | 1.18
Participants | 168,960 | 37,370
Keystrokes recorded | 136,857,600 | not reported as a total
Percentile thresholds reported by the authors | top 10% > ~78 WPM; bottom 10% < ~26 WPM | 75% below 43.98 WPM
Source | Dhakal, Feit, Kristensson & Oulasvirta, CHI 2018, doi.org/10.1145/3173574.3174220 | Palin, Feit, Kim, Kristensson & Oulasvirta, MobileHCI 2019, doi.org/10.1145/3338286.3340120
Both studies used the same task - transcribe a displayed English sentence - so the device comparison is unusually clean. The mobile study compares itself to the desktop one directly and reports that average performance is about 15 WPM slower on a phone.
WPM | Percentile | CPM | Keystrokes per hour
20 | 6th | 100 | 6,000
30 | 14th | 150 | 9,000
40 | 28th | 200 | 12,000
50 | 47th | 250 | 15,000
60 | 66th | 300 | 18,000
70 | 82nd | 350 | 21,000
80 | 92nd | 400 | 24,000
90 | 97th | 450 | 27,000
100 | 99th | 500 | 30,000
Computed from a normal distribution with mean 51.56 and standard deviation 20.2. It is an approximation - real typing speed is mildly left-skewed - and it is validated by reproducing the study's own reported deciles (about 26 and 78 WPM) to within one percentile point. Enter any score to convert it.
The full curve at 5 WPM steps is available as typing-speed-benchmarks.csv (columns: wpm, percentile, percentile_rounded, cpm, keystrokes_per_hour). Reuse it with attribution. The same curve, the Python and JavaScript percentile functions and the source table are published as a repository at github.com/hello532/typing-speed-benchmarks, so a citation can point at the code as well as the page.
From | To | Formula | Example
WPM | CPM | × 5 | 40 WPM = 200 CPM
CPM | KPH | × 60 | 200 CPM = 12,000 KPH
WPM | KPH | × 300 | 40 WPM = 12,000 KPH
KPH | WPM | ÷ 300 | 10,000 KPH = 33.3 WPM
Key depressions/hour | WPM | ÷ 300 (corrections count) | 8,000 KDPH ≈ 26.7 WPM
The factor of five is the characters-per-word convention, not a physical constant. It exists so that a score on a long-word passage and a short-word passage can be compared.
Role | Advertised band | Basis
General office / admin | 40-55 WPM | Range across advertised clerical postings
US federal clerk | 40 WPM, 5 minutes, ≤3 errors | Published federal clerical standard
Data entry clerk | 8,000-12,000 KPH | Range across advertised postings
Legal secretary | 60-75 WPM | Range across advertised postings
Medical transcription | 65-80 WPM | Range across advertised postings
Court reporter (stenotype) | 225 WPM | Certification standard, not a keyboard
These are not measurements of a population; they are what employers and certifying bodies publish. Two employers in the same sector commonly differ by ten WPM, so read the posting rather than the table. Detail per role: typing speed requirements by job.
There is no average speed by country, no average by gender, and no "average for a 12-year-old" figure here, because we could not find a primary measurement for them that we were willing to cite. Sites that publish those numbers rarely link a study.
There is also no traffic or leaderboard statistic: this site stores results in the visitor's browser, so it has no server-side dataset to aggregate and will not pretend to have one.
Preferred form: "Typing.Rerivo, Typing Speed Benchmarks, https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-speed-benchmarks.html (accessed DATE)". The underlying numbers should be cited to the papers above, not to this page - the page is a convenient summary, not the source.
If you reuse the CSV, keep the column names and note that the percentile column is a normal approximation of the CHI 2018 distribution.
## Frequently asked questions
51.56 WPM on a desktop keyboard, from the CHI 2018 study of 168,960 volunteers. On a phone the measured average is 36.17 WPM from a 37,370-person study.

## German Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/german-typing-test.html

Real German sentences with the characters that actually slow typists down: ä, ö, ü, ß and the comma-heavy clause structure. Works on a QWERTZ keyboard, no sign up, results stay in your browser.

German adds four characters that English does not use: ä, ö, ü and ß. On a QWERTZ keyboard they sit on dedicated keys to the right of P and L, so they need a reach rather than a modifier - which means they interrupt the hand position less than a Shift combination, but they are pressed less often and therefore practised less.
The second difference is length. German compounds produce long words (Geschwindigkeitsmessung, Tastaturbelegung), and long words mean more consecutive keystrokes per word with no space to reset the hand. Typists who are comfortable at 60 WPM on English often measure 50-55 on German text at the same accuracy.
German-language typing tests usually report two figures. Wörter pro Minute (WPM) counts five characters as one word, the same convention used in English. Anschläge pro Minute (CPM, sometimes Zeichen pro Minute) counts every character, which is what German office job adverts often quote.
Anschläge/Min | Wörter/Min | Einordnung
150 | 30 | Anfangsniveau, Übung nötig
200 | 40 | Solide für Büroarbeit
250 | 50 | Gut, über dem Durchschnitt
300 | 60 | Schnell, für Sekretariat und Datenerfassung
400 | 80 | Sehr schnell, obere 10%
The conversion is arithmetic: WPM = Anschläge ÷ 5. Nothing about German text changes the formula, only the character mix.
German-speaking countries use QWERTZ: Y and Z are swapped relative to QWERTY, and the umlauts sit on their own keys. If you type on a QWERTZ keyboard, this test works as-is, because the browser reports the character your operating system produces, not the physical key.
If you are learning German on a QWERTY keyboard, enable the German layout in your operating system before practising. Typing German text on an English layout means hunting for the umlauts, which trains the wrong habit and produces a score that does not transfer.
Start with one-minute rounds on sentences, then move to five minutes once accuracy holds above 97%. German rewards rhythm more than speed: the comma clauses give you natural places to breathe, and typists who rush through them accumulate errors on the endings.
If your goal is a specific job, check what the advert quotes. Office and Verwaltung roles typically ask 200-300 Anschläge pro Minute; Datenerfassung is quoted in keystrokes per hour, which you can convert on the WPM to KPH converter.
For the general benchmarks behind these bands, see the average typing speed page; for the English version of this test, English typing test.
## Frequently asked questions
200-250 Anschläge pro Minute (40-50 Wörter pro Minute) is solid for office work. Office and administrative roles commonly ask 200-300, and data entry is quoted in keystrokes per hour.
Yes. The test compares the characters your operating system produces, so a German layout with umlauts and ß on their own keys works without configuration.
German compounds produce longer words with more consecutive keystrokes, and the umlauts are pressed less often than letters, so they stay less practised. A 10% drop at equal accuracy is normal.
On a QWERTZ keyboard they have their own keys to the right of P and L. On a QWERTY keyboard, add the German layout in your OS settings rather than using Alt codes, which do not train the correct motion.
Forty words per minute. Anschläge ÷ 5 = Wörter pro Minute, the same five-characters-per-word convention used by English typing tests.

## French Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/french-typing-test.html

Real French text with the characters that decide accuracy: é, è, ê, à, ç, ù, œ and the space before a colon. Works on an AZERTY keyboard, and the score is reported in mots par minute and caractères par minute.

Three things. First, accents: é, è, ê, à, ç and ù each have their own key on AZERTY, and œ (as in cœur) is a separate character again. Second, punctuation spacing: French typography puts a space before : ; ! ? and inside guillemets, so a correct sentence has more keystrokes than the English equivalent.
Third, apostrophes. French elides constantly (l'oiseau, qu'il, d'accord), and the apostrophe key on AZERTY sits on the fourth row, reached with the right little finger. That single reach accounts for a large share of errors in French typing tests.
French tests report mots par minute (MPM) and caractères par minute (CPM). The word count uses five characters per word, the same convention as English, so a French and an English score are comparable - provided both tests count characters the same way.
Caractères/Min | Mots/Min | Repère
150 | 30 | Débutant, entraînement nécessaire
200 | 40 | Correct pour le travail de bureau
250 | 50 | Bon, au-dessus de la moyenne
300 | 60 | Rapide, secrétariat et saisie
400 | 80 | Très rapide, 10% supérieurs
French keyboards are AZERTY: A and Q swap, Z and W swap, M moves next to L, and the accented letters replace the number row. If you use an AZERTY keyboard, this test works directly, because the browser receives the character your system produces.
The detail that catches people is the space before double punctuation. A French sentence writes « Bonjour : voici » with a space before the colon, not « Bonjour: voici ». Typing tests that use real French text include that space, and typists trained on English punctuation lose accuracy on it until they notice.
One-minute rounds first, then five minutes once accuracy is above 97%. Add a round with quotes once a week, because that is where the guillemets and the double punctuation appear together.
French office and secrétariat postings commonly quote 40-50 mots par minute, and some public-sector concours include a bureautique exercise rather than a formal typing score. Saisie de données roles are quoted in caractères par minute or keystrokes per hour - convert with the WPM to KPH converter.
For benchmarks across languages, see average typing speed; for the English version, English typing test.
## Frequently asked questions
40-50 mots par minute (200-250 caractères par minute) is solid for office work. Secretarial and data-entry roles often ask for 50-60 MPM, with accuracy above 97%.
Yes. The test compares the characters your operating system produces, so accented letters and ç work directly on an AZERTY layout without configuration.
French typography requires a space before : ; ! ? and uses guillemets, which adds keystrokes. If you learned English punctuation, the extra space is a habit you have to build.
On AZERTY, accents have their own keys and œ is typed with a dedicated combination. Add the French layout in your OS settings rather than using Alt codes, which do not train the right motion.
Fifty mots par minute. Characters ÷ 5 = words, the same convention used by English typing tests, so the two scores are comparable.

## Touch Typing Course: 12 Lessons
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/touch-typing-course.html

Twelve lessons, each with one drill and one pass criterion. You start on the home row and finish typing full sentences without looking, in four to six weeks at 15 minutes a day. No account, no software to install.

On this page
Before lesson 1: set up, and accept the dip
Lessons 1-4: the rows
Lessons 5-8: capitals, punctuation, digits, letter pairs
Lessons 9-12: words, sentences, control, test
How long this actually takes
Why this order, and what the evidence says
Sit so your elbows are near 90 degrees, feet flat, screen at eye level. Put the keyboard flat, not tilted. Find the two bumps on F and J with your index fingers, and rest your thumbs on the spacebar.
Expect to get slower for the first week. Typing with ten fingers means abandoning a system that already works, and the new one takes about 300-500 repetitions per key before it stops needing attention. That dip is the cost of the ceiling you are removing, not a sign that it is not working.
Lesson | Drill | Pass criterion
1. Home row | asdf jkl; repeated, hands covered for the last two rounds | 95% accuracy, no looking down
2. Home row + G, H | Words built only from asdfghjkl; | 95% accuracy at 20 WPM
3. Top row | qwerty uiop added, one minute at a time | 95% accuracy, 25 WPM
4. Bottom row | zxcvbnm added, then full alphabet words | 95% accuracy, 30 WPM
Cover your hands for at least one round per lesson. Looking down is the habit that caps most people at 35-40 WPM, and it is far easier to prevent now than to break at 60.
5. Capitals. Shift with the hand that is not typing the letter. Drill sentence case until the Shift press stops breaking rhythm.
6. Punctuation. Full stops, commas, apostrophes and question marks in real sentences, not lists of symbols.
7. Digits. Reach the number row with the correct finger. This is the slowest lesson for most adults and the one data-entry work actually needs.
8. Letter pairs. th, he, in, er, an, re, on, at. Practising transitions moves 40-60 WPM faster than practising words, because that is where the hand movement lives.
Pass criteria for this block: 96% accuracy on a two-minute round with capitals and punctuation intact, and 97% on a one-minute numbers round.
Lesson | Drill | Pass criterion
9. Words | Top 200 common words, typed as whole units | 40 WPM at 97%
10. Sentences | Three-minute rounds, normal text | 45 WPM at 97%
11. Speed control | 30-second sprints at maximum, then a slow accuracy round | Sprint peak 10-15 WPM above your sustainable pace
12. Full test | Five-minute net score, unfamiliar keyboard if possible | A number you can reproduce twice
Lesson 12 is not about hitting a target. It is about being able to reproduce a score, because that is what an employer's test will ask of you.
For an adult starting from two-finger typing: home row secure in one to two weeks, all rows in three to four, and full sentences without looking in four to six. Reaching 60 WPM usually takes two to four months after that, because speed comes from accuracy plus repetition rather than from pushing.
Children need longer on the motor side and shorter on the reading side. The published classroom bands put grade 5 at roughly 25-35 WPM, which matches the same lesson path at a slower pace.
The order is rows first, then modifiers, then transitions. Rows build the map; modifiers build the reach; transitions build speed. Skipping to sentences before the map is automatic produces the hunt-and-peck pattern with extra steps.
One published finding is worth knowing: Feit, Weir and Oulasvirta (CHI 2016, doi.org/10.1145/2858036.2858233) found that consistent finger use and preparing the next keypress predict typing speed more than which specific finger presses which key. That is why the drills here emphasise not looking and rhythmic preparation over rigid finger doctrine.
Lesson 1 assumes you can already find the home row; if you cannot, spend a week on keyboard practice first and come back.
## Frequently asked questions
Four to six weeks at 15 minutes a day gets an adult from two-finger typing to full sentences without looking. Reaching 60 WPM typically takes another two to four months of regular practice.
Close to it. Research on typists (Feit et al., CHI 2016) found that consistent finger use and preparing the next keypress predict speed more than which specific finger presses which key - so consistency matters more than doctrine.
You are replacing a working habit with an unfamiliar one. The dip lasts one to two weeks; the ceiling it removes (around 35-40 WPM for two-finger typing) never comes back.
For at least one round per lesson. Looking down is the habit that caps speed, and preventing it is much easier than breaking it later.
No. Lessons run in the browser, results stay on your device, and there is nothing to install. Each lesson links to the test mode it needs.

## Typing Consistency Score
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-consistency-score.html

Two typists can average 60 WPM and be very different: one runs 58-62 the whole minute, the other swings between 40 and 80. Consistency is the figure that separates them, and it predicts your five-minute score better than your peak does.

Speed is sampled once per second during the round. Let those samples be a series of speeds with mean m. Consistency is one minus the coefficient of variation, expressed as a percentage:
consistency = 100 × (1 − standard deviation ÷ mean)
So a round that holds 60 WPM with a standard deviation of 3 reads 95. A round that averages 60 but swings with a standard deviation of 12 reads 80. It is clamped to 0-100, and a round with fewer than two samples reports 100 rather than an error.
The number appears in the results panel as Consistency (labeled 安定度 / 稳定性 / استحکام in other interface languages) and in the share image.
Average WPM is an average of a curve, and the curve has shape. A typist whose speed collapses in the last ten seconds has a stamina problem; one whose speed spikes at the start and settles has a pacing problem; one whose speed oscillates throughout is reading word by word instead of ahead.
Consistency separates those cases. It also explains a common frustration: two people with the same one-minute score can have completely different five-minute scores, and the one with the higher consistency usually keeps more of it.
Consistency | What it looks like | What to do
90-100 | Nearly flat; the average is the truth | Nothing - work on speed instead
80-89 | Mild variation, usually around difficult words | Drill the words that cause the dips
70-79 | Visible dips; the average overstates your sustainable pace | Slow down 10% and hold it for a full minute
under 70 | Large swings, often burst-then-recover | Accuracy work first; the swings are usually corrections
Metronome typing. Type to a steady rhythm - one word per beat - for 30 seconds. The goal is not speed but flatness; you will feel the urges to sprint and to recover.
Slow-hold rounds. Pick a pace you can hold for the entire round without a single sprint, and finish at exactly that pace. Most typists discover their sustainable pace is 10-15% below their peak.
Dip hunting. After a round, look at the graph and find the lowest second. Type the words around that point again, slowly. Dips concentrate on the same few sequences - usually one hand doing two awkward reaches.
On very short rounds (15 seconds) there are too few samples for the figure to mean much. On very hard text, low consistency is expected and correct - the dips are the difficulty, not a technique failure.
For benchmarking, keep using net WPM plus accuracy. Consistency is a diagnostic for how you got the number, not a replacement for it.
## Frequently asked questions
Above 85 is steady, 90+ is nearly flat. Below 70 means your speed swings enough that the average overstates what you can sustain over five minutes.
One minus the coefficient of variation of your per-second WPM, as a percentage: 100 × (1 − standard deviation ÷ mean). It is clamped to 0-100.
For sustained work, yes. A steady 55 holds up over a ten-minute test; a spiky 60 often drops to 48. For passing a short screening test, speed matters more.
Accuracy measures errors, consistency measures rhythm. You can be accurate and still accelerate and stall, usually because you read word by word rather than looking ahead.
Slow-hold rounds: pick a pace you can maintain for the whole round and finish at exactly that pace. It teaches the difference between peak and sustainable speed.

## Why Am I Stuck at the Same Typing Speed?
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/why-am-i-stuck-at-the-same-typing-speed.html

A plateau is not one problem. Where you are stuck tells you what is stuck: at 40 it is usually the look-at-keyboard habit, at 60 it is corrections, at 80 it is consistency. Here is the diagnosis by band.

On this page
First, check that you are actually stuck
Stuck at 30-40: the habit ceiling
Stuck at 50: the reading bottleneck
Stuck at 60: the accuracy tax
Stuck at 70-80: variance, not peak
If none of that applies
Measure the same way three times: same length, same text mode, same time of day. If the three scores sit within 3 WPM, you are consistent and the plateau is real. If they swing by 10, you do not have a plateau - you have noisy measurement, and the fix is a fixed protocol rather than a new drill.
Then check the length. A one-minute score improves faster than a five-minute score, so a plateau on a five-minute test looks like progress on a one-minute one. Decide which number you are tracking and stay with it.
Almost always two habits: looking at the keyboard, and backspacing through every slip. Both are cheap to fix and both feel worse before they feel better.
Covered rounds: hands hidden, 30 seconds, once a day. Expect accuracy to drop 10-20% for a week.
No-backspace rounds: finish with mistakes in them. Most people at this level gain 3-5 WPM immediately.
At 50 WPM your fingers are no longer the limit; your eyes are. You read the word you are about to type, so the hands wait for the eyes on every word. Faster typists read one to three words ahead and let the hands run on a buffer.
Drill: before starting a line, read it silently once, then type it without re-reading. It feels wrong for three rounds and then it stops feeling wrong. Add 15-second bursts to raise your top end, because a 50 average with a 55 peak has no room to grow.
At 60 WPM a 2% error rate costs about 5-6 net WPM over a five-minute test. That is the arithmetic that keeps people at 55-60 for months: they gain speed, lose accuracy, and net out where they started.
Drill: 30-second rounds at 90% of your maximum, with an error budget of one. Stop the round when the budget is blown rather than pushing to the timer. The skill being trained is accuracy at speed, which is different from accuracy at rest.
Above 70 the ceiling is consistency. Ten rounds might range from 68 to 84; the average is 74 and the peak is irrelevant. Narrowing the spread is what raises the average.
Drill: type ten one-minute rounds and record all ten. Work on the lowest quintile - the rounds where you were tired, distracted or on a hard passage. Slow-hold rounds (pick a pace, hold it exactly) and hard-text rounds do more here than any speed drill.
Then the constraint is probably outside the keyboard: sleep, screen position, keyboard feel, or the fact that you only practise in one-minute bursts and never test endurance. Try one ten-minute round a week - many "plateaus" turn out to be a stamina problem that a short test cannot see.
The band-by-band plans are on the 40, 50, 60 and 70 WPM pages; the diagnostic line is consistency.
## Frequently asked questions
Usually because the practice repeats what you already do well. Plateaus have band-specific causes: habits at 40, reading ahead at 50, error tax at 60, variance at 70+.
Ten to fifteen minutes a day, with one variable changed per week. Longer sessions at the same routine mostly build fatigue.
Slightly, and briefly. A mechanical keyboard can be worth 3-8 WPM for some typists, but it will not break a plateau caused by looking down or reading word by word.
Not to break a plateau. The switch costs weeks of being slower, and most people return to the same speed on the new layout because the limiting habit moved with them.
Two to six weeks if you change the drill, months if you keep repeating the same practice. The signal that a drill is working is accuracy rising before speed does.

## Best Keyboard Layout for Programmers
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/keyboard-layout-for-programmers.html

Programmers do not type prose, they type symbols wrapped in words. That changes the layout question: the letters are already solved, and the brackets, braces, quotes and operators are what a layout helps or hurts.

A rough count of ordinary source code: letters are still the majority of characters, but the shifted symbol row ( ) { } [ ] ; : " ' = + - _ / \ | carries a disproportionate share of the awkward reaches, and those reaches are where errors cluster.
So the question is not "which layout is fastest for English" - it is "which layout puts the symbols you type most under the fingers that can reach them without leaving the home row".
Layout | Letter changes | Symbol changes | Cost of switching
QWERTY | None | None - symbols where every tool, shortcut and tutorial expects them | Zero
Dvorak | Substantial reordering for English comfort | Number row rearranged; brackets moved | Weeks of being slower; shortcuts assume QWERTY positions
Colemak | 17 keys moved; keeps Z X C V in place for shortcuts | Mostly unchanged | Weeks, but lower than Dvorak
Programmer Dvorak | Dvorak letters | Number row replaced with symbols; digits shifted | High - digits need Shift for every number
Programmer Dvorak looks attractive on paper because symbols get the unshifted number row. In practice the digits then require Shift, which is a bad trade for anyone who types numbers - and most code contains them.
For most programmers, stay on QWERTY. The reason is not that it is optimal; it is that every editor shortcut, every bracket-matching habit and every tutorial assumes it, and your bottleneck is thinking, not the 60-70 WPM you already type.
Consider a change only if all three hold: you are past 60 WPM on QWERTY, you type code for several hours a day, and your error report shows the symbol reaches as the main source of mistakes. Even then, expect a month of being slower before any gain.
Practise the symbols you actually type. Bracket-and-quote drills beat layout changes by a wide margin.
Let the editor do the brackets. Auto-pairs, snippets and formatters remove keystrokes; a layout reorders them.
Learn five shortcuts properly. Duplicate line, move line, go to definition, rename symbol, format document.
Code typing pools to practise on: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, Go, SQL. The general comparison is on Dvorak vs QWERTY.
## Frequently asked questions
Not measurably. It reorders letters for English comfort and moves brackets, which breaks shortcut muscle memory. The evidence for a coding gain is anecdotal rather than measured.
It puts symbols on the unshifted number row, which sounds ideal until you need a digit - then every number requires Shift. For most codebases that is a bad trade.
Only if you are already past 60 WPM, type code for hours a day, and want comfort rather than speed. It keeps Z X C V in place, so shortcuts survive better than with Dvorak.
Practising symbols, using snippets and formatters, and learning editor shortcuts. Layout changes come last, if at all.
Most sit at 60-90 WPM on prose and 40-55 on real code, because code is symbol-dense. No employer screens for it.

## Go Typing Practice
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/go-typing-practice.html

Go is deliberately plain, and that is what makes it a good typing drill: short declarations, braces on every line, := and error checks appear so often that they become the rhythm of the language.

Three things. Braces open on the same line as the statement, so almost every line ends with a reach to the right hand. Short declarations (:=) put the colon and equals in sequence, two keys that are not adjacent. And error checks repeat the same three-line idiom constantly, which makes it the single most valuable sequence to automate in your fingers.
The upside is regularity. Once you can type `if err != nil {` without thinking, a large fraction of Go becomes the same motion with different identifiers.
Thirty-six lines of ordinary Go: a package declaration, grouped imports, a struct with a receiver method, an HTTP server start, JSON decoding with the standard error check, context with timeout, a goroutine range loop, a select, slices.SortFunc with a comparison function, sync.WaitGroup, error wrapping with %w, a type switch, a test helper with t.Fatalf, and a mutex with defer.
They are deliberately short. Go lines are short, and the drill should teach the shape of the language rather than test your endurance with a long expression.
Start with the three highest-frequency sequences: `if err != nil {`, `for _, v := range`, and `defer x.Close()`. Type each twenty times slowly, then in a normal round. Automation of those three is worth more than raw speed.
Then add the punctuation that bites: the colon-equals, the ampersand for addresses, and the backtick for struct tags - which needs the key most typists have never used.
Same engine, different grammar: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, SQL, and Excel formulas. For layout questions, see keyboard layout for programmers.
## Frequently asked questions
No one measures it formally. Most developers type prose at 60-90 WPM and real Go at 45-55, because braces and short declarations add right-hand reaches.
Go is brace-dense and every block closes with a reach, while Python uses indentation. Go also repeats the error-check idiom, which is fast only once it is automatic.
Yes - 36 lines of ordinary Go covering goroutines, channels, context, error wrapping, generics-era slices helpers, struct tags and tests.
`if err != nil {`, `for _, v := range` and `defer ...Close()`. Those three sequences cover a large share of real Go lines.
Two weeks of five-minute daily rounds usually shows 4-7 WPM on Go content, mostly from the brace reach and the := sequence becoming automatic.

## Wrist Pain From Typing
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/wrist-pain-from-typing.html

Most typing-related wrist discomfort comes from position and pace, not from the keyboard itself. This page covers the setup changes that help, the break pattern that matters, and the symptoms that are not a typing problem at all.

On this page
What usually causes it
Setup, in order of impact
The break pattern that actually helps
Pace and tension
Symptoms that are not a setup problem
What to change first if you only change one thing
Four factors account for most typing-related wrist and forearm discomfort: wrist extension (hands bent upwards because the keyboard sits too high), ulnar deviation (hands angled outwards towards the arrow keys), shoulder elevation (a desk that is too tall, or a laptop on a table), and unbroken duration (two hours without standing up).
None of those are about willpower or typing speed. They are geometry and timing, which is why they respond to setup changes rather than to practice.
Keyboard height. Elbows at roughly 90 degrees, forearms level or slightly downward, wrists straight. If your wrists bend upwards, the keyboard is too high - lower the desk or raise the chair.
Wrist support that supports, not presses. A palm rest should support the heel of the hand between bursts, not compress the wrist while typing. Resting the wrist on a hard desk edge is the single most common cause.
Shoulders down. If your shoulders creep up, the desk is too tall for the chair, or the monitor is too low and you are leaning in.
Keyboard angle. Flat, or slightly negative with the back edge raised. The little feet at the back tilt the keyboard the wrong way for wrist position.
Thirty to forty-five minutes of typing, then two to three minutes away from the keyboard with the hands doing something else. Micro-breaks beat a single long break, because the load is cumulative and the recovery is what matters.
A useful rule: every time you stop to think, take your hands off the keyboard. Most typists rest their hands on the keys while thinking, which converts thinking time into sustained static load.
Speed work can produce tension without producing pain at the time. If you notice yourself gripping the keyboard, pressing hard on the keys or holding your breath during a timed round, that is a sign to slow down rather than push.
Typing tests reward bursts, but sustained work rewards relaxation. The typists who can type for six hours are not the fastest in a one-minute test; they are the ones who never tense up.
See a clinician rather than adjusting your desk if you have any of: numbness or tingling in the fingers that persists after you stop typing, pain that wakes you at night, weakness or dropping objects, swelling, or pain that continues at rest for more than a week.
Those patterns are not explained by keyboard geometry, and no ergonomic change or typing drill addresses them. This page is about workstation setup, not about diagnosis or treatment.
Move the keyboard down until your wrists are straight, and stop resting them on the desk edge while typing. That single change addresses the most common cause and costs nothing.
If the discomfort continues after two weeks of the setup change plus regular breaks, treat it as a reason to get advice rather than a reason to buy a different keyboard.
## Frequently asked questions
Sustained typing in an awkward position can produce discomfort in the wrists and forearms. It is usually related to keyboard height, wrist angle and unbroken duration rather than to typing itself.
For support between bursts, yes; while typing, no. A rest that compresses the wrist during typing can make things worse - the goal is a straight, floating wrist.
Every 30-45 minutes, for two to three minutes away from the keyboard. Micro-breaks are more effective than one long break at the end of the day.
It can reduce the force needed per keystroke for some people, but it does not fix wrist angle or duration. Setup comes first.
For persistent numbness or tingling, night pain, weakness, swelling, or pain at rest lasting more than a week. Those are not explained by keyboard position.
